The Finnair Plus program has just launched its newest promotion on purchased Avios, offering up to a 50% discount, which is an opportunity to acquire Avios for as little as 1.06 cents each. This is the best offer from the program of the year, and you can use this to acquire any “flavor” of Avios at an advantageous rate.

Strategically buying points for premium travel can be a great value, especially with a specific use in mind, so this is an offer I’d seriously consider.

Between 12:01AM EET on November 2 and 11:59PM EET on November 16, 2026, Finnair Plus is offering a limited time promotion on purchased Avios. If you purchase Finnair Plus Avios, you can receive the following deal:

Beyond the discount, you can also receive tier points toward status equivalent to 10% of the Avios purchased. This is of course useful if you’re going for elite status with Finnair, but otherwise, is of limited value.

Now, here’s where it gets interesting — Finnair lets you select the currency in which you want to buy Avios (you can find the option to switch currencies at the top of the screen), and the price differs:

So based on current exchange rates, you’re best off paying in JPY, followed by USD, followed by EUR. If you maxed out the promotion with a 50% bonus and paid in JPY, the best deal you could get would be to pay $2,110 for 200,000 Avios, which comes out to 1.06 cents per Avios (in USD), inclusive of all taxes and fees.

Note that this offer is only available to Finnair Plus members who joined the program before October 30, 2026, and have a minimum balance of 50 Avios in their account (though those Avios can be transferred from another “flavor” of the currency).

When Finnair Plus offers a promotion on purchased Avios, it’s common to see either a 50% bonus or a 40-50% discount. The 50% discount gives you the absolute best price, so this is definitely the time to buy Avios, if interested.

Since the purchase of Finnair Avios can potentially be billed in a foreign currency, there is one other great option. The Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card (learn more) offers 3x points on foreign purchases, so that’s a fantastic card for this kind of purchase.

Awards also have surcharges, though they’re at least mild. If you have a connecting itinerary, you’ll only be charged the surcharge correlated to the most expensive segment flown.

When your award booking includes a connecting flight, Avios are charged separately for each flight, except for flights within Finland and Northern Europe. For example, a Frankfurt to Helsinki to New York business class award would cost you 82,500 Avios (20,000 Avios plus 62,500 Avios). One awesome thing is that Finnair Plus has an award seat guarantee, meaning there’s pretty consistently award availability when booking far in advance.

Finnair Plus also allows redemptions on partner airlines, though the pricing isn’t particularly attractive, for the most part. The more important thing to keep in mind is that it’s possible to transfer Avios between the various “flavors” of the currency.

Therefore this promotion is also an opportunity to earn Avios that you can transfer 1:1 to programs like Aer Lingus AerClub, British Airways Club, Iberia Club, Qatar Airways Privilege Club, etc. That opens up more redemption opportunities.

This is the best price of the year from Finnair Plus on purchasing Avios (and the best price for purchasing any current of Avios this year, for that matter).

#6222. Update: American Airlines Pilots Union Retracts Warning Not To Eat Dessert

Update: the American Airlines pilots union has retracted: PHX ​Crew ​Meal Update Yesterday, APA ​Aeromedical was advised by the ​PHX ​Flight ​Office that ​a dessert ​included ​with ​some crew meals may ​have contained ​alcohol.   Out of ​an abundance of ​caution, APA issued an immediate ​advisory recommending that crewmembers ​not ​consume the dessert, ​specifically ​the ​tiramisu, ​until ​additional information ​could be obtained. ​Following coordination ​with ​AA ​Corporate ​Safety, PHX Inflight, ​the catering ​provider, and ​other ​involved ​parties, APA has confirmed ​that ​the desserts ​in question ​are safe ​to ​consume ​and ​do not pose a ​risk to ​aviation safety.   We appreciate the ​PHX ​Flight ​Office ​for promptly ​raising the concern and ​working with ​both American Airlines ​and APA to investigate the potential ​issue. The ​initial ​advisory ​was ​issued ​based on the information available ​at ​the ​time ​and ​with crew ​and ​flight ​safety ​as ​the priority. ​We appreciate your patience ​while additional fact finding ​was ​conducted.   For those pilots ​involved ​in a HIMS ​program ​we ​would like to ​use ​this ​as an opportunity to ​remind you that ​consuming ​certain ​food additives ​and extracts in large quantities may pose a ​risk to ​abstinence ​monitoring. Please consult ​the APA ​HIMS Subcommittee ​for additional ​information.   As ​always, ​please reach out to APA ​Aeromedical ​with any ​questions or ​concerns. American Airlines pilots in Phoenix are being warned not to eat the tiramisu on their crew meal trays because it contains alcohol. Their union says it can’t determine how much is in a serving or what that might mean if a pilot is tested. Aviation watchdog JonNYC shares the warning from the Allied Pilots Association’s Aeromedical–HIMS Committee. It covers crews based in or transiting Phoenix, where the contracted caterer has put the dessert on some crew meal trays. The contracted catering provider has included tiramisu containing alcohol on some crew meal trays. Because the dessert is not cooked after the alcohol is added, alcohol may remain in the finished product. We recommend that no crew member consume this dessert. The committee says it’s working with the Phoenix Flight Office to have the item removed and replaced. Until then, pilots should accept an incomplete meal. They’re telling pilots who ate it and are concerned about being fit to fly to contact their union reps. JonNYC’s October 30, 2026 post sharing the Phoenix crew meal alert How Does Alcohol End Up In A Pilot’s Crew Meal? One imagines someone selected a dessert option without checking the recipe, or there was a communication breakdown between the airline and caterer. I’ve written before that American’s pilots have traditionally received the same meals as first class passengers. A dessert can be perfectly fine for a passenger and not fine for the person in the cockpit. American Airlines Meal Alcohol isn’t necessary to make tiramisu. Alcohol doesn’t always cook off – it can leave a substantial amount behind though the quantities in the individual portioned dessert would be small. Last year, I covered the union telling pilots to obtain replacement meals in the terminal before departure when their food hadn’t been loaded. Here, the meal arrived, but the union is telling them not to eat all of it. Could A Small Tiramisu Show Up On An Alcohol Test? Alcohol in food can enter the bloodstream but that doesn’t mean it would be detectable or a pilot was impaired. A small dessert with a few grams of alcohol, where it gets eaten and the pilot winds up being randomly tested several hours later, probably doesn’t produce anything detectable based on FAA discussions of how the body eliminates alcohol. However, there are a couple of additional scenarios: Alcohol left in the mouth. This can temporarily inflate a breath reading. Federal testing procedures require at least a 15-minute wait before a confirmation test in order to address mouth alcohol. They’re not taking an immediate reading after a bite! Abstinence monitoring. Some pilots returning to flying after alcohol treatment undergo separate testing for alcohol metabolites. Those tests can detect an exposure after the alcohol itself has cleared. It’s abstinence testing that would be an actual concern. A Delta Pilot Fought The FAA Over Alcohol In His Lunch In Erwin v. Federal Aviation Administration, a Delta pilot in alcohol monitoring attributed a positive urine test to pulled pork cooked in beer. The restaurant confirmed using beer, which hadn’t been disclosed on the menu. The agency withdrew his medical authorization. Delta required another treatment program and a last chance agreement if he wanted to keep his job. The appeals court sent the case back because the agency hadn’t adequately addressed his evidence. I’ve written about the strict requirements for pilots returning after alcohol treatment. American has even apologized for photos of bartenders dressed as pilots mixing cocktails in its inflight magazine. They pulled the magazine from planes, back when they had magazines on planes. “The Tiramisu? What is it?” “It’s a little dessert in the front of the plane where the pilot’s career used to be, but that’s not important right now.” Topics on this pageAllied Pilots AssociationAmerican AirlinesFAAFederal Aviation AdministrationTiramisuDelta Air LinesPhoenix+2 more More From View from the Wing

Yesterday, APA ​Aeromedical was advised by the ​PHX ​Flight ​Office that ​a dessert ​included ​with ​some crew meals may ​have contained ​alcohol.

Out of ​an abundance of ​caution, APA issued an immediate ​advisory recommending that crewmembers ​not ​consume the dessert, ​specifically ​the ​tiramisu, ​until ​additional information ​could be obtained. ​Following coordination ​with ​AA ​Corporate ​Safety, PHX Inflight, ​the catering ​provider, and ​other ​involved ​parties, APA has confirmed ​that ​the desserts ​in question ​are safe ​to ​consume ​and ​do not pose a ​risk to ​aviation safety.

We appreciate the ​PHX ​Flight ​Office ​for promptly ​raising the concern and ​working with ​both American Airlines ​and APA to investigate the potential ​issue. The ​initial ​advisory ​was ​issued ​based on the information available ​at ​the ​time ​and ​with crew ​and ​flight ​safety ​as ​the priority. ​We appreciate your patience ​while additional fact finding ​was ​conducted.

For those pilots ​involved ​in a HIMS ​program ​we ​would like to ​use ​this ​as an opportunity to ​remind you that ​consuming ​certain ​food additives ​and extracts in large quantities may pose a ​risk to ​abstinence ​monitoring. American Airlines pilots in Phoenix are being warned not to eat the tiramisu on their crew meal trays because it contains alcohol. Their union says it can’t determine how much is in a serving or what that might mean if a pilot is tested.

Aviation watchdog JonNYC shares the warning from the Allied Pilots Association’s Aeromedical–HIMS Committee. It covers crews based in or transiting Phoenix, where the contracted caterer has put the dessert on some crew meal trays.

The contracted catering provider has included tiramisu containing alcohol on some crew meal trays. Because the dessert is not cooked after the alcohol is added, alcohol may remain in the finished product.

We recommend that no crew member consume this dessert.

The committee says it’s working with the Phoenix Flight Office to have the item removed and replaced. Until then, pilots should accept an incomplete meal. They’re telling pilots who ate it and are concerned about being fit to fly to contact their union reps.

JonNYC’s October 30, 2026 post sharing the Phoenix crew meal alert

One imagines someone selected a dessert option without checking the recipe, or there was a communication breakdown between the airline and caterer.

I’ve written before that American’s pilots have traditionally received the same meals as first class passengers. A dessert can be perfectly fine for a passenger and not fine for the person in the cockpit.

Alcohol isn’t necessary to make tiramisu. Alcohol doesn’t always cook off – it can leave a substantial amount behind though the quantities in the individual portioned dessert would be small.

Last year, I covered the union telling pilots to obtain replacement meals in the terminal before departure when their food hadn’t been loaded. Here, the meal arrived, but the union is telling them not to eat all of it.

Alcohol in food can enter the bloodstream but that doesn’t mean it would be detectable or a pilot was impaired. A small dessert with a few grams of alcohol, where it gets eaten and the pilot winds up being randomly tested several hours later, probably doesn’t produce anything detectable based on FAA discussions of how the body eliminates alcohol. However, there are a couple of additional scenarios:

It’s abstinence testing that would be an actual concern.

In Erwin v. Federal Aviation Administration, a Delta pilot in alcohol monitoring attributed a positive urine test to pulled pork cooked in beer. The restaurant confirmed using beer, which hadn’t been disclosed on the menu.

The agency withdrew his medical authorization. Delta required another treatment program and a last chance agreement if he wanted to keep his job. The appeals court sent the case back because the agency hadn’t adequately addressed his evidence.

I’ve written about the strict requirements for pilots returning after alcohol treatment. American has even apologized for photos of bartenders dressed as pilots mixing cocktails in its inflight magazine. They pulled the magazine from planes, back when they had magazines on planes.

“It’s a little dessert in the front of the plane where the pilot’s career used to be, but that’s not important right now.”

#6221. Boeing 747-400 Vs. 747-8: How The Last 2 Jumbo Generations Compare

Jeang Herng & ajuangon | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

For more than half a century, the Boeing 747 has served as the flagship of the global aviation industry, shaping long-haul travel as we know it today. Since entering commercial service with Pan Am in 1970, the four-engined, partially double-decked jet has become one of the most recognizable aircraft in aviation history. Over the years, Boeing continued to develop the type, introducing multiple different variants, each with their own unique features and characteristics.

The last two generations of the jet were the 747-400 and 747-8, which entered passenger service in 1989 and 2012, respectively. Although both share the 747's distinctive hump and overall design, the 747-8 was substantially different from its predecessor, incorporating new engines, wings, and other technical improvements. Interestingly, however, the older 747-400 proved considerably more commercially successful than its successor.

After introducing the original 747-100 in 1970, Boeing continued to develop the aircraft to meet airlines' changing requirements. This resulted in several variants, including the 747-200, the shortened 747SP, and the 747-300, which introduced the stretched upper deck that would become standard on the 747-400 passenger version.

However, the introduction of the 747-400 marked one of the most important developments in the aircraft's history. The aircraft made its first flight on April 29, 1988, before entering commercial service with Northwest Airlines in February 1989. Compared to earlier variants, the 747-400 featured a revised wing design with six-foot-tall winglets, more efficient engines, and a redesigned two-pilot glass cockpit, eliminating the need for a flight engineer. The aircraft was also available with engines from three different manufacturers: General Electric, Pratt & Whitney, and Rolls-Royce.

Boeing eventually delivered 694 aircraft from the 747-400 family, including passenger, freighter, and combi variants, making it the best-selling 747 generation. Boeing delivered the final passenger aircraft to China Airlines in April 2005, while production of the freighter variants continued until 2009. By then, Boeing had already launched the aircraft's successor, the 747-8.

Although both aircraft look very similar, the most noticeable difference between the 747-400 and 747-8 is their size. The 747-400 measures 231 feet, 10 inches (70.66 meters) in length, while the 747-8 is considerably longer at 250 feet, 2 inches (76.3 meters). Boeing achieved this by stretching the fuselage ahead of and behind the wings, creating additional space for passengers and cargo. The passenger version, officially known as the 747-8 Intercontinental, also features a longer upper deck than its predecessor.

The 747-8 also has a larger wingspan: 224 feet, 5 inches (68.4 meters), compared to 211 feet, 5 inches (64.4 meters) on the 747-400. However, the most recognizable difference is the aircraft's wingtips. While the 747-400 features traditional upright winglets, the 747-8 uses raked wingtips similar to the 787 Dreamliner that extend backward from the wing, improving aerodynamic efficiency.

Specifications of the Boeing 747-400 Vs. 747-8

GE CF6, Pratt & Whitney PW4000, Rolls-Royce RB211

According to Boeing's original announcement, the 747-8 Intercontinental was designed to accommodate 467 passengers in a typical three-class configuration, compared to 416 passengers on the 747-400. However, these figures depend heavily on the configuration selected by each airline. For example, Lufthansa currently operates its 747-8s with 364 seats, including eight First Class and 80 Business Class seats. Its older 747-400s have a total capacity of 371 passengers.

Discover the surprising differences between the 747-400 and 747-8 models.

Besides the increased size, the 747-8 incorporated substantial technical improvements over the 747-400. One of the most important changes was the introduction of four General Electric GEnx-2B engines, developed using technology from the 787 Dreamliner program. Unlike the 747-400, which was available with engines from three manufacturers, Boeing offered the newer generation exclusively with General Electric engines.

Furthermore, Boeing redesigned the aircraft's wings, incorporating new airfoils, improved high-lift devices, and an increased wingspan. The 747-8 also introduced fly-by-wire technology for certain flight controls, including the spoilers and outboard ailerons. According to Boeing, these improvements allowed the 747-8 Intercontinental to achieve approximately 16% lower fuel consumption per seat than the 747-400, while generating a 30% smaller noise footprint. The manufacturer also claimed that the newer aircraft offered almost identical operating costs per flight, resulting in 13% lower costs per seat-mile.

Actual fuel consumption per passenger depends, of course, on the cabin configuration, passenger load factor, flight distance, and operating conditions. Moreover, while the 747-8 was considerably more efficient than its predecessor, it still required four engines, making it more expensive to maintain than newer twinjets with similar passenger capacities.

Furthermore, the 747-8's larger capacity also disadvantaged routes with insufficient passenger demand. While the newer aircraft offered lower costs per available seat-mile, airlines still needed to fill enough seats at profitable fares to benefit from these improvements. Smaller twinjets offered greater flexibility, allowing carriers to adjust capacity to individual markets without operating a four-engined airplane.

The Queen of the Skies lives on: Lufthansa's unique reasons for keeping both the 747-400 and 747-8 in its fleet.

While the 747-8 incorporated several technologies developed for the 787 Dreamliner, Boeing deliberately retained much of the 747-400's cockpit design. This allowed airlines already operating the older aircraft to introduce the 747-8 without requiring lengthy pilot retraining. The 747-400 had already introduced a glass cockpit, replacing many analog instruments on earlier variants with electronic flight displays.

The newer 747-8 retained the same basic flight deck layout, while incorporating updated liquid-crystal displays and several improvements to its avionics. Additional features included a new flight management computer, electronic checklists, improved navigation systems, and an airport moving map. Both jets also share the same pilot type rating, allowing pilots qualified on the 747-400 to transition to the 747-8 through an approved difference training program.

See every flight within 20 miles of you right now and where they're all going.

From an airline perspective, this was an important advantage, particularly for carriers operating both versions simultaneously. Lufthansa, for example, has operated the two types alongside each other for more than a decade. The passenger cabin, however, received a more substantial redesign, incorporating features from the 787 Dreamliner, including larger overhead luggage bins, revised cabin architecture, and improved lighting.

Exploring the design of the Boeing 747-400F.

Despite all the improvements introduced with the 747-8, the aircraft never came close to its predecessor's commercial success. While Boeing delivered 694 aircraft from the 747-400 family, only 155 examples of the 747-8 were produced, including just 48 passenger aircraft. This was partly because the newer generation entered a market where demand for quad-jet passenger jets was already declining.

When the 747-400 entered service in 1989, airlines had relatively few alternatives capable of transporting large numbers of passengers over intercontinental distances. However, by the time the 747-8 entered service in 2012, the 777-300ER had already established itself as a popular alternative. Furthermore, the introduction of the Boeing 787 and Airbus A350 allowed airlines to operate long-haul services with smaller aircraft and lower operating costs. Lufthansa became the launch customer for the passenger 747-8, introducing the plane in June 2012, while Korean Air and Air China also ordered the type.

The 5 Largest Boeing 747 Operators In 2026

Although Boeing ended production of the 747 in late 2022, both generations will continue to operate commercially in 2026. Lufthansa currently operates 18 747-8s and eight 747-400s, making it the largest remaining passenger operator of the aircraft. Korean Air and Air China also continue to operate the 747-8, while Rossiya Airlines remains an operator of the older 747-400. However, with airlines increasingly replacing their remaining 747s with newer twinjets, the number of passenger aircraft in service continues to decline.

Interestingly, the freighter version of the 747-8 proved considerably more successful than its passenger counterpart, accounting for 107 of the 155 aircraft produced. Cargo carriers such as UPS Airlines, Cargolux, and Atlas Air continue to operate the newer generation alongside older 747-400 freighters. In addition to its increased payload capacity, the 747-8F retains the 747's distinctive nose-loading capability, allowing airlines to transport oversized cargo that cannot be loaded through conventional side doors. The last 747 ever produced was a 747-8F delivered to Atlas Air on January 31, 2023, ending more than five decades of production.

#6220. Save On Air France-KLM Flights With Amex Offers (Targeted)

The Amex Offers program has just rolled out a great new targeted offer for the purchase of Air France-KLM flights, which could be worth considering for anyone planning travel. We’ve seen this offer in the past, and I’m happy to see it return, as I always get significant value from it. However, this offer isn’t quite as lucrative as past ones.

With a new targeted Amex Offers deal, you can earn a $250 statement credit when you spend $2,500 or more with Air France-KLM by December 15, 2026. (Enrollment required)

It’s possible that there’s also a version of the offer for 25,000 bonus points rather than a $250 statement credit, and if so, I’d consider that to be more valuable. That’s because based on my latest miles & points valuations, Amex points are worth 1.7 cents each, so I’d value the 25,000 points at $425.

For what it’s worth, in the past when I’ve purchased sustainable aviation fuel with Air France in order to earn XP (the metric by which you qualify for status), that triggered an Amex Offers deal. So at least anecdotally, that seems to work. Furthermore, taxes and carrier imposed surcharges on award tickets also seem to qualify.

I’m always happy to see this offer available, though let me note that this isn’t as lucrative as in the past. In past situations we’ve seen a $200 statement credit or 20,000 bonus points after spending $1,000+, so as a percentage return, this definitely isn’t as good.

This Amex Offers deal is targeted, though it’s possible you’ll see it on multiple of your cards. If so, I’d highly recommend registering your American Express Platinum Card® for this offer. That’s because the Amex Platinum offers 5x points on airfare purchased directly with airlines on up to $500,000 per calendar year and then 1x.

Based on my valuation of 1.7 cents per Membership Rewards point, the 5x points offers an incremental 8.5% return on spending. On top of that, the Amex Platinum offers valuable travel protection, should you experience irregular operations.

In other words, if you took advantage of this offer with the Amex Platinum for a $2,500 ticket, you’d receive a $250 statement credit plus 12,500 points. By my valuation, that’s a return of $462.50 on $2,500 of spending, which comes out to an 18.5% return.

There’s a new targeted Amex Offers deal for a $250 statement credit when you spend $2,500+ on an Air France-KLM ticket. If you’re planning travel on Air France or KLM, this has the potential to be a solid deal. Ideally you’ll see this offer on the Amex Platinum, so that you can really maximize your points.

Were you targeted for this Amex Offers deal, and if so, do you plan on taking advantage of it?

#6219. American Airlines Charges Solo Travelers More On Up To 1/3rd Of Flights—Booking For Two Can Be Cheaper

American Airlines is charging a solo traveler $496 for a one-way flight from Miami to Charlotte. But put two people on the reservation and the same main cabin ticket drops to $155 per person. Three people can fly for less than the price of one. And when two people travel together, a $100 basic economy fare becomes available that the solo passenger can’t even buy. This isn’t an isolated example. Kyle Potter at Thrifty Traveler compared fares for one passenger and two on 5,000 domestic nonstop one-way flights, 1,000 on each of the five largest U.S. airlines. They found a higher fare for a solo passenger on 33.5% of American Airlines flights in their sample and 10.6% of United Airlines flights. They didn’t find this on any of the 1,000 flights they checked on each of Delta, Alaska Airlines and Southwest Airlines. The average difference on affected flights was more than $90 on American and over $64 on United. They also found the restriction on some roundtrip and short-haul international itineraries as well. Why Airlines Want To Know How Many People Are Traveling I’ve written about this pricing before. It’s a way for airlines to charge different customers different prices for the same seat (price discrimination). A business traveler is more likely to book alone, often with an employer paying for the ticket. A couple or family traveling together is more likely to be paying out of pocket and be price sensitive. The airline can make a cheaper fare available when at least two people travel together, hoping to fill seats with leisure travelers while collecting more from people willing to pay the higher price. It’s using the number of passengers on the reservation as a proxy for the kind of trip you’re taking. That’s a crude proxy. I’ve flown alone to meet my family when we’re coming from different places. Friends going on vacation together may buy their tickets separately. A parent may fly out later to join the rest of the family, or a passenger may be traveling alone for a funeral. Airlines used to separate business and leisure travelers with advance purchase requirements, roundtrip fares and Saturday night stays. Low cost carriers offered cheap fares without those conditions, making it harder for the big airlines to keep charging a premium to business travelers. Some of those restrictions have returned in certain markets, but basic economy has become a principal way to separate travelers: the most price-sensitive customers accept restrictions that many business travelers won’t. Requiring a companion is another way to do it. The lower fare has an accompaniment restriction in the fare rules. American calls its version Multi-Pax Fares, for eligible passengers who book and travel together. Is It A Solo Penalty Or A Family Discount? Passengers are angry because they see someone else paying far less for the same seat on the same flight, and the only way to get that price is to bring another person along. That feels especially unfair when you’re traveling alone because you have to, not because your company is buying the ticket. The fare rule isn’t something most people would know to look for, either. The defense is that this can also be described as a lower price for two passengers traveling together. Scott McCartney made the comparison to a retail discount and suggested calling it a family or couples discount when he and former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker discussed the practice. Parker’s argument was that different prices can help fill a plane while producing enough revenue to operate the flight. The airlines aren’t raising fares per se, they’re just deciding more carefully whom they want to offer the lowest fares to. The idea is to charge each passenger as close as possible to what they’re willing to pay. No more great deals on airfare, but the idea is that if you buy the ticket you valued the travel more than the cost. The airline captures more of the surplus though. When Delta and United initially pulled some of these fares after the practice drew attention last year, the cheap fares disappeared. That didn’t make cheaper for everyone right away at least. Tim Carney has argued for family pricing at places like museums and parks, where charging for every child can make an outing prohibitively expensive. But American’s fare isn’t limited to families or children. Two unrelated adults can qualify, while a parent flying separately to meet their spouse and kids won’t. I don’t think airlines should be barred from offering different prices. But passengers need to know how the price is determined, especially when airline competition is limited. Otherwise, they’ll follow their usual techniques from past (wrong) advice when making bookings. In the Thrifty Traveler sample, the practice was more common on routes where American and United faced no nonstop competitor, and especially common in American’s Charlotte and Philadelphia markets. Search For The Number Of People Actually Traveling When I’m comparing flights for a family trip, people often search for one passenger first, not bothering to adjust the number of passengers in the search box until settling on their flights I want. Now a fare search for one person may miss a lower price available when you’re booking for two or more. Search with the actual number of travelers, and compare the total price. You can also search for one passenger to see how those prices differ. There’s a reason the old advice was sometimes to search for one person first. Suppose there’s only one seat left at $100 and the next fare is $200. A search for two passengers may price both at $200, or $400 total. If you book separately, one passenger might get the $100 seat and the other the $200 seat, for $300 total. But when the $100 fare requires two people on the same reservation, a solo search won’t show it at all. Check both ways, and compare the total for everyone before booking. And what about buying two tickets and then canceling one? I previously suggested that as a possible workaround. American’s published instructions say that when a cancellation leaves only one passenger on a multi-passenger fare, the remaining ticket has to be repriced to an eligible fare. I’d still try splitting the record. If the FTC is against AI pricing, I guess this is the next best price-discriminatory option.

A new definition of “business class” since I’m guessing AA feels most of those single flyers are on company expense reports vs personal.

I wonder what happens if someone buys two seats to have a free seat next to them.

The issue is transparency. If pricing isn’t transparent, people will suspect that they are being cheated.

Are they not offering a discount for multi ticket purchase. The retail industry does. Buy one get 2nd 50% off Buy one soda get second for $1 more A case of beer is cheaper the buying a six pack per unit 7 nights in a hotel is cheaper the 7 nights at 7 different hotels Buying anything at bjs or costco

This reminds me of ads for cell phone service. They always tout low monthly charges, but note in smaller print that pricing is based upon multiple lines.

If faced with a fare increase for one person such as you note, is it possible to buy 2 tickets and spread out in Economy at the discounted price or did their study only look for 2 travelers?

If an itinerary shows 2 travelers and 1 cancels within 24 hours does the entire itinerary gets cancelled??

I don’t suppose United allows the second passenger on one of these fares to be “EXTRA SEAT”?

Sidetracking a little bit, but remaining on the topic of pricing, I do not trust the Bonvoy App. Why, because of the following experience:

(1) Last week, my girlfriend asked me about where to stay near LAX before a flight. She wanted a price $150/all-in and below. So I went in, found a hotel using the AAA discount, that was $150/all-in. It was a cancellable rate. (2) Two days later, she called me and said, I tried to cancel and I have done a non-cancelable rate. (3) I thought odd, so I went in, and the price was now $163/night but cancellable. Even after I change it to special rates, the price didn’t change. Wow, I thought, the price sure went up. (4) Then I thought, well maybe I made a mistake in my search, so I redid the search. Now the price was $147/night, but cancellable. (5) I went off, had a cup of coffee. I thought, maybe I will take a picture, in case my girlfriends asks me again. Now the price was $134/all-in night cancellable. I took a screenshot of it. (6) Then I remember when I made was about to make a cancelable reservation at the airport, before I realized that the cancellation date on the Bonvoy app, was that night, not the night before the reservation. (7) Actually, when I have started a search, then gone back to the Bonvoy App, I have accidentally booked reservations, with an earlier cancellation date then I thought. I found out when they charged my credit card a week before the stay. Now I triple check the cancellation dates before booking.

There might be a rationale answer for this. However, my warning is to be very careful about pricing and change dates on the Bonvoy App. Circling back to airline pricing, if Bonvoy is doing it, then one wonders if the airlines are more honest than Bonvoy. I thought I would pass that along.

(Of course, I would be happy if Albert Wonders, who has suggested that I am a liar and a groper, ignores that above. He can trust the Bonvoy app and airline pricing 100%). If anyone else wants to criticize my experience above, just remember the universal rule that “No Good Deed Goes Unpunished.”

I wonder if I were to book a flight for me and my traveling companion and then cancel my companions portion, what would happen to the price?

@Gary: “Search with the actual number of travelers, and compare the total price. You can also search for one passenger to see how those prices differ.”

I learned early on that if there’s only one seat left in, say, Fare Bucket “Q”, when booking for two passengers, the airline will only show you fares in the higher priced “N” bracket.

Generally I’ve always priced out tickets both ways, just to play it safe (or should I say, “play it cheap?”). Sometimes it is cheaper to book my wife and I on the same reservation; sometimes it’s less expensive if we book separate reservations and then “link” them together on the airline’s website.

Very okay with OPM flyers being charged more. And as a reward we get a shiny elite card. Noone loses.

So can you buy the 2 seats and have extra space?

Some movie theaters don’t allow single men to see movies.

Interesting since every time I book for my partner and myself I find the fare goes up when I book for two than booking for one. We only book business/first fares so that might be why, but we’ve now gone to booking each ticket in our owh FF account and then calling to have the itineraries merged.

Round trip requirements are also coming back. With Spirit out of the picture and LCCs struggling, more and more routes price higher as one ways.

So now to really test fares, you have to do all of the following:

*Check to see if pricing fares for more than 1 person will be higher if booking together (fare class availability) or higher if booking solo (multiple passenger fares) *Compare one-ways across multiple carriers to round trips on a single carrier (you used to be able to just check each one way and get the best price, now you have to price out the round trip separately as well) *Compare fare types across each airline offering comparable fares to see what they do and don’t include *Ponder upgrades: you were in the market for economy, but upgrading looks so cheap… but wait… that’s the basic version of premium… *Once you make a decision, you’re forced to price out whether their “extras” packages (some combination of seats and bags) is more beneficial than buying what you need a la carte across each passenger

In this era of “segmentation” consumers are just suckers. How many variations of fares, fees, and bundles can they create to cause confusion and extract every possible penny?

I always travel solo. Thats if I even feel like traveling. This was an eye opener!

I wonder if people who purchase multiple tickets are more likely to also pay to reserve their seats so they can sit together then the Solo traveler. So the airline therefore anticipates making up that lost revenue on them.

#6218. United’s CEO Loves New American Airlines Boarding Gates—Here’s Why They Make Flying Worse

He saw it as something worth copying. When American announced the equipment, I thought it would make flying worse.

Kirby says he’s flown American, Delta and Southwest at least three times each over the past year, looking for things they do better than United. He lives in Dallas, and is regularly spotted on American but Southwest is based at Dallas Love Field as well.

American supplied this rendering when it announced the gates in April:

The glass barriers open after the system validates a boarding pass. American says the equipment can control the pace at which passengers enter the jet bridge, reduce manual work (cost savings on gate agents), and let employees spend more time helping customers (or just pocket the labor savings). The airline has since opened its new DFW Terminal C pier with the technology at all nine gates.

Airports are increasingly moving to e-gates, where facial recognition is used to confirm identity. So far this has mostly been used for international departures. The government wants more than a person looking at you and confirming it against the photo in your passport.

At many international departure gates, a camera is mounted at the gate or held by a government customs officer or airline staff member, to take a live photo of each passenger during boarding.

That image is sent to the Customs and Border Protection cloud-based Traveler Verification Service, which compares each person’s mugshot to a gallery built from your passport or visa photo and compares it to the flight manifest. The government has already checked the flight manifest and decided who can travel and who can’t. Now they want to match people against the manifest. If there’s a match, you’re allowed to depart the country. If there’s no match, you get a manual document check.

The biggest boarding bottlenecks aren’t actually the act of scanning a barcode. In fact, without human assistance each passenger may take longer to scan and wait for the gate to open.

Too many carry-ons, limited overhead bin space, gate-checking bags, families bunching up during preboarding and standby processing at the gate seem to be bigger issues. These gates do not solve any of that – just queue management and access control. The worst part of the experience is actually what Kirby says is his standard for judging this:

“I think of air travel for customers through the lens of traveling with small children,” Kirby said. “I have seven kids. I know what it’s like. I’ve tried to make it easy for people to travel with young children because if we do that, it’s going to be great for everybody.”

It is after all the day after Halloween. So I am wondering, if Chucky has a passport. If I put on a Chucky mask that I purchase at Halloween store, would I be able to get past one of those automated gates.

I am saying it in a humorous manner, but one wonders how easy those automated gates are to fool. Or for that matter, the Global Entry automated portals.

If the boarding gates allow the airline tom “just pocket the labor savings”, then by all means they should be installed.

Maximizing the return on shareholder investment is the only Scott Kirby, or any CEO, or any employee gets paid.

All too often “jouranlists” and “activists” seem to think private, publicly traded corporations are some kind of public service or charity.

Also, when I was flying to St. Lucia on American Airlines, I went through an automated gate. I remember being concerned that I could not see my name pop up. If American Airlines did not think I flew, then it would cancel my return ticket. Also, I would not get my points. It worked fine, but still the concern of mistakes continue.

Kirby is moving into obsessed territory with everything AA.

Can you imagine if Kirby gets fired at United. He will probably have a nervous breakdown.

These have been in use in Asia and Europe for a long time. They work great. I’ve never had an issue with them. And if you’re in an airport, your face is likely being recorded dozens if not hundreds of times anyway these days.

Anyone flown United Polaris recently? It is a mediocre product with outdated and worn out equipment and entertainment. The food is not as bad as it was but is still not good. Planes are old for the most part.

Kirby is giving new definition to the term “paying lip service”.

It’s funny the lead theory is it’s worse for passenger used it yesterday it was awesome with no issue – got to love if AA is doing something it must be bad – good news Kirby obsession is still live

So you get the experience of writing on the subway.

Disagree with Gary on this one. I am not a fan of facial recognition but having experienced this overseas quite a bit I think (with certain exceptions that Gary flagged) it makes for a more orderly boarding process. On the other hand, I’m old enough to remember when humans actually interacted with each other and I much prefer that way of doing things. Unfortunately human interaction is going the way of the dodo.

Two thoughts: (1) I’ve regarded these as a waste of /somebody’s/ money, especially since they tend to slow up the process.

(2) Why is every third post you reporting some other thing that Scott Kirby said? Is he paying you by the post or word or something? Seriously – just do a “Scott Kirby talked out of his rear roundup” each week or something.

#6217. Save On Etihad Flights With Amex Offers (Targeted)

The Amex Offers program has just rolled out a great new targeted offer for the purchase of Etihad Airways flights, which could be worth considering for anyone planning travel (that’s not to say you should or shouldn’t plan travel on Etihad, for a variety of reasons — I’m just sharing a deal!).

To my knowledge, this is the first time that we’ve seen an Amex Offers deal for Etihad purchases, so it’s nice to see another airline join the Amex Offers “circuit.”

With a new targeted Amex Offers deal, you can earn a $200 statement credit when you spend $1,000+ or more with Etihad Airways by December 31, 2026. (Enrollment required)

It’s possible that there’s also a version of the offer for 20,000 bonus points rather than a $200 statement credit, and if so, I’d consider that to be more valuable. That’s because based on my latest miles & points valuations, Amex points are worth 1.7 cents each, so I’d value the 20,000 points at $340.

Let me emphasize that while the terms suggest that you need to book an Etihad flight through the US website that originates in the US, I’ve had similar Amex Offers triggered in the past for flights that didn’t originate in the US, so it’s anyone’s guess how that’s actually enforced here.

This Amex Offers deal is targeted, though it’s possible you’ll see it on multiple of your cards. If so, I’d highly recommend registering your American Express Platinum Card® for this offer. That’s because the Amex Platinum offers 5x points on airfare purchased directly with airlines.

Based on my valuation of 1.7 cents per Membership Rewards point, the 5x points offers an incremental 8.5% return on spending. On top of that, the Amex Platinum offers valuable travel protection, should you experience irregular operations.

In other words, if you took advantage of this offer with the Amex Platinum for a $1,000 ticket, you’d receive a $200 statement credit plus 5,000 points. By my valuation, that’s a return of $285 on $1,000 of spending, which comes out to a 28.5% return.

There’s a new targeted Amex Offers deal for a $200 statement credit when you spend $1,000+ on an Etihad ticket. If you’re planning travel on Etihad, this has the potential to be a solid deal. Ideally you’ll see this offer on the Amex Platinum, so that you can really maximize your points.

Were you targeted for this Amex Offers deal, and if so, do you plan on taking advantage of it?

If you're used to cruising in the Caribbean, shore excursion prices on your Alaska cruise might surprise you.

Want to take a helicopter ride to the top of a glacier to enjoy a dogsled ride? It'll cost upward of $700 per person. Excited about an authentic Alaska fishing experience? That's a more than $400 tour. A nearly three-hour scenic train ride on the White Pass and Yukon Route Railroad starts at more than $150 per traveler.

Not only are tours so pricey because Alaska is a remote destination (where it costs more to fly in goods and materials), but also because Alaska is part of the U.S., where wages and tour insurance costs can be higher than in the islands. Plus, many Alaska excursions involve seaplanes, helicopters, specialized boats and other equipment that only add to the price of your onshore experience.

For many, an Alaska cruise is a once-in-a-lifetime trip, and many tours are worth the splurge. But you don't have to spend money hand over fist in every port. Whether you're trying to balance your budget with a few cheaper days or you simply don't have the resources to spend big every day of your vacation, you'll want to seek out cheap or free things to do in Alaska's cruise ports.

Luckily, you have plenty of options. I know because I've spent many a day exploring independently in Alaska's ports. Plus, I consulted with Alaska's tourism representatives to bring you a comprehensive list of free (and cheap) things to do in Alaska on a cruise.

Skagway is known for its gold rush history, but you don't need a pricey tour to immerse yourself in the town's storied past. Klondike Gold Rush National Historical Park has four free museums open to visitors, including the Visitor Center Museum (with interactive exhibits), the Moore House Museum (former home of the first family to live in Skagway, with two restored Victorian-era rooms), the Jeff Smiths Parlour Museum (a former bar with a shady past) and the Mascot Saloon Museum (a restored gold rush saloon).

If you're fully embracing the old-timey vibe, you'll want to belly up to the bar at the Red Onion Saloon. Once, it was Skagway's signature bordello, but now it's the place to sling back an Alaska-brewed beer or snack on apps and pizzas named after former good-time girls. For a reasonable $20 a person, you can sign up for a Quickie Tour of the venue's supposedly haunted brothel museum. Ghost sightings don't cost extra!

One of my favorite things to do in Skagway is stretch my legs on a hike, and there are several trailheads within easy walking distance of your cruise ship. Options include the Upper and Lower Dewey Lake, Reid Falls and Gold Rush Cemetery, and Icy Lake and Upper Reid Falls trails. The National Park Service kindly lists its hikes by distance from Skagway's Historic District, as well as by level of difficulty. No guide is needed, and you don't have to pay to access the trails.

Related: Alaska cruise guide: Best itineraries, planning tips and things to do

Window shopping is a popular activity along the main streets by Juneau's cruise docks, but you might be tempted to blow your budget on souvenirs. (Look for sales, especially during end-of-season sailings, if you want to buy gifts for less.)

Typically, you can pay $60 for an all-day pass up and down Juneau's Goldbelt tram*, or if you're in good shape, you can hike from your ship to the top of the tram on the Mount Roberts Trail for free. I did this hike on my recent Alaska cruise, and while it's not technical, it is steep and can be muddy after a rainstorm. Make lots of noise just in case bears are on the trail.

At the top, you can visit the Chilkat Theater to watch a free movie about the region's Tlingit people. If you're too tired to hike back down, you can get a ride back on the tram for $20.

However, the Goldbelt tram has been closed since late April 2026 for maintenance. Visitors can still go to the base of the tram to watch Tlingit artists carve totem poles, weave ceremonial robes and perform cultural dances for no charge.

Other hikes accessible from your ship include the Gold Creek Flume Trail and the Perseverance Trail.

If a stroll through downtown is more your speed, self-guided tours of Juneau come free of charge. The Juneau Voices project features audio installations at 11 spots around town where you can learn about the city through the stories of Native Alaskans. Or grab a map from a tourist welcome center and follow this walking tour to see the city’s highlights.

You can also find a PDF guide to Juneau’s totem poles online.

If you prefer to get your history and culture indoors (not a bad plan in Alaska, given the temperamental climate), Juneau offers a few museums with modest admission fees that are worth checking out.

The Juneau-Douglas City Museum offers a mix of permanent and temporary exhibits on the area's history and art. Admission is $7, but you might need a cab if you're not up for a 20-minute walk. The museum also runs a free walking tour of the Alaska State Capitol Building.

Also, a 20-minute walk from the port is the Alaska State Museum, where you can learn about the cultures of the Tlingit, Haida and Tsimshian peoples. Admission is $14. For more information on Native Alaskans and their cultures, visit the Sealaska Heritage Institute's Walter Soboleff Building ($10 admission) and its gift shop, which features local art. Don't miss the signature totem pole and handcrafted clan house.

If you’re keen for a scenic uphill walk, head up Basin Road to the Last Chance Mining Museum ($5) to learn about the gold rush in a historic mining building.

*At the time of writing, Goldbelt tram is closed but has plans to reopen soon. Check availability and prices before you plan.

Related: Alaska cruise mistakes you never want to make

Ketchikan is best known for its Creek Street Historic District, built on a wooden boardwalk above the salmon-filled Ketchikan Creek. Stroll for free by its historic buildings, shops and restaurants, or pay $10 to stop into Dolly’s House for a glimpse into the city’s former red-light district.

Not far from Creek Street, the Tongass Historical Museum and Totem Heritage Center immerses you in the area’s history for a modest $6 fee (children and military are free). From there, you can embark on a self-guided, 1 1/2-mile Ketchikan Salmon Walk to learn about the fish’s impact on the town (and maybe even spot some, in season, at the Salmon Ladder). The walk will take you past the Totem Heritage Center (also $6, or get a combo ticket to both museums for $9), with its collection of 19th-century totem poles rescued from nearby islands.

If you’re feeling adventurous, you can skip the tour and head out to the Saxman Native Village on your own. It’s 2 miles south of Ketchikan, so it's walkable — but for a few bucks, you can take a city bus there instead. It costs just $5 to wander the park on your own and see the 25 replica totem poles, as well as Native carvers working on new poles using traditional techniques.

Icy Strait Point is a manufactured cruise port near the town of Hoonah. It was created to offer everything cruisers could possibly want in a port, so all the activities are planned to get you to part ways with your hard-earned cash. That said, there are still plenty of things to do in Icy Strait Point for free or cheap.

A free gondola ride transports visitors from one cruise pier area to the other, but if the line is long or you’re afraid of heights, you can walk the same path on nature trails instead. Keep your eyes out for wildlife.

The port has tons of beach access, so you can wander Icy Strait’s shores, stop for scenic photos and look for marine life free of charge. At the Hoonah Cannery building, you can browse the Hoonah Packing Co. Cannery Museum exhibits interspersed among the shops, or get tickets to the Native dance show for $20 per person at the on-site ticket booth.

From the cannery, it’s a 1 1/2-mile (roughly 30-minute) walk to Hoonah, an actual town where many of Icy Strait Point’s workers live and home to Alaska's largest Tlingit village. You can also take an affordable $10 shuttle to town, where you can admire the totem poles and sip a local beer at Icy Strait Brewing.

Related: The best Alaska cruise shore excursions — from heli-hiking to whale watching

Sitka offers a compelling mix of Native Alaskan and Russian history and culture, and a self-guided tour of the key sites in town won't cost you much (if anything at all).

You can get a free tour of the Russian Bishop’s House, an example of 19th-century architecture during Russia’s colonization of Sitka. Baranof Castle State Historic Site (Castle Hill) was occupied throughout the centuries by Tlingit people and later by Russian settlers, and it was the site chosen for the transfer of Alaska from Russia to the U.S. You can check out the views and the informative signs for free.

St. Michael Cathedral National Historic Landmark is an exact replica of the first Russian Orthodox church in the Americas. Because the site has an active congregation, visitors can view its collection of 17th-century religious artifacts for a limited time each day.

Museums with small admission fees include the Sitka History Museum (featuring exhibits on local history) and the Sheldon Jackson Museum (showcasing a collection of Alaska Native artifacts). If exploring old cemeteries is your thing, you’ll want to stop at the more than 200-year-old Sitka Russian Cemetery, with gravestones made from the ballast of Russian ships.

The Sitka National Historical Park’s visitor center and grounds (with walking trails and totem pole installations) are open to all, free of charge. It’s a scenic spot for an easy nature walk, or you can come inside to learn more about Sitka’s Russian and Tlingit cultures or join a ranger program.

You don’t need a tour to gawk at eagles, hawks, owls and falcons at the Alaska Raptor Center. Admission is $16, though it is a bit of a walk from downtown. Watch injured birds relearn how to fly, and take a stroll through the center’s forested grounds.

Finally, you can attend various dance performances at affordable ticket prices. The Alaska Storytellers dance show ($15) celebrates traditional and modern Russian dance, while the New Archangel Dancers' performances highlight Russian folk dances. Or, step into a Tlingit clan house to enjoy the music, costumes and choreography of the Naa Kahidi Tlingit Dancers.

You don’t need to spend a fortune on tours to explore Alaska's culture and history or enjoy its natural splendor. You’ll find plenty of free things to do in port on an Alaska cruise. However, I do encourage you to budget for a few tours, whether it’s to travel beyond the port area into Alaska’s wilderness or to immerse yourself in an activity, such as dog sledding, kayaking, fishing, or whale or bear watching. You won’t regret spending the money on amazing experiences and memories.

#6215. Ouch: Flying Blue Makes Earning XPs Through SAF 50% More Expensive

The Air France-KLM Flying Blue program has just rolled out a quiet devaluation, and it’s one that many savvy Flying Blue members won’t be happy about. The airline group has increased the cost to contribute toward sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), and in turn, has reduced the ability to earn elite status through this method. And we’re not talking about a minor price increase either…

Personally I consider Air France-KLM Flying Blue elite status to be valuable, not just for the SkyTeam Elite Plus perks, but also for the more Air France- KLM specific benefits, like access to more award availability.

Earning Flying Blue elite status is based on the concept of XPs (“experience points”), and how many of those you rack up. One really innovative thing that Flying Blue has done is that it has been possible to earn XPs through environmental contributions:

As I see it, this is a win-win — this program can genuinely help you earn status, while doing something that’s good for the environment, and also contributing to Air France-KLM’s long term environmental goals.

Well, seemingly overnight, Flying Blue has increased the cost to purchase SAF, and in turn, earn XPs. With these changes, you earn one XP for every €15 contributed toward SAF, compared to the previous amount of €10.

A 50% overnight increase is rough. It gets even worse than that, though. There’s no longer any “rounding” with this, so for short haul economy flights you might find that you’re not offered any XPs if the contribution amount is €14, and you’re offered one XP if the amount is €28.

The past year or so has definitely been rough for the overall value of the Flying Blue program, including for elite members:

This is of course all frustrating, though I guess the other side of the equation is that Flying Blue Platinum status has become more valuable over time, but primarily through punitive measures:

How do we make sense of increasing the cost to contribute to SAF, and in turn, earn XPs? I wonder if Flying Blue management thinks that people will still buy SAF at the same rate as before? I know I certainly won’t, though maybe I’m in the minority (I’ll instead increasingly earn XPs through Flying Blue’s co-branded credit card in the US, since that opportunity was recently improved).

For that matter, I’m curious to what extent the number of people buying SAF matters to Air France-KLM? Does this materially contribute to any environmental initiatives, or is it not a priority?

I still get value from my Flying Blue Platinum status, and don’t have plans to change my strategy. Honestly, that partly comes down to how hard it has become to find award availability in business class on long haul flights through other programs.

But I’m definitely slowly becoming less enthused by the program. Then again, I guess that sums up the reality of miles & points more broadly — this isn’t what it once was, and it’s getting harder and harder to make the case for being loyal. It’s no different than World of Hyatt, where they’re clearly trying to cash in. I guess that is the goal of any for-profit business, eh?

Flying Blue has just devalued the rate at which you earn XPs for SAF contributions. You used to earn one XP for every €10 contributed, while you now earn one XP for every €15 contributed. A 50% increase in cost overnight is huge.

I always thought this was a unique aspect of the Flying Blue program, since it’s a win-win for consumers, the airline group, and the environment. Obviously they’ve decided on a different equation now, and for us members, this isn’t good news.

What do you make of this change to Flying Blue when it comes to earning XPs for SAF?

This has become an all too familiar script. Devalue a program, wait a few months, find another way to devalue it, and repeat. Flying Blue is hardly alone. Numerous frequent flyer programs have followed the same playbook. I'm sure these programs analyze member behavior after each devaluation and, seeing little meaningful impact, feel emboldened to do it again. But loyalty erodes gradually. At some point, members will stop chasing status, accumulating miles, or going out of their way to remain loyal. The real danger isn't that members will get angry and leave. It's that they'll simply stop caring. And indifference is far more damaging to a loyalty program than outrage.

While I really don't like the idea of changing the rules without any prior notice (something that, unfortunately, is quite typical of Flying Blue, which has implemented several devaluations without warning), I actually hope they would just remove XP from SAF contributions which would of course almost stop any purchases of SAF as we know that most buy this SAF for XP and not for the environment.... Nowadays, obtaining Elite status through SAF contributions has become far too easy, and let's not forget all status matches that have become quite the norm unfortunately. AF lounges are already overcrowded, and anyone willing to spend enough can potentially reach Platinum without even flying so much on revenue tickets, simply by purchasing award tickets and buying SAF contributions. At the very least, they could introduce a cap on the number of SAF-related XPs that count towards status qualification.

Was there no notice of this change? If not, it's quite disappointing, and something to which (one would think) the head of the FB program would have been sensitive.

Great development! FF status should be for people who actually, you know, fly frequently! Not for those who buy their way there with SAF or credit card sign-up bonuses.

#6214. American Airlines Spent Years Making Its Cabins Worse—Now It’s Racing To Win Passengers Back From United And Delta

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby says one of his biggest competitive advantages won’t last. Other airlines will catch up with Starlink internet. He says he’s investing anyway, because two or three years is enough time to get passengers to try United, discover other things they like, and move their loyalty and credit card spending. That answers the argument Doug Parker made at American Airlines in 2017 for not investing in product: better products just get copied so can’t offer an enduring advantage. Delta spent nearly two decades showing how investment in the operation, product and employees could work together. United has improved more than any other U.S. airline over the past decade. American has made an impressive amount of progress since its premium pivot roughly 21 months ago. But it’s trying to win back customers while losing money, carrying heavy debt, and with fuel costs up. They’re in a race against time to show results before Wall Street gets impatient. I attended American’s September 2017 media and investor day. The airline’s theory was that competitors would match a better product, leaving corporate culture and employees to differentiate the airline. Take care of employees, who would take care of customers, who would take care of shareholders. (Of course American alienated all three groups.) They didn’t explain how that was going to happen. There were nicer employee facilities coming, help using their health and wellness benefits, and they spent a disproportionate amount of time on company-sponsored weight loss programs. I left without understanding the mission employees were supposed to rally around, or how American would install its workforce with a desire and knowledge to deliver exceptional service. Meanwhile, American was preparing to fly its new domestic interior with less legroom, less padded seats and no seatback screens. At that same media day, they didn’t even think they needed native booking in their mobile app. Sending customers to a mobile website was good enough. A year later, Parker told employees: we work really hard to match our service to our competitors, and they do the same to us. He described watching what competitors put onboard, including meals, to ensure American was comparable. He was surprised by the idea that customers might choose United or Delta because of a different inflight product. In contrast, Richard Anderson became Delta CEO in 2007. Along with Glen Hauenstein and Gil West, he built an airline around keeping its promises to passengers and driving hard bargains with its counterparties. Anderson later explained how much of the advantage came from line maintenance. An older airplane could be reliable if mechanics could work on it where it spent the night, fix recurring problems and have it ready in the morning. Delta also worked toward eliminating involuntary denied boarding. A customer who bought a ticket, arrived on time and followed every instruction shouldn’t be told they weren’t going to travel because the airline had sold too many seats. Finding enough volunteers protected the relationship with that customer. They leaned into seatback screens. Their non-union crews were somewhat friendlier than at competitors. Then Delta made itself relevant in the markets where customers had the most money to spend. The 2011 LaGuardia slot swap with US Airways was one of the great airline asset trades. Parker’s airline gave Delta 132 daily LaGuardia slot pairs in exchange for 42 pairs at Washington National and $66.5 million. Required divestitures reduced Delta’s net gain (they eventually got the slots back that were transferred to WestJet) but it gave them the platform to build the New York business. Delta fleeced Parker. US Airways strengthened Washington, but when it merged with American it had to give up slots there anyway. The combined airline couldn’t keep all of both carriers’ holdings. American – once headquartered in New York – would never be able to position itself in New York the way that Delta had. Delta invested in facilities at LaGuardia, JFK and Los Angeles. That all positioned Delta to overtake American in cobrand credit card spend. I’ve been critical of how much Delta has coasted on that reputation. Its operational advantage isn’t what it was (they’re still a bit more reliable than peers but when things go south they struggle to recover, and no longer go months without a mainline cancel). Their 767s out of New York are arguably the actual worst product across the Atlantic and among those who compete for premium transcon business. And Delta’s success despite weak mileage value shouldn’t have taught competitors to devalue their own programs. Delta offered a better experience – that’s eroding – and had strong positioning in some of the best spend markets, and lack of competition in their other key markets (Atlanta, Upper Midwest, Salt Lake). Kirby took a long time to arrive at his current view. He was president of American when it cut meal service in 2014. Planning for the domestic interior without screens began while he was still there, even though the first aircraft with that interior entered service after he left. He initially carried the same approach to United. They cut full domestic first class meals on flights under four hours outside the dinner window, before customer complaints forced a reversal. They eliminated Polaris wine flights and cocktail carts, then reduced business class staffing by one flight attendant and moved to pre-plated entrees. Some of United’s early product investment was probably overboard – greenlighting most everything when Oscar Munoz came back from medical leave. The later United NEXT commitment to screens, bigger bins and a better domestic cabin, combined with sustained investment in its mobile app, represented a different approach under later Kirby. Most passengers sit in coach. Improving their experience gets them to pay more and builds a reputation that qualifies the airline for their future purchases in business. Even business class passengers internationally are often coach passengers domestically, and bad experiences in domestic form the bulk of a passenger’s opinion when it coms time to buy long haul business. The app is part of the coach product just as well as the premium cabin one. Passengers can manage changes, get help improving their seat assignment and receive clearer explanations when something goes wrong. It gives them more control over their trip. They use it repeatedly, and it’s reason they may hesitate to move their flying elsewhere even after another airline matches the cabin. By 2025, Kirby was explaining a different test for food spending. He told Brian Sumers: Every year we’re going to consciously spend more for customers in a bet that we’ll just win more brand-loyal customers. He couldn’t prove exactly how much additional ticket revenue better food would generate. He was willing to make the investment anyway. The old approach could identify the savings from moving a meal window by 15 minutes, while the revenue lost through a series of small disappointments was much harder to see. United’s network rebuilding started earlier. Kirby restored domestic connectivity that had been cut back under Jeff Smisek, and explicitly explained in October 2017 that better connections would help sell credit cards. If United’s schedule didn’t work for someone, that person wasn’t going to take the card. American went the other way in New York, Chicago and Los Angeles. Retreating made the airline less useful in the country’s most valuable spending markets. Offering a less desirable product alienated customers from spending on the American card. And an airline’s route accounting can miss this. A Chicago customer’s work trips may be what persuade them to get an airline’s card, even if they eventually redeem the miles for Hawaii. Credit the Hawaii flight with all the benefit, cut Chicago because it looks weak, and you lose the spending that generated the miles in the first place. In contrast, aviation watchdog JonNYC shares excerpts attributed to Chief Commercial Officer Andrew Nocella laying out where the airline sees itself: United reached 50% of revenue from Chicago-based passengers in the second quarter of 2026, according to Nocella, and gained share in its other hub cities as well. It expects to largely complete United NEXT’s connectivity goals at its midcontinent hubs by summer 2027. More attention then shifts to coastal gateways and international expansion, including a planned return to New York JFK next year. Premium capacity will grow faster than main cabin capacity as United adds Airbus A321neo and A321XLR aircraft at scale. Comments by Andrew Nocella, shared by JonNYC United’s hubs in some of the best cities for card spend and long haul pre-existed Kirby (and those cities are more contested than other airlines face in their most important hubs). Kirby’s Starlink explanation in his Cheeky Pint interview describes how he plans to accelerate United’s gains. John Collison characterized the opportunity as a two-to-three-year window to win customers, and Kirby agreed. Other airlines will eventually have comparable low Earth orbit connectivity. American, Southwest, Alaska and even Frontier are all adding Starlink (and Southwest expects to complete its install around the time United does). they’re going to try us for Starlink, and they’re going to stay because all the other technology, and everything else is better. A temporary advantage can generate a customer relationship that outlasts it. And the biggest gap will be with Delta, which has committed to Amazon Leo that will maybe start becoming available in 2028, and where they’ve committed only to eventually outfit 500 aircraft. Delta’s current wifi is generally poor now that demands on the system by giving it away free have overwhelmed available bandwidth. Parker was right that competitors could copy a feature. Copying the feature doesn’t on its own win back the customer. American is finally reversing course. I first reported its explicit premium pivot in January 2025. In roughly 21 months they’ve changed an extraordinary amount, from better coffee and wine to improved lounges, new business class suites and more attention to the coach experience. They’ve committed to bringing back domestic seatback screens and adding more first class and extra legroom seats. They’ve announced Starlink installations beginning early next year. They’ve even instructed employees to stop involuntarily bumping passengers, giving airport leadership more authority to secure volunteers. American is changing what it asks employees to prioritize, and giving them tools to do it. And Flagship Dining at Los Angeles is finally reopening after more than six years, with access expanded to qualifying business class passengers. It’s a defensive move because Delta’s business class lounge is so much better, and United’s even had been better than American Flagship. I want this to work. I’ve spent years criticizing American because it had so much potential to be better. They’re making real changes and some customers will come back simply because the airline stops giving them reasons to avoid it. But matching what they already get elsewhere likely isn’t enough – American needs a value proposition for what they deliver to customers that no one else will. That’s Delta’s reliability argument (paired with service and screens that for years others eschewed). That’s United’s Starlink argument (paired with a stronger global network). American entered the pandemic with heavy debt after spending more than $12 billion on share buybacks under Parker. Borrowing while returning that much cash to shareholders left it weaker than competitors. It has too much debt service, less room to borrow, and less well-positioned to do acquisitions. The risk is that investors demand results before enough customers have experienced the improvements, or demand cuts to the spending that could produce real results. American’s domestic seatback screens won’t begin arriving on new aircraft until 2028, and the broader fleet project extends into the next decade. It needs the improvements it can deliver sooner to get customers back onboard and spending more before then. The interest and fuel bills are arriving now. Then Delta made itself relevant in the markets where customers had the most money to spend. The 2011 LaGuardia slot swap with US Airways was one of the great airline asset trades. And Delta’s success despite weak mileage value shouldn’t have taught competitors to devalue their own programs. More attention then shifts to coastal gateways and international expansion, including a planned return to New York JFK next year. It needs the improvements it can deliver sooner to get customers back onboard and spending more before then. The interest and fuel bills are arriving now.
