Not until Robert Isom is gone and AA has true leadership will this airline ever recover. Morale is miserable in ALL work groups. Airlines are all alike and it simply comes down to the people that take care of the customers. Whenever I have to fly AA I brace myself for the absolute worst experience. After being scolded asking for a third glass of water during a dinner service in business class I simply have had enough. Like TWA, Braniff, Eastern and Pan Am before them there’s plenty of room in the desert to park planes when it’s all said and done.

I bet NO. We don’t forget the barking dog tapes. They treat passengers like dogs

American’s on time performance and overall reliability remains at the bottom end of the industry peers, slightly above JetBlue. That’s not good.

The fleet is enormous, and a lot of it still flies around in the Parker-era bare bones aesthetic, which is not aging well.

American’s finances are challenged by the buy-backs, yes, and the massive 2011 re-fleet which was needed, but very costly.

American has to work harder in NYC, Chicago, and LA to win back premium customers and position itself not as one that has matched DL and UA but does something a bit better. The wealth on credit card spend in America does not sit in Charlotte or the Sun Belt. It resides in the big blue cities that MAGA hates. Just look at United’s route map and rising premium revenue, and you can see why. It’s hubs are in the right markets.

Delta’s performance in NYC is slipping. Too much flying to Europe is performed on 767-300ERs and 767-400ERs, and A330CEOs that have old, dated cabins. Ground staff at JFK are often rude but Delta still has the ability to find a revenue yield premium like the rest cannot.

Alaska is the winner in the service wars. They have the best employees and give them the authority to do their jobs. That’s not to say that AS hasn’t backslid the last two years but their recent announcement indicated they still get what’s important.

Is that enough to grow to the size of the big three? No not so long as airport slots are constrained. But where they fly Alaska asks for and appears to get a premium which indicates that passengers are willing to pay more to fly with them.

Bigger picture whatever happens the customer is going to see substantial benefits from AA’s change in direction not only when they fly AA but other carriers as well because premium flyers obviously don’t take well to being abused and with loyalty no longer very valuable are much more likely to go with the airline with whom they have had good experiences.

That marginal revenue the airlines have been able to extract by upselling has come at a cost. No longer beholden the carriers have to perform in order to get a passenger’s repeat business.

Ironic but a good outcome for those of us who fly frequently and want more than just a cheap seat.

To respond to another commentator… you’re wrong about Alaska. They absolutely suck. Their Firsr Class food is a joke. And Alaska is already dumbing down Hawaiin Airlines, a once great airline. American will catch up over time. Delta is sliding. Their seats on the a321 Neo in First Class are absolute garbage… there is a metal box for electronics that sits right between the 2 “First Class” seats, severely impeding your legroom. The seats are cheap and you feel like you’re sitting on concrete after a couple of hours. And Delta’s WiFi is pure garbage too.

The US Airways/Doug Parker take over was an unmitigated disaster. The US Air planes right after the merger were horrendous. Charlotte, Phil, PHX are not DFW, MIA, ORD for corporate travel. I get AA was bankrupt and Arpey and Carty before him were not Crandall and Parker had the upper hand of a profitable airline, at that time. Going forward the legacy US AIR team needs to be moved out and bring in fresh blood that can make American Airlines great again.

Bob I agree the box on the floor is terrible and don’t make excuses for it. I’ve not had the same reaction you have to the seats. Are you referring to F or Y?

I haven’t had the same reaction to their food in F. In your opinion how would you say it compares to UA, AA and DL?

It’s not all about ‘systems’. The people at Delta are so friendly and helpful – that can’t be replicated. The 757-400s are being replaced by new planes. That is coming.

Sometimes I fly AA from Heathrow having flown from Boston with BA. The difference in the cabin crews is night and day. The BA staff are sharply dressed, polite, efficient and friendly, while the AA cabin crew look like they have been let out of their nursing homes. Slovenly and sullen are two traits that come to mind. No airline is perfect so as long as I get from A-B safely I’ll put up with cabin crew who couldn’t care less

(Reading the room, whispering to myself… ‘but, I liked the new Flagship Suites’…)

I’m a flight attendant. Employee moral at AA is low. AA expects flight attendants to be punching bags. We even have a lesson in our quarterly training on “how to apologize to passengers”. I no longer tell people that I work for American

Please bring back meals on flights 700+ miles! I’m begging you!

So how does Kirby justify Basic Business where United is very intentionally driving off premium passengers while also destroying loyalty? I’m not an insider but I’d love to hear how alienating premium customers makes your airline more premium.

I don’t want to be rude or mean however it was UNIONS which wanted the so-called “merger” between AA and US. In fact, I remember blogging (back when I used to blog on WordPress.com) about how the APA head was bragging about it and how its going to eventually cost them in the long term.

Horton was doing a fantastic job getting AA back on track – in fact, he was the one who was responsible for the blockbuster aircraft deals with both Boeing and Airbus.

The unions simply didn’t like the way Horton ran AA which is a shame as he’s one of the only people I’ve ever heard who not only was able to get bondholders their 100 cents to the dollar, but didn’t have shareholders wiped out during BK.

As the saying goes, “you reap what you sow”.

As an American Airlines retiree I agree with Texas Fly Girl. When someone asks I tell them I worked for airline and hope they don’t ask which one. It is embarrassing the downfall since the arrival of Parker and the USAIR guys.

#6213. Emirates Airbus A380s Finally Return To 17-Hour Route: See Map Now

On November 1, Emirates finally reintroduced Airbus A380 service from Dubai International Airport (DXB) to Houston George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH). The major Texas airport has superjumbo service again.

The relaunch of double-decker quadjet flights to IAH came two days after the Gulf giant began flying the equipment to Glasgow again. The Scottish city last saw the A380 in early March, so the return was significant.

The United Arab Emirates' largest operator has a reasonably long history of flying to IAH. OAG data shows that the first service took place 19 years ago, in December 2007, when the Boeing 777-200LR — which was designed for such ultra-long missions — was deployed. The larger 777-300ER, which also has significant freight capacity, materialized in March 2012. Then it was the turn of the A380.

The superjumbo first arrived in IAH in December 2014, seven years after the route began. It was deployed daily until early 2020 and returned in December 2022. Flightradar24 shows that the double-decker flew to IAH until February 2026, when the war in Iran meant that the type and the route were temporarily paused.

After a month-and-a-half gap, service from DXB to IAH returned in May 2026, with the 484-seat A380 used. The superjumbo was deployed until August 24, 2026, after which the 276-seat 777-200LR, the original equipment to IAH, was once again flown. With 43% fewer seats for sale, the equipment swap to the Triple Seven would have helped with higher loads, although first class was not available and there were considerably fewer business seats.

On November 1, Emirates reintroduced superjumbo service to IAH. While the great circle suggests 7,098 nautical miles (13,146 km) each way, this is, as always, theoretical. It does not take account of real-world operations. Avoiding Iranian, Ukrainian, and Russian airspace, for example, increased the distance to around 7,211 nautical miles (13,355 km), which is a pretty insignificant increase.

The route continues to run daily on the 484-seat A380 with the following schedule. There are 14 seats in first, 76 in business, 56 in premium economy (40" pitch; 2-4-2), and 338 in economy (32"; 3-3-3). While unsurprising, the number of economy seats (338) is far more than the total capacity of the 777-200LR (276 seats), which operated until October 31.

EK211: 9:40 AM-4:40 PM (17 hours and 00 minutes)

EK212: 7:00 PM-7:45 PM+1 (14 hours and 45 minutes)

It contributes to the country having a record number of superjumbo flights. Find out more!

Between December 2007 and February 2026, US Department of Transportation data shows that Emirates transported just over 3.5 million round-trip passengers between DXB and IAH. In the 12 months to February this year, 249,000 passengers were carried, with a very low load factor of just 66.0%. Questions must be asked about whether that government figure is accurate. Nonetheless, with first class and so many business seats, the yield performance must make the long and expensive route worth serving.

Booking data suggests that about 70% of the route's traffic connected to another flight in DXB. ​​​​​​​Predictably, India was by far the most popular country market, followed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, the Philippines, Thailand, Kuwait (for oil), Malaysia, Iran, Bangladesh, and Singapore. The top ten cities were Houston to/from Mumbai, Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Karachi, Delhi, Manila, Chennai, Dammam (for oil), Ahmedabad, and Kochi.

#6212. Belavia Can Once Again Do Business With Boeing, As US Lifts Sanctions On Belarus

Belarusian national carrier Belavia has faced sanctions from the United States and European Union for quite some time, due to a combination of the “hijacking” of a Ryanair flight, along with the country’s support for Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Well, if Belarusian media is to be believed, these sanctions are now being lifted, so the country’s airline can once again buy planes from Boeing…

Belarusian state owned national news agency BelTA is reporting that the United States Department of Commerce has granted Boeing a license to resume full cooperation with Belavia. This was announced by Valentin Rybakov, the Belarusian representative to the United Nations. If true, this means that Belavia can once again purchase planes and parts directly from Boeing.

This all seems to be related to a visit to Belarus by an American delegation in September, where the country’s president, Alexander Lukashenko, met with US Special Envoy John Cole. This meeting included a larger lifting of sanctions. It also comes at a time when we’re seeing the Trump administration increasingly lifting sanctions on Russia in relation to the invasion of Ukraine.

In 2021, the United States imposed sanctions on Belarus, after the country engaged in what was referred to as a state sponsored hijacking. A Ryanair Boeing 737 was flying between Greece and Lithuania, and as the plane approached Belarusian airspace, an air traffic controller claimed there was a bomb onboard, and that the plane needed to divert to Belarus.

As it turned out, an opponent of the Belarusian government was onboard, so the real motive with this was to have him arrested. Obviously this violates all sorts of international laws and aviation treaties, which is why action was taken against the country. Then in 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, additional sanctions were imposed against Belarus, given its support for Russia.

Obviously having sanctions imposed on you by both the United States and European Union makes it challenging to buy new aircraft, given the aircraft manufacturing duopoly we have (unless you consider the aircraft manufacturers in China and Russia to be competitors).

So most of Belavia’s aircraft acquisitions in recent times have been smuggled into the country using shady middlemen. For example, in 2025, Belavia acquired Airbus A330s through an imaginary Gambian airline, as one does.

Belavia can reportedly once again buy aircraft and parts from Boeing, after the United States lifted sanctions that were imposed around five years ago, when the country hijacked a Ryanair plane. This easing of sanctions comes as part of a larger reversal by the Trump administration, as it takes less of a stance against Russia and Belarus.

It’ll be interesting to see what comes of this, and if Belarus places some big Boeing aircraft order in the near future…

What do you make of the US lifting sanctions on Belarus on the airline front?

#6211. Chase credit cards: Best time to apply based on offer history

With many of the best credit cards on the market, earning a generous welcome bonus is a quick way to receive a lot of value. These cards from Chase are no exception.

It's important to know, however, that welcome offers often change.

Let's say you're considering adding a new Chase card to your wallet. When is the best time to apply so you can earn the best offer? We have you covered.

Read on to learn more about the welcome offer history across both Chase's cash-back cards and those earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points.

Below are some of the most popular Chase credit cards, along with their highest-ever offers and our recommendations for when to apply.

Note that these are all publicly available offers; some individual, targeted bonuses may be higher than the offers listed here. Additionally, some of these offers may no longer be available.

Also, keep in mind that Chase factors in its 5/24 rule when you apply. Other factors can dictate whether or not you're eligible for a Chase welcome bonus.

Consider your current wallet setup and cross-check with the terms of whichever card you decide to apply for.

The Chase Freedom Flex is a solid no-annual-fee, cash-back option for cardholders who want to maximize rotating quarterly bonus categories (on up to $1,500 in combined spending each quarter; activation is required each quarter).

If you have a card that earns Ultimate Rewards points, the cash back you earn on the Freedom Flex (and any Chase cash-back card, with the exception of the Ink Business Premier, which doesn't combine rewards with any other Chase card) can be turned into Ultimate Rewards points.

Here are the recent offers we have seen on the Freedom Flex.

The best bonus we've seen on this card is the current one: Earn a $250 bonus after spending $500 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

We suggest applying for this card when the bonus offers at least $200 cash back.

The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers a flat 1.5% cash back on most purchases, with simple bonus-earning categories for certain everyday purchases. The card doesn't charge an annual fee.

The Freedom Unlimited's bonus offer has matched the offer on the Freedom Flex in the past, but they aren't always identical. So, it's worth comparing the two if you decide to apply.

Here are the recent offers we have seen on the Freedom Unlimited.

$200 plus up to $600 on grocery purchases

This card has offered two welcome bonuses that could be considered the highest, and it depends on what you prioritize.

One bonus offered unlimited double cash back for the first 12 months from account opening. The other offered a $200 bonus after spending $500 on purchases in the first three months from account opening, plus 5% cash back on grocery store purchases (not including Target or Walmart; on up to $12,000 spent on these purchases) during the first year.

This card could be worth applying for when the bonus offers double cash back for the first year, or at least $200 plus a bonus category for extra earnings during the first year.

The Chase Sapphire Preferred Card is a solid entry-level travel rewards card for anyone ready to dive into the world of Chase Ultimate Rewards points. The card provides good value for many at a modest $95 annual fee.

Here are the recent offers we have seen on the Sapphire Preferred.

*The bonus offer value is based on TPG's October 2026 valuations and is not provided by the credit card issuer.

The best offer allowed new cardholders to earn 100,000 points after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening (no longer available).

The best time to apply for the Sapphire Preferred is any time the bonus comes with at least 75,000 points.

Learn more: Chase Sapphire Preferred Card

The premium Chase Sapphire Reserve offers a host of benefits and is a great option for Chase Sapphire Lounge access and elevated earning rates in multiple travel categories. It comes with a $795 annual fee.

Here are the recent offers we have seen on the Sapphire Reserve.

*The bonus offer value is based on TPG's valuations and is not provided by the credit card issuer.

The highest-ever offer on the Sapphire Reserve allowed new cardholders to earn 150,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening (offer no longer available).

It's good to apply for this card anytime it's offering at least 125,000 points.

The Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business is a premium business card option for business owners looking for top-tier perks. The card charges a $795 annual fee.

Here are the recent offers we have seen on the Sapphire Reserve for Business.

*The bonus offer value is based on TPG's valuations and is not provided by the credit card issuer.

The highest welcome offer is also the current offer: Earn 200,000 bonus points after spending $30,000 on purchases in the first six months from account opening.

When at least 200,000 points are on offer.

Learn more: Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business

The Ink Business Cash earns bonus cash-back rewards for business owners in popular spending categories, such as office supply stores, internet, cable and phone services, for no annual fee.

Here are the recent offers we have seen on the Ink Business Cash.

The highest offer we've seen allowed new cardholders to earn $1,000 cash back after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first four months from account opening (no longer available).

It's a good time to apply when the welcome bonus exceeds $750.

Learn more: Ink Business Cash Credit Card

Small-business owners who are Chase Ultimate Rewards points enthusiasts could find their perfect match in the Ink Business Preferred Credit Card. For a $95 annual fee, you can collect Chase points across multiple bonus categories.

Here are the recent offers we have seen on the Ink Business Preferred.

*The bonus offer value is based on TPG's valuations and is not provided by the credit card issuer.

The highest offer we've seen in the Ink Business Preferred's history gave new cardholders the opportunity to earn 120,000 bonus points after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

The best time to apply for the Ink Business Preferred is any time the welcome bonus is at least 100,000 points.

Learn more: Ink Business Preferred Credit Card

The Ink Business Premier is Chase's top-tier business cash-back card, offering unlimited 2% cash back on business purchases on top of other bonus categories for a $195 annual fee.

Here are the offers we have seen on the Ink Business Premier.

This card's welcome offer has remained the same since its launch, so the highest offer is the current offer of $1,000 cash back after spending $10,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

If the Ink Business Premier ever runs a limited-time offer above its typical $1,000 (the only offer we've seen in its history), it could be worth applying, depending on the spending requirement.

Learn more: Ink Business Premier Credit Card

For business owners seeking a flat-rate cash-back card, the no-annual-fee Ink Business Unlimited is a good option to consider.

Here are the recent offers we have seen on the Ink Business Unlimited.

The highest offer we've seen allowed new cardholders to earn $1,000 cash back after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first four months from account opening (no longer available).

It's a good time to apply when the welcome bonus exceeds $750.

Learn more: Ink Business Unlimited Credit Card

Chase is the issuer of the only two Hyatt cobranded cards on the market — one personal card and one business card. These two cards will occasionally offer elevated welcome bonuses.

If you're interested in one of Chase's Hyatt cards, check out our guide to the offer history on the World of Hyatt cards to help you decide when to apply.

IHG loyalists have three card options, all cobranded with Chase. Two of the cards are personal cards, and there's one option for business owners.

If you're interested in one of Chase's IHG cards, see our offer history guide for IHG cards to help you make your decision.

Marriott credit cards are in an interesting position within the industry, since they're issued by both Chase and American Express. Chase issues three Marriott cobranded cards, two of which are currently open to applicants.

If you're interested in one of Chase's Marriott cards, take a look at our guide to Marriott cards' offer history to decide when to apply.

All Southwest Airlines credit cards are cobranded with Chase, which issues three personal options and two business cards for Southwest loyalists. These cards will receive new welcome offers somewhat frequently.

If you're interested in one of Chase's Southwest cards, our guide to the offer history of Southwest cards can help you choose a time to apply.

Chase issues all United Airlines credit cards, which often feature solid bonuses for frequent flyers. The Chase-United suite includes four personal card options and two business cards.

If you're interested in one of Chase's United cards, see our guide to the United cards' offer history to decide when to apply.

Welcome bonuses often fluctuate, so if you're interested in applying for a new card, it's worth checking out its offer history and comparing it to the present offer.

Since so much of a card's value is found in the welcome offer, you may find that the best strategy is to hold off until a lucrative limited-time bonus appears so you can earn a large number of bonus points or cash back.

#6210. Hotel Guests Report Mold And Mice—It Still Passed Inspection The Next Day

A mother says mice crawled across her sleeping three-year-old at a Wyndham hotel near the Albany, New York airport. Other residents reported mold, cockroaches and soaked carpets. The hotel passed a county health inspection the next day even though the inspector recorded six violations. The rooms with violations weren’t occupied on the day the inspector arrived and were supposed to be repaired before being rented. We trust hotels to do some very basic things: Change the sheets Clean the bathroom Make sure the door locks And the brand on the hotel is supposed to give you confidence! Baymont by Wyndham Latham Albany Airport markets rooms to travelers. It also houses people placed by county social services. That’s often a good indication… One woman, staying with her nine month old daughter, described cockroaches, mice, mold and bedbugs in some rooms. Other residents described wet carpets and a strong smell. A guest said she’d filmed mice crawling over her sleeping child and had stopped letting the girl sleep in her own bed. There were complaints about mouse droppings and dead flies on a bed, and mold and dead flies in a refrigerator. The County moved some social service clients. Another county with one room there relocated their client as a precaution and suspended use of the hotel. What The Inspection Found Albany County inspected the hotel October 13, finding no public health hazards, but six violations: A removed smoke detector. Three exterior doors that didn’t self-latch. A stained bathroom ceiling tile. Evidence of pests in a room. The plan to fix the rooms before renting them helps explain how the hotel could continue operating, though a missing smoke detector matters even in an empty room. And it seems to me that pests in one room can easily spread. There were earlier maintenance concerns, too. A March 13, 2025 entry in New York’s inspection database notes water stains and possible active leaks at this property. You’re Supposed To Be Able To Rely On A Brand A big part of what a hotel brand sells is confidence that somebody has vetted the property. You know what you’re getting. The hotel may be franchised but it’s supposed to deliver to brand standards. Years ago I covered an Inside Edition investigation that found three of nine hotels tested hadn’t provided completely fresh sheets between guests. The beds were re-made with the previous guest’s used sheets. Then came pandemic promises of enhanced cleaning. Inside Edition went back in 2020, using washable marks visible under ultraviolet light. It reported unchanged bedding at a Hyatt Place and a Hampton Inn in Times Square. At Trump International, the sheets had been changed, but the report said a pillowcase hadn’t. More recently, I covered a Hyatt Place guest who went through three rooms and still wound up with filthy bedding. Hyatt refunded the stay and provided 15,000 points. You’re not supposed to have to even check recent reviews and traveler photos, and pull back the bedding immediately on arrival. I Wouldn’t Let An Airline Choose Where I Sleep, Either I’ve made the same argument about hotels airlines provide during overnight delays. I’ve reported on roaches, floors was so dirty they turned guests’ feet black, and worse. Airlines offering lowest-cost rooms aren’t necessarily delvering places you’d ever want to stay. Years ago I covered an Inside Edition investigation that found three of nine hotels tested hadn’t provided completely fresh sheets between guests. The beds were re-made with the previous guest’s used sheets.

Then came pandemic promises of enhanced cleaning. Inside Edition went back in 2020, using washable marks visible under ultraviolet light. It reported unchanged bedding at a Hyatt Place and a Hampton Inn in Times Square. At Trump International, the sheets had been changed, but the report said a pillowcase hadn’t.

More recently, I covered a Hyatt Place guest who went through three rooms and still wound up with filthy bedding. Hyatt refunded the stay and provided 15,000 points. You’re not supposed to have to even check recent reviews and traveler photos, and pull back the bedding immediately on arrival.

#6209. The ICE arrest of a pro-Trump evangelical has MAGA in an uproar

Samuel Sey spent the past two years telling American Christians that the Bible demands what Immigration and Customs Enforcement does. âChristian ethics do not denounce deportations,â the conservative Christian blogger and podcaster wrote in Feb. 2025. âThey demand it.â Immigration was a privilege and not a right, he argued, and America âdoesnât owe anything to people born outside of the country â including me.â Should his own residency ever be ended, he allowed, that would be âinconvenient â not unjust.â

Now Sey, who is originally from Ghana and grew up in Canada, has found himself swept up in the very deportation apparatus he spent years cheering on.

The resulting uproar has exposed a particularly ugly contradiction in the MAGA movement: Its most enthusiastic defenders of mass deportation suddenly understand the human cost of immigration enforcement when the person facing removal belongs to their own. On Oct. 21 federal agents arrested Sey at the Columbus airport. He now sits in the Butler County Jail on an ICE hold. The Department of Homeland Security says he entered the country legally in 2022 but overstayed by more than four years, that he has no pending applications and that he accepted voluntary departure. Seyâs wife â who was born in the U.S., as were the coupleâs three children was born in the U.S. â says he entered legally and has spent years working with a lawyer to secure permanent status. His friends call the whole thing a clerical error. The conservative movement that amplified him is tearing itself apart over what to feel about his detention, because the answer exposes what its immigration politics were always made of.

âThis has been probably the darkest 24 hours Iâve ever experienced on social media,â wrote Joel Berry, the former Babylon Bee managing editor who calls himself a right-wing Protestant evangelical Trump supporter. âThere is a segment of the so-called âChristianâ nationalist crowd that has given itself completely over to Satan.â

For a political coalition that has built its entire identity around the demonization of undocumented immigrants and the ruthless execution of mass removals, the detention of one of their own foot soldiers has triggered a profound internal fracture.

Christian conservative influencers like The Blazeâs Allie Beth Stuckey and The Daily Wireâs Megan Basham immediately flooded social media to sound the alarm and rally support for their fallen comrade. Berry rushed to set up a GiveSendGo crowdfunding campaign that quickly hauled in more than $30,000 to cover legal fees. The right-wing influencers rallying around Sey have suddenly discovered that an immigrant can be a good person, that the governmentâs account might be incomplete and that separating a father from his children can be devastating.Â

As Salonâs Amanda Marcotte has extensively documented, Stuckey has built a lucrative career railing against what she dismissively derides as toxic empathy whenever progressives advocate for basic human decency toward migrants and asylum seekers. Being so empathetic toward one set of people that you are blinded to everyone else, she has written, âisnât just misguided, itâs evil.â Yet when Sey was taken, Stuckey asked her followers to empathize with his family. âAs you can imagine, his wife, whoâs at home with their 3 babies, is devastated and also trusting the Lord to help them find a resolution quickly. Please pray for all of the Seys,â she wrote on X. Berry, who produces the Jeremy Boreing podcast, which Sey was traveling to record when he was arrested, once declared that âthe only due process owed to an illegal alien is deportation.â Now he says that Sey âis in my tribe, and he is my brotherâ and âwould make an excellent American.â

But the reactions from the broader MAGA grassroots suggest that despite Seyâs relentless pandering to white Christian nationalists, he was never truly seen as an equal member of the tribe. âLord, we thank you sincerely. We thank you for the arrest of Samuel Sey,â Joel Webbon, a prominent Texas pastor, said following the podcasterâs detention. âWe thank you for shutting his mouth from spewing out more lies and slander against your servants and your church here in these United States of America.â Webbon described Sey as an âillegal alien wrongfully in our countryâ who lectures Americans about their heritage.Â

Sey has spent much of the past year feuding with a set of conservative pastors who promote antisemitic and pro-segregation theology. #6208. Trump’s right. Bill Maher is a man without a party — or a point

Donald Trump is bad at a lot of things — negotiations, concealing criminal behavior, standing normal — but he’s not bad at everything. As much as it might bug some of us to admit it, there are a few areas where the president excels. He has an incredible gift for crafting earworms, and his Queens cadence and variable-volume delivery has wriggled its way into American speech patterns. He’s skilled at crafting funny putdowns, pithy nicknames and jabs that hit what his rival politicians are sensitive about and exploit the pressure points of expensive, futile campaigns.

But Trump’s greatest skill is his ability to sniff out a loser. The son of a slumlord coming from the outer boroughs, he was starting with two strikes against him when he attempted to make a jump into Manhattan’s high society. If he wanted to join the rarefied air of the sons and daughters of The 400, he couldn’t be seen associated with anyone who would count as a mark against his judgment. Trump developed a sharp sense of who was on the wane and on the rise, and he worked hard to only mingle with the ascendant.

It worked. His surname became synonymous with big-money deals, success and opulence despite a string of bankruptcies, casino closures and failed direct-to-consumer businesses. Trump kept away from maiden horses, in part because he ate dirt so often. So you can trust that when he calls Bill Maher a “complete and total loser,” he knows what he’s talking about.

Trump railed against the host of HBO’s “Real Time” on Sunday night in a Truth Social post that expanded beyond essay length. He bashed Maher for his ratings and accused the host of lying about Trump’s approval rating. He pushed back against Maher’s criticism of the war in Iran. Most cuttingly, the reality TV veteran accused Maher of leaning heavily on canned applause and a laugh track to sell the idea that he’s funny.

“[Maher] lies about everything,” the president wrote, “and I believe he lied to me when I asked him, with all the applause and laughter he gets after almost everything he says, about things that aren’t funny or even any good, what Laughter Machine does he use?”

Maher prodded Trump in a monologue last Friday after attending a White House dinner alongside Kid Rock and ESPN’s Stephen A. Smith. The host made a note of Trump’s plummeting approval ratings and recent commentary on men’s physiques at his rallies. “It’s just a little odd that Trump keeps gushing about men’s bodies, and how handsome they are, and their jawlines, and their asses, their physiques,” Maher said. “I’m a little hurt. I was there for dinner for four hours last week, and not a peep. Nothing.”

On Truth Social, Trump accused Maher of turning up looking bedraggled and drunk for the controversial dinner at the “seductive and beautiful” White House. The president said that he “learned nothing” from Maher, but he clearly hoped the host would leave with a more favorable outlook on the MAGA movement. Afterward, Trump said Maher returned to his set and his “laughing machine” and offered slightly tamer critiques in the days that followed, before the host supposedly turned on him for the cameras.

“He reverted back to his former self, and his old ways,” Trump wrote. “What he spouts isn’t what he believes. He has to cater to his base, which is mostly composed of Losers, and people who don’t like working.”

In true Trump fashion, the post was lengthy and melodramatic. But at the heart of his burn-book slams, he did hit on a real question: Who is Bill Maher for?

In true Trump fashion, the post was lengthy and melodramatic. But at the heart of his burn-book slams, he did hit on a real question: Who is Bill Maher for?

The snarky libertarian has the carriage of an overeducated yuppie. Despite his frequent protestations, his smarm and suits pushed him to one side of the country’s rigid two-party binary. (He didn’t name his first show “Politically Incorrect” to rile the GOP, after all.) Maher’s outrage over the War on Terror and 2002 cancellation by ABC jammed him into an awkwardly fitting box of “liberal cause celebre.” As neoconservatives pushed an uberpatriotic theocracy in the aughts, his bad faith documentaries, which were aimed at evangelicals, kept up the illusion that he was on the side of progressives. But Maher has never been a lefty, or even particularly committed to any beliefs beyond his freedom to smoke weed.

In recent years, he’s crowed to anyone still listening that he’s open to MAGA’s overtures. He’s frequently come out on the side of reactionaries when the question centers around gender nonconforming people or Islamophobia. Outside of his dinner at the White House, Maher has railed against progressive candidates and offered his vote to Republicans, provided they tone down their rhetoric around the Big Lie.

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only, written by Amanda Marcotte, now also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

That particular problem is unsolvable, at least as long as Trump is alive and in power. While the president’s popularity might be waning with voters, he still has the ability to sink Republicans who cross him. That leaves Maher in an unenviable position, inching toward a conservative party that could take or leave him. He’s gotten crankier and more prone to cribbing Fox News talking points at a time where the center of the Democratic Party is rushing to the left. His constant trashing of rising progressive stars will be hard to forget if the expected blue wave materializes in the Nov. 3 midterms.

All this means that the proud libertarian has found himself with fewer friends than ever. Cozying up to Trump only got him publicly mocked by the president as a “hopeless guy” and a “coward.” The liberal commentariat reacted negatively to Maher’s first dinner with Trump in 2025, with Keith Olbermann claiming that the comedian had always been a “shameless opportunist.” This year, Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee Dr. Abdul El-Sayed called out Maher’s history of religious intolerance.

With Trump realizing that Maher’s not worth the effort to woo and the next generation of party stars outright hostile to him, it’s unclear what role Maher has to play. “Aren’t these flyover states stupid?” isn’t enough of a stance to warrant having the mic when the current administration is disappearing people off the street. Maher’s punch-left, pat-right comedy has been stale for years, but he’s still insisting he’s owed a platform. He’s a blunt comic whose rotation of tired jokes have left him with no one to pass his joint to.

Perhaps Trump summed up the problem of Maher best, in a barb buried deep in his Sunday night tirade. Maher clearly views himself as a bold truth-teller, willing to take on both the empty-headed conservatives and the too woke progressives. Trump’s approval-obsessed brain looks at a guy who has alienated anyone who might support him and only sees one thing: “You’re not transformative,” he said. “You’re a loser!”

#6207. Transfer Amex Points To Virgin Atlantic Flying Club With 30% Bonus: Worth It?

The Amex Membership Rewards program has just launched a new 30% transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. While Flying Club is in some ways a niche program, this is a deal that has the potential to offer outsized value, and I’m sure it will interest many people. I’d probably speculatively take advantage of this, except for the fact that I moved a bunch of points last year when there was a 40% transfer bonus.

Between November 2 and November 30, 2026, the American Express Membership Rewards program in the United States is offering a 30% bonus on points transfers to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club.

Ordinarily points transfer at a 1:1 ratio (in 1,000 point increments), while through this promotion you’d get 1,300 Flying Club points for every 1,000 Membership Rewards points transferred. Transfers are generally instant.

For context, Amex seems to offer a transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club once or twice per year. The last promotion we saw was over the summer, and this is the second offer so far in 2026. When we do see these offers, they’re typically in the range of 30-40%, so this is on the low side of that range, but could still represent a great deal.

Virgin Atlantic is definitely a frequent flyer program with more niche redemption opportunities. In addition to being able to redeem Flying Club points for travel on Virgin Atlantic, there’s also good value to be had for redemptions on Air New Zealand, All Nippon Airways, and Delta.

In late 2024 we saw Flying Club introduce dynamic award pricing for travel on Virgin Atlantic. While the changes are a mixed bag, what’s exciting is that on the low end, redemptions are cheaper than ever before. It’s now possible to fly one-way Virgin Atlantic Upper Class between the United States and the UK for under 30,000 points, and that’s before a transfer bonus.

Beyond that, Virgin Atlantic has several airline partners, some of which are more lucrative than others. Probably the best use of Flying Club points is for travel in ANA first & business class. You can find the redemption rates below.

Paying 45,000-47,500 Flying Club points for a one-way business class ticket between the United States and Japan is a phenomenal value to start with. Then when you consider the 30% transfer bonus, that means you could be paying significantly fewer Amex points. First class can also be a good deal.

All Nippon Airways’ new first & business class are amazing products as well. The major catch is that availability can be really tough to come by.

Through November 30, 2026, Amex is offering a 30% bonus when you transfer points to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. This is definitely more of a niche program, but with a specific use in mind, there’s a lot of value to be had.

With the 30% bonus, award travel on Virgin Atlantic will be an even better value. There’s also lots of value to booking on partners, ranging from SkyTeam airlines, to Air New Zealand, to All Nippon Airways.

Do you plan on taking advantage of this Amex transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club?

#6205. Passenger Says Delta Flight Attendant Photographed Her Sleeping—‘You Might See It On Facebook’

Tasia Jewel had just arrived in Mexico City and checked into her hotel when she shared the story. She’d been at the Formula One race in Austin, stayed in Texas rather than going home, and was exhausted. She slept for about an hour and a half or so on the roughly three-hour flight.

Then she got to the aircraft door. She says three or four male flight attendants were standing there saying goodbye to passengers. One told her:

Hey, yo friend, I took a picture of you while you were sleeping.

She says the other crewmembers laughed with one adding, “Yeah, she was knocked out.” And the first flight attendant repeated, “You might see it on Facebook.”

Here’s her account, flagged by Paddle Your Own Kanoo:

The woman acknowledges he could have been joking. She also says she hadn’t spoken to him at all on the flight.

My first reaction was that, while Delta has built up its Austin flying, they don’t actually operated Austin – Mexico City. But in a follow-up video she says she flew from Dallas to Atlanta to Mexico City with the flight in question being Delta 602. She says she chose Delta’s Boeing 757 because she didn’t want the Aeromexico Boeing 737 MAX.

And she reports that Delta responded well to her complaint. Her original video caption said she’d filed a complaint. In later replies, she reports a phone call, an apology and an investigation. I guess what matters here was whether there was a fundamental breach or a bad joke. Either way, she says she felt unsafe.

I’ve written about a sleeping passenger who said a man photographed her, where the crew intervened and police met the flight. Here, the person allegedly taking the photos was an employee she was supposed to go to for help.

And last year I covered a flight attendant who caught a passenger secretly filming her and sending her image to someone else. It’s easy to understand why that bothered her. But a passenger can have the same objection when the roles are reversed.

I don’t want a ban on taking pictures inside an aircraft. Passengers need to be able to document how they’re treated. Delta’s customer photography guidance recognizes that people take photos and videos, while asking them to avoid interfering with safety and to be “respectful in your intent” when including employees. Employees ought to show customers that same consideration.

#6204. Elvis borrowed from Black artists. Now his songs’ owners are suing AI

Depending on who you talk to, Elvis Presley was either the king of rock ânâ roll or a no-good thief.

The legendary singerâs legacy has gone through about as many re-evaluations as Presley himself had jumpsuits. His long-held status as an originator of rock music was obviously not quite the whole story. A minute of research, or just an honest accounting that nearly all his early rockabilly hits were cover songs, puts the lie to the idea that Elvis was a drawling bolt from the blue.Â Â

He took the genre to new heights of popularity, with a hip-swinging style and a (white) babyface, but the music that Elvis sold so well predated him by decades. The prehistory of rock ânâ rollÂ  is full of names who might have become stars if they were gifted with his baby blues or discovered by a relentless schemer on the level Col. Tom Parker.Â

Then, as something of a corrective to the idea that Elvis was the end-all, be-all of early rock music, the revisionist idea that he was nothing more than a Pat Boone-type, a watered-down middling talent whose success only came on the backs of better Black originators took hold in the sort of circles that like to argue about music history. That was, of course, just as false. Presley was a remarkable performer with a magnificent voice and an ear for hits. His reliance on songwriters was not unusual for its time, with the idea of performers also being their own primary songwriters only arising by way of the rock bands like the Beatles who emerged in Elvisâ wake.Â

That conception of Elvis has also faded in recent years, in no small part thanks to Baz Luhrmannâs glitzy, campy 2022 biopic. But you could forgive some people for rolling their eyes when they saw the news that the companies that own the rights to Presleyâs music and likeness were suing Anthropic, accusing the AI companyâs chatbots of lifting scraping hundreds of Elvisâ songsÂ  in service of creating AI-generated pseudo-music. How could the owners of this catalog, of all people, object to well-funded operations cranking out simulations?

The lawsuit, filed earlier this month in a San Francisco federal court, accuses Anthropic of engaging in âcopyright infringement at a scale never seen before.â The owners of Elvisâ catalog claim that Anthropic used their songs as training data without permission or payment. They make the point that Presleyâs music isnât unique in this regard, alleging that Anthropic has done pretty much the same thing with all manner of recorded music, in blatant defiance of copyright law. Anthropic software could never have created songs that sound so similar to Presleyâs out of whole cloth, the plaintiffs say, and instead relied on ill-gotten data.

Anthropic software could never have created songs that sound so similar to Presleyâs out of whole cloth, the lawsuit claims, and must have relied instead on ill-gotten data.

âAnthropic has essentially put to the test the adage of whether monkeys and typewriters could, provided enough time, recreate Hamlet,â the lawsuit states. âAnthropic found a workaround. Rather than training its monkeys (the AI models) from first principles, Anthropic found mimicry (i.e. copyright infringement) to be the much easier pursuit.â

The plaintiffs say they tested Claude, asking it to crank out modern updates to Presley hits. The results were âvery close to the originals: same structure, same hooks reused with light rewording, and full sets of verses/choruses/bridges.â

âThatâs edging past âinspired byâ into reproducing the copyrighted song, even when the words are swapped out,â they wrote.Â

The proprietors of Presleyâs material are demanding more than $41 million in damages. Anthropic has denied any wrongdoing.

âWe disagree with the claims and intend to defend this case fully,â Anthropic said in a statement.

Given the AI industryâs hostility toward intellectual property rights, itâs not a stretch to imagine that a major player may have trained its models on some of the most famous songs in recorded music history. Itâs also not hard to imagine the estates of Big Mama Thornton and Arthur Crudup â should any such entities exist â scoffing at those headlines.

But even if we concede that Elvis was elevated to stardom in large part becauseÂ  a racist public was unwilling to buy the same songs from Black artists, and even if we picture the late king as a conniving tyrant extracting unconscionable wealth from an underclass of geniuses who remained unrecognized, the rights holders are right to cry foul. Thatâs because stealing, begging or borrowing material in service of an artistic creation made by real people is enormously different from some corporation doing it to build a better Mechanical Turk.Â

Want more from culture than just the latest trend? The Swell highlights art made to last. Sign up here

Presley was a lot of things: a hick from Tupelo who loved R&B and gospel in equal measure, a white performer of Black music who undoubtedly benefited from the segregated pop charts, a tragic figure whose opioid addiction and poor health led to an early death. But he was also a man, flesh and blood. Anything he could create by virtue of his expelling air through his vocal chords carries more intrinsic value than a billion Claude prompts (which is doubly true true once you know that all of these AI companies operate at a loss).Â  If you need convincing, just look at his 1977 performance of âUnchained Melody.âÂ

The song itself is no great feat. Its creation was a purely commercial affair, written for the soundtrack of a â50s prison movie that no one remembers. A weepy ballad about longing for a lost love while behind bars, it had been recorded many times over by the time an ailing Elvis brought it out during a concert in Grand Rapids, Michigan. Overweight and profusely sweating, the visibly failing superstar belts the Righteous Brothersâ version of the song while seated at the piano, with a band member holding the microphone. Barely two months before his death, Presley gives everything heâs got left to the songâs central question: âAre you still mine?âÂ

Even from this distance, nearly a half-century later, itâs still capable of raising the hair on your arms. That moment, a brief section of a borrowed song from a washed-up and dying man, carries more weight than even the most faithful AI recreation or iteration. That moment is exactly why rights holders have a duty to push back against any attempts for AI companies to pretend their chatbots are included in the old chestnut that âgreat artists steal.â

#6203. The 10 best places to visit in November 2026

November is peak shoulder season: The weather can be unpredictable (but you can get really lucky), crowds are small nearly everywhere and prices are often the lowest they'll be all year for many destinations. It is an ideal time to travel in many ways, if you're willing to risk less-than-ideal weather in some places.

Thanksgiving also takes place in the U.S., and if you are not obligated to visit family, you can enjoy a wonderful four-day vacation without missing any school or work. And for those who love Christmas markets and lights, several spots start their displays at the end of the month.

Here are 10 great destinations to consider for your November getaway.

This stunning desert and mountain region enjoys cooler weather in November that's ideal for hiking in the Atlas Mountains. Meanwhile, the nearby city of Marrakech is as vibrant as ever, with more people coming out in the less-than-scorching temps that linger all summer. Wander the souk, stroll the gorgeous gardens, and visit architectural highlights without breaking a sweat.

Nov. 18 is Morocco's Independence Day, and this year's Marrakech Coffee & Tea Festival will run Nov. 5-7, with more than 400 exhibitors and various workshops and classes. This year's Marrakech International Film Festival runs from Nov. 20–28.

Use points to stay at the Park Hyatt Marrakech, which opened in 2025 (rates from $594 or 25,000 World of Hyatt points per night), or check out the new Riad Beij, in the heart of the Medina (rates from $168 per night). To stay in the Atlas Mountains, you can use Virgin Red points at the luxe Virgin Limited Edition Kasbah Tamadot (rates from $577 or 140,000 Virgin Red points per night).

TPG tip: Marrakech has increased seasonal direct flight access, including a direct flight from Newark on United Airlines, which launched in 2024, and from Atlanta on Delta Air Lines, which debuted at the end of 2025.

Oaxaca's celebration of Dia de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, is legendary, especially in Oaxaca City, where festivities and commemorations take place every year from Oct. 31 to Nov. 2. Expect elaborate costumes, parades, street festivals, cemetery and altar visits, and plenty of music, food and drinks.

After the city festivities, plan to stay at one of the region's design-forward hotels. Boutique hotel 7 Casa Laurel opened in April this year, and Casa Yati opened in Ventanilla on the beach last summer. La Valise Mazunte is a member of Small Luxury Hotels of the World with just six suites and a villa (rates from $400 or 130,000 Hilton Honors points per night).

TPG tip: You can fly directly to Puerto Escondido on United Airlines' Houston-to-Puerto Escondido route, which debuted in 2025. American Airlines launched its direct flights to Puerto Escondido from Dallas-Fort Worth in December 2025.

November is the very beginning of the dry season in Thailand, so it's a good time to beat the winter crowds and score good airfare and hotel pricing. Nov. 24 is Loy Krathong, the beautiful floating lantern festival that lights up the Bangkok waterways on the night of the full moon in the 12th month of the Thai lunar calendar. Various events happen along the Chao Phraya River, in public parks and at cultural landmarks.

The city, which has several new hotels this year, with something for almost every loyalist. Voco Bangkok Surawong opened in January 2026 (rates from 19,000 IHG One Rewards and $137 per night). Canopy by Hilton Bangkok Sukhumvit opened in August 2026 (rates from 45,000 Hilton Honors points and $170 per night). The long-delayed Fairmont Bangkok Sukhumvit finally opened, also in August, with LEED Gold certification, a jasmine-inspired spa, seven food and beverage outlets and 474 rooms (rates from 12,345 ALL Accor points and $278 per night).

TPG tip: Last year, United Airlines launched a new daily flight to Bangkok via Hong Kong from Los Angeles and San Francisco, making it the only domestic airline to offer a daily one-stop flight to Bangkok from the U.S.

Looking for an adventure? November is the last month of the dry season to visit the Amazon, so there's still time to squeeze in an adventure before the end of the year. If colorful birds, jaguars, river dolphins and caiman sightings aren't enough for you, the first-ever Global Citizen music festival in the Amazon, in Belem, is Nov. 1. Global Citizen Festival Amazonia brings Brazilian music stars Anitta, Seu Jorge and Gaby Amarantos and Coldplay's Chris Martin together with Indigenous leaders to amplify climate action campaigns.

TPG tip: Avianca flies to Belem via Bogota, Colombia, from New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), and LATAM flies there through Sao Paulo/Guarulhos International Airport (GRU). Book a room at Ibis Styles Belem Batista Campos ($67 per night) or Grand Mercure Belem do Para ($474 per night). Both are members of Accor Live Limitless.

If you've dreamed of a vacation in St. Barts but thought you couldn't afford it, November may be the best time to visit the gorgeous Caribbean island. You'll enjoy warm weather, beat the winter crowds and enjoy better prices on hotels and flights. And while the French island is known for always having excellent food, November brings even more culinary star power to the isle.

The Saint-Barth Gourmet Festival is Nov. 9-15 and features five chefs from Michelin-starred restaurants, including chef Amaury Bouhours of Restaurant Le Meurice Alain Ducasse and Thibault Sombardier of Les Parisiens.

TPG tip: Getting to St. Barts can be a bit of a journey if you don't have a private jet (ahem), but Cape Air flies twice daily from well-connected St. Thomas.

Looking to the other hemisphere is always a good idea, and in Australia, they're experiencing the other shoulder season: spring. In Western Australia, this means gorgeous wildflowers and some excellent festivals worth traveling for.

Foodies should plan to attend the world-renowned Pair'd Margaret River Region food and wine festival (Nov. 19-22), which brings world-class wine, food and music to the Margaret River region. This year's lineup includes chefs Rodney Scott, Matt Abe, and Mindy Woods, as well as wine writer Erin Larkin.

TPG tip: Hyde Perth opened in March of this year (rates from $239 per night) as the first Hyde hotel in Australia, a brand from Ennismore (also behind the Hoxton, Mama Shelter, Delano, and 25Hours brands) that also has locations in London, Ibiza, Dubai, and Miami.

Some November trips require compromising on the weather, but not in the desert. Palm Springs in November is ideal: With a daytime high of 79 degrees Fahrenheit and a low of 52 degrees Fahrenheit at night, you'll still avoid its peak tourist months, which begin in January. It's also ideal weather to hike in nearby Joshua Tree National Park.

Though most Pride events occur in June, the Palm Springs Pride Festival is a fall event. This year, it runs from Nov. 6–8, with the big parade on the final day. Expect live music, comedy, local vendors and artists, and plenty of food and drink stands in several areas across the downtown area. The Sunset Music and Comedy Festival runs concurrently each night at the Agua Caliente Casino.

There are several new and improved attractions in the desert: The Palm Springs Air Museum recently completed a $2.5 million renovation, and reopened in September, featuring a turbine-inspired façade, new exhibits, and the Ronald M. Auen Learning Center, and DSRT Surf, a manmade surf lagoon that creates the perfect wave, every time, opened this summer in Palm Desert.

TPG tip: The iconic La Quinta Resort & Club celebrates its centennial in 2026, with special events and guest experiences all year long. It's now a part of Hilton's Curio Collection, so you can use and earn rewards points there (rates from 85,000 Hilton Honors points and $329 per night)

Florence in summer can be a hot, crowded mess, but come November, there are fewer crowds and mild weather (although rain is likely). It's also truffle-hunting season in Tuscany.

Film lovers should mark Oct. 31-Nov. 8 for the Festival dei Popoli, Europe's oldest international documentary film festival. And Nov. 29 brings runners from around the world to the Estra Firenze Marathon. Finally, most Christmas markets open around the city in the last week of November.

TPG tip: The city recently welcomed Borgo Pignano Florence, set on a 5-acre estate with 11 historic buildings and 32 rooms and is part of Relais & Chateaux. La Resérve Firenze opened Oct. 15 inside a restored 15th-century palazzo. If you want to use points, W Florence (rates from $507 or 70,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night) opened last year.

Rev your engines for the Las Vegas Grand Prix, when Formula 1 racing comes to Sin City from Nov. 19-21.

Outside the hugely popular event, you can find some hotel and flight deals this November. And there's still plenty to do in November beyond F1. At the Sphere, you can catch the 4D version of "The Wizard of Oz" daily throughout the month, or see Metallica Nov. 4-7, the Eagles Nov. 13-14 and 27-28.

Christmas also starts early in Vegas on Nov. 5, when the 3-acre Cactus Garden at Ethel M Chocolate Factory opens its annual lights show, and Nov. 14 at the Bellagio Conservatory, where they pull out all the stops to create a lit-up floral winter wonderland.

Foodies should also be excited: Taylor Swift favorite and NYC hotspot The Corner Store is opening its second location at the Cosmopolitan of Las Vegas on November 9.

TPG tip: United restored its nonstop service between Cleveland and Las Vegas in September, with five flights a week and budget airline Breeze Airways added a daily route between Las Vegas and John Wayne Airport in Orange County.

November is the tail end of hurricane season so the possibilities of one hitting are slim—and there are great deals to be had, and usually, excellent weather. Miches — located on the northeast coast of the Dominican Republic — has been increasing its number of high-end all-inclusive resorts, and it's typically much less crowded than Punta Cana, which is near the airport.

Hilton loyalists can turn Hilton Honors points into an all-inclusive stay at Zemi Miches Punta Cana All-Inclusive Resort, Hilton's first Curio Collection all-inclusive resort in the country. Hyatt has also planted its all-inclusive flag in Miches with two openings: Dreams Playa Esmeralda Resort & Spa and Secrets Playa Esmeralda Resort & Spa. At Dreams, families and kids are welcome to enjoy the beautiful beaches, pools, and many restaurants and bars, while Secrets is adults-only.

TPG tip: No matter where you stay, let the hotel arrange your transportation from Punta Cana International Airport for ease and affordability. The transportation area at this airport can be overwhelming, and after a long flight, who doesn't want everything made easy?

#6202. Airline Passengers Are Getting Scam Emails With Real Confirmation Numbers—Some Frontier Customers Are Entering Credit Card Details

Frontier Airlines passengers are reporting emails from scammers using their real flight details and confirmation numbers, promising refunds or claiming their bookings haven’t been paid for – and telling them to enter their credit card information to complete purchases or confirm return of funds. Frontier reported an active phishing campaign targeting its customers. That doesn’t tell us where the reservation information came from. A reader sent me a refund email that claims a ticketing error caused duplicate taxes and fees and failed to apply a promotional credit. It promises a full refund after the customer confirms the original payment card. The message even supplies an explanation for why an airline that already charged you supposedly needs your card again: Because the settlement batch for this reservation has already closed, our payment system needs the original payment method confirmed so the refund can be routed back to your card. A closed settlement batch ordinarily means the merchant needs to process a refund rather than void the original transaction. In other words, it’s a made up reason meant to sound plausible. These Emails Are Using Real Reservation Details In a Frontier GoWild! Pass Holders discussion, numerous passengers say they received these emails. Several report that the confirmation numbers matched actual bookings. That includes trips already taken and travel still upcoming. One customer says the supposed refund was about five times what they’d paid. Another reports receiving both versions: a refund offer for a completed trip and a warning that payment hadn’t gone through for an upcoming reservation. A separate Reddit discussion reports the payment problem version, with an email that contained real flight information and confirmation number. Passengers report responding with their credit card numbers. One passenger says they tried several other cards before the site accepted the card originally used to book the flight. And of course a rejection message doesn’t mean the site didn’t collect the card number. Frontier Has Disclosed A Database Incident I wrote in July about a breach affecting 11,482 people. Separately, a security researcher reported that a confirmation number and last name could expose sensitive passenger information through Frontier’s systems. There’s also an October 2 notice from Frontier about a security incident involving its customer care database covering information submitted through its customer care form. They changed the database configuration and are ‘improving monitoring’. Security firm VenariX analyzed leaked samples associated with a group claiming Frontier among its victims. They found booking codes, flight numbers and dates, and evidence pointing to overly broad access permissions on Microsoft customer service portals. This Approach Has Been Used Against Hotel And Cruise Customers I’ve covered hotel scams where the sender knows the guest’s reservation details and uses them to demand payment or card verification. Knowing the hotel, dates and guest’s name makes the message much more persuasive. Norwegian Cruise Line customers reported a similar campaign in October, with messages containing real booking information and demanding payment verification. Norwegian issued its own warning. What To Do If You Received One Frontier won’t email asking you to reconfirm a reservation, re-enter card details, or supply payment information to receive a refund. Check the trip through Frontier directly. Open the app or type the airline’s website address yourself. Use contact information obtained there if something looks wrong. If you entered a card, contact its issuer. Lock it while you report the exposure and arrange a replacement. Include every card you tried, even ones the page said it rejected. Don’t assume leaving before clicking Submit protected the information. Web forms can collect what you type before submission. If you supplied a password, change it through the legitimate site. Change it elsewhere if you reused it. Check the reservation. Make sure the itinerary and contact information remain correct. Frontier’s published instructions say a confirmation code and last name can provide access to changes and cancellations, so changing your frequent flyer password may not close that separate route into a booking. Always check the sender information on an email. That can be spoofed but most scammers don’t go to that level of effort. #6201. Scary mommies are everywhere, but this time with more nuance

In the opening sequence of âOther Mommy,â Ursula (Jessica Chastain) is making lunch for her daughter, Bela (Arabella Olivia Clark), when she asks if the girl would like to âcome into her heart.â

Itâs an odd request, but thatâs because this version of Ursula is not actually Ursula. She is an entity that Bela calls Other Mommy â who looks exactly like her real mother, except that Other Mommy can contort her body into freaky spider-like shapes that scare the hell out of Bela and her stay-at-home father, Russ (Jay Duplass). Also, Other Mommy seems to want to kill or otherwise possess Bela, which is not exactly maternal. Other Mommy promises to nurture Bela, but clearly she represents the worst type of matriarch imaginable: one who is frightening, controlling and dangerous.

The scary mommy has been an archetype in storytelling for as long as stories have existed. Weâve seen it in fairy tales, animated films produced by studios ranging from Disney to Laika (in a way, âOther Mommyâ is just âCoralineâ in live-action form), multiple seasons of Ryan Murphy shows, and, of course, everywhere in the horror genre, from âPsychoâ toÂ  âHereditary.â But the scary mommy is really having a moment this spooky season.

In addition to âOther Mommy,â Hulu is streaming a new series called âPhonyâ that has a similar premise: a kid â this time a teenage boy played by Sam Nivola â believes his mother (Connie Britton) has been replaced by an imposter who looks like the real thing but has sinister intentions. Two other streaming series, âCrystal Lakeâ on Peacock and âCarrieâ on Prime Video, place two of the horror genreâs most famous scary mothers in new contexts. Even real life has given us a scary mommy for the ages: Donna Arthur. The estranged mother of Democratic Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton remained married to Cledith Arthur, who was charged with raping Acton as a child. Donna Arthur later criticized her daughter in a recent attack ad produced by Actonâs Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy. It should be no surprise that there has been intense backlash to that ad. Society and pop culture, not to mention basic decency, have taught us, over and over, to be horrified by a vicious mother.Â Â

Whatâs notable about the latest batch of scary mommy releases is that, for the most part, they offer more nuance in their depictions of motherhood than previous examples of the trope often allow. The moms in these movies and shows are, generally, not entirely demonized even if they sometimes do monstrous things.

(Universal Pictures) Jessica Chastain in âOther Mommyâ

Society and pop culture, not to mention basic decency, have taught us, over and over, to be horrified by a vicious mother.Â Â

âOther Mommyâ comes closest to outright blaming its central maternal figure for all the bad things that happen in her home. (Spoilers ahead.) The powers held by the bad version of Ursula seem to grow the more that Bela feels neglected by real-life Ursula, who works constantly and often gets home late. While she loves her daughter, Ursula ultimately admits that she hadnât initially wanted kids. âIâm sorry for not being the kind of mother that you deserve,â she tells Bela in one of the filmâs key moments.

Director Rob Savage and screenwriter Nathan Elston do not solely blame Ursula for the problems within her family unit. Her husband is a bit of a slacker who gets high in the middle of the day, and the Other Mommy, a shapeshifter, assumes other forms aside from that of Ursula, including Belaâs babysitter. But the movie strongly suggests that Other Mommy would not have shown up at all if Ursula had simply given her daughter more attention, which is more of a tradwife-adjacent take than I expected walking into the theater. Oddly enough, âVerity,â released in theaters a week before âOther Mommy,â has a lot more fun slyly toying with and ultimately negating the idea that a professionally successful mother (Anne Hathawayâs best-selling author Verity Crawford) must secretly resent her children.

Want more from culture than just the latest trend? The Swell highlights art made to last. Sign up here

The three aforementioned scary mommy streaming series go much farther out of their way to depict their respective parents as flawed individuals who do care about their kids. In much of the first season of âPhony,â Connie Brittonâs Ellen comes across as a totally caring and attentive mom to her boy Sonny. His suspicions about her arise after heâs injured in a car accident and becomes convinced that she looks slightly different post-crash. (CGI alters Brittonâs features just enough to make her appear noticeably off.) But she has a very close relationship with him and, even after her supposed heel turn, makes a sincere effort to get him treatment when he begins to struggle emotionally. Her biggest sin is perhaps being too protective of him and overly involved in his life. The only reason she is scary is that Sonny thinks she might be and weâre not sure whether to believe him.

âCrystal Lakeâ and âCarrieâ have the unenviable task of taking scary mommies we already know and helping us understand their motivations in new contexts. âCrystal Lake,â an eight-episode prequel to the original âFriday the 13th,â delves into much â perhaps too much? â more detail about how and why Pamela Voorhees (Linda Cardellini in this version) descended into grief and homicidal madness following the drowning death of her son, Jason, at Camp Crystal Lake. In the 1980 âFriday the 13thâ the identity of the murderer of all those horny young counselors isnât revealed until late in the movie, when we realize Pamela, bitter that the camp has reopened, is the perpetrator. Reminder: the homicidal, goalie-masked version of Jason Voorhees doesnât appear onscreen until âFriday the 13th Part III.â So even though we all think of Jason as the villain of the franchise, one could reasonably argue that the OG baddie is Pamela, the person responsible for most of the kills in the first film and, arguably, for influencing Jason to keep on killing. Jason Voorhees is, according to previous lore, a literal son of a bit*h.

In âCrystal Lake,â the Linda Cardellini version of Pamela Voorhees still slaughters numerous people, but sheâs more than just a one-dimensional crazy bit*h. Sheâs complicated and more capable of selflessness than the first movie takes the time to suggest when itâs not busy knifing poor Kevin Bacon in the chest. The series, by contrast, invites us to feel empathy toward her, or at least acknowledge the suffering she endured in her life even before losing her son.

âCarrie,â developed by Mike Flanagan, the streaming worldâs master of horror, attempts something similar but even more extreme. It moves the familiar story about a bullied, sheltered teenage girl to the present. The plot points that are key in Stephen Kingâs novel and its subsequent adaptations remain. Carrie (Summer H. Howell) is still taunted in the girlsâ locker room after she panics over getting her period, and she still loses it in a way that turns the senior prom into a massive, telekinetically-generated disaster. But all of this happens in a world where social media exists, and some of the mean girls at Carrieâs high school wield it like a bucket of pigâs blood that can be dropped on anyone, at any time. The bullying is both more insidious and more soberingly recognizable.

Whatâs notable about the latest batch of scary mommy releases is that, for the most part, they offer more nuance in their depictions of motherhood than previous examples of the trope often allow.

As in the original, Carrieâs mother, Margaret, is a conservative Christian who wants to shelter her daughter from the outside world as much as possible. But unlike the most well-known version of that character, portrayed by Piper Laurie in Brian DePalmaâs 1976 adaptation, Margaret is not a melodramatic, over-the-top, completely irrational zealot.Â

As portrayed by an excellent Samantha Sloyan, Margaret still punishes Carrie by frequently shoving her into a prayer closet, but sheâs also more grounded in her humanity. Sheâs conservative in a more modern sense: sheâs driven by conspiracy theories, overly protective of her daughter, mistrustful of the government, and deeply Christian even though she does not always act like it. There are also times when Margaretâs opinions are actually correct, as in the first episode when Carrie starts going to public school and must participate in a shooter drill for the first time. Margaret confronts the principal and tells him that Carrie was rattled by the drill and that the whole exercise is traumatizing to students. I never thought I would watch any adaptation of âCarrieâ and say to myself, âYou know, Margaret White makes a good point.â But there I was, saying exactly that.

(Robert Falconer/Prime) Samantha Sloyan as Margaret White in âCarrieâ

We need your help to stay independent.Become a member to support Salonâs progressive journalism. Join today!Not every element in these films and shows works, nor do any of them completely whitewash their charactersâ more deplorable tendencies. But as a collective, they signal that itâs important to look beyond our cultureâs tendency to demonize mothers and women in general. Simply being a good mom or a terrible one (within, you know, non-murderous reason) is not the only thing that defines a woman. Weirdly, this fact is also made clear in the most talked-about film of the moment, âYou Can See Everything,â in which Elizabeth Holmes, who genuinely seems to love her children, also uses them as a shield in the documentary.

In the very first scene, we see and hear her partner, Billy Evans, talking on the phone about his hopes that directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim will show a more relatable, likable side of Holmes and prove she is not a monster. As the camera pans out, we eventually see that Holmes is sitting in the room with him. She is holding a baby, the youngest of her two kids, and gently snuggling with the child.

âLook at this nice mom taking care of an infant; surely sheâs a nice lady who would never defraud anyone or even tell a single, small lie,â the image desperately wants to tell us. But in the end, even being a good mom isnât enough, on its own, to persuade most rational viewers that Elizabeth Holmes is completely innocent of everything of which sheâs been accused. Because just as a scary mommy may have some valid reasons that explain some of her behavior, a seemingly caring mommy can also be kind of scary.
