#6200. United went big on credit cards in 2026. More changes are coming, MileagePlus boss says

Before he ran United Airlines' MileagePlus program, Jarad Fisher was the type of traveler who went "all-in" for elite status.

He read TPG, collected miles and occasionally went on ambitious end-of-year "status runs."

"My wife thought I was nuts," he joked, recalling an epic out-and-back trip to Hawaii 12 years ago — where he never even left the airport — in order to qualify.

Now, Fisher is in charge of United's loyalty program as it undergoes one of its biggest transformations in recent memory.

Ironically, one of his first orders of business was eliminating flight segments as a status metric.

Starting in 2027, "Premier Qualifying Flights" are out. That means United loyalists will no longer be "graded" on how many actual flights they rack up.

Instead, the carrier will rely exclusively on PQPs, which are based on a combination of members' spending, both on flights and on their United credit cards.

United has framed the change as a way to make qualifying for status simpler — though it could make it more challenging for some United flyers.

It will also end the need for eleventh-hour "segment runs" that once had frequent flyers (like Fisher) crisscrossing the country in December to rack up enough elite-qualifying flights.

"That was an old relic," he said, speaking about United's recent changes in an exclusive interview with TPG.

"You're taking seats away from people who actually want to get to a certain destination. It's not great for the environment. It's not a great use of time," he explained. "We thought it made more sense for them to have one, consistent metric."

That's not the only change United has made to MileagePlus in 2026.

Earlier this year, the carrier upended several of its loyalty policies, heavily tilting its program toward members who carry one of its credit cards.

Together, these moves were among the most aggressive any U.S. airline has made to nudge flyers toward its cobranded credit cards.

It's part of a larger strategy Fisher often sums up with this mantra:

"It's good to fly United, it's great to be a MileagePlus member," he said. "But the best way to engage with us is to be a MileagePlus member and actually have one of our cards."

Speaking publicly this year, United's chief commercial officer, Andrew Nocella, has hinted that United's loyalty shakeup isn't done.

It appears some changes may have to wait until the airline can re-negotiate its credit card deal with banking partner Chase.

"While we continue to work under a long-term cobrand contract," Nocella said on an earnings call in April, "We're making changes to what we can control today."

United's current Chase deal is set to run through 2029, according to past TPG reporting.

For now, the carrier has significantly upped the incentives for customers to carry one of its cards in the first place: Over the past year, United's cobranded credit card holders have clearly gained the upper hand in its program.

Fisher said the airline plans to continue adapting the program in ways "that will be more consistent" with that ethos in the coming years.

"And so I think as a function of that, we're looking at not only the core loyalty program, we're looking at our partnerships," he said. "And we're trying to make it so that we will continue to be — not just the best airline loyalty program — but we're really aspiring to be the best loyalty program in the world."

What future changes could MileagePlus members ultimately see when they go to redeem miles, earn on their Lyft rides or enter a United Club?

And Fisher will play a big part in those decisions, after taking the helm of MileagePlus this year with an intriguing pedigree.

Seven years ago, he was heavily involved in the launch of Apple Card.

Before that, he spent time at top rival Delta Air Lines, helping turbocharge its partnership with American Express — which today is the industry's most lucrative tie-up, set to bring Delta $9 billion this year.

That resume has Fisher thinking beyond earn rates and status benchmarks as he looks to build on changes that gave United flyers plenty to digest in 2026.

"We're really trying to think about what will truly help us break away from the pack," he said of the carrier's future plans.

Of course, that's easier said than done in the airline world.

Flight delays are inevitable. Loyal flyers can grow frustrated when they go to book a redemption and are shocked by how many miles they'll need.

Not to mention, complimentary status upgrades don't clear as often as they used to, as first-class seats are increasingly filled by customers who actually paid for their tickets. By the way, balancing paid first-class seats with those long upgrade queues is a dilemma Fisher said the airline is "consistently looking at."

"More folks are paying for [premium seats], which of course is putting pressure on the system," he acknowledged.

But for an airline that has made plenty of waves in recent years — from its on-board internet to its international routes — it's safe to say United won't shy away from trying new things on the loyalty front, either.

And it's a likely bet that customers who carry its credit cards will benefit most.

"If you think about the amount of time people spend with us, and on board our aircraft, we want them to feel known. We want them to feel recognized," he said. "You will continue to see us become even more focused and deliberate about that approach."

By taking advantage of low-cost domestic award tickets (such as flying from Houston to Orlando for as little as 3,500 miles), you can stretch the miles you earn with your credit cards to help you plan your upcoming trips.

Or, go big and start saving miles toward a fancy United Polaris business-class flight.

#6196. Patrick Stewart, “Star Trek” and “X-Men” star, dies at 86

English actor Patrick Stewart, who became world-famous as the star of “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and the “X-Men” movies, died on Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles. He was 86. Kelly Bush Novak, his longtime spokesperson, announced that he died from Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia, which is marked by features of Parkinson’s disease.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” Bush Novak wrote. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

Stewart’s distinctive baritone voice and striking bald head made him one of the most familiar actors to American audiences, but until the late 1980s, he was virtually unknown in the U.S. Before his casting as Capt. Jean-Luc Picard on “Star Trek: The Next Generation,” he had spent decades as a classical theater performer in Britain, especially in the works of Shakespeare. He joined the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966, where he met fellow actor Ian McKellen, who would become a longtime friend and collaborator.

Over the course of his career, he received four Emmy nominations for his television work, as well as two Laurence Olivier Awards and a Tony nomination for his role in “Macbeth.” In 1996, he won a Grammy for best spoken word album for children for “Prokofiev: Peter and the Wolf.” He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010.

We need your help to stay independent.Become a member to support Salon’s progressive journalism. Join today!

Later in his career, Stewart reprised his role as Picard in various “Star Trek” films and a recent spinoff series. His role as professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” film series from 2000 to 2017 helped propel his career to new heights and usher in a new era of superhero films. He is set to appear as Xavier in “Avengers: Doomsday,” which will be his final on-screen film appearance.

“I think I’ve been in denial about my life for a very long time,” Stewart told The Guardian in 2023. “I never really took on board how successful I had become. Even today I sometimes think, ‘You’re a lucky son of a b**ch, Patrick,’ when something unexpected or good happens to me.”

Stewart was born on July 13, 1940, in Mirfield, England, a small town in West Yorkshire. He is survived by his wife Sunny Ozell, an American singer, whom he married in 2013; his son, Daniel, also an actor; and his daughter, Sophie.

Visit Norway turned a presidential insult into one of its most-viewed pieces of content this year. After President Donald Trump called Norway a "shit house country" at a Michigan rally following the Nobel committee's decision not to award him a peace prize, the destination marketing organization tweaked an existing web page about scenic public toilets along Norway's tourist routes, adding that the country makes restrooms "great again!" Page views ran more than 540 times higher than the previous week, topping 80,000 views from more than 170 countries since Monday, with roughly 4,000 views an hour as of Friday morning. Christine Baglo, editor-in-chief for Visitnorway.com, told Skift that about 90% of the traffic was organic and that the team spent less than $10,000 on sponsored posts on Facebook and Instagram, with a Times Square ad on the toilet theme planned for Saturday. Baglo credits a seven-person "always-on" team that works more like an editorial desk than a campaign-driven marketing arm. Americans accounted for about a quarter of page visitors, in a year when Norway posted a record 14.2 million foreign guest nights, up 14% from 2024.

#6194. Hearing probes charges of FBI agents lying to Congress

A federal magistrate allowed an unusual, dayslong examination this week of the effort to charge two former FBI officials with lying to Congress amid concerns about partisan prosecution ahead of the coming election.

The extended preliminary hearing delved into the details of the Justice Department’s case and focused on errors in the complaints against the pair, involvement by FBI Director Kash Patel in targeting the two and the case’s testifying FBI agent’s own misgivings about the political nature of the charges. After the hearing, which stretched across three days and ended Thursday, Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia did not immediately act and said he would issue a written ruling Monday on whether the case could move forward.

The complaint alleged Nicole Floris and Bradley Benavides lied to Congress on two occasions in 2023 about their knowledge of investigations into President Joe Biden’s son Hunter Biden and a now-infamous laptop.

Floris’ attorney Mary Dorman urged the judge to address the “elephant in the room here.”

“The evidence is mounting that this prosecution is about some political football and not the law or the facts in this case,” Dorman said.

Usually the federal government avoids such hearings by proceeding with an indictment instead of a complaint. Regardless of the result of this week’s hearing, the government would need to seek an indictment to proceed with the case. Faruqui noted that there have been less than a half-dozen such hearings in the D.C. District Court in the last decade.

Under federal law, the government has 30 days from filing the complaint to secure an indictment. If the government does not secure an indictment, the case could be dismissed.

The case turns on what the pair told the House Judiciary Committee as it investigated what the FBI did in its probes of Hunter Biden in the lead-up to the 2020 election. The complaint alleges the pair misled the committee about a laptop left at a Delaware computer repair shop, as well as the involvement of the Foreign Influence Task Force in the FBI’s response to stories about the laptop ahead of the election.

Across the three-day hearing, Ron Safer, an attorney for Benavides, criticized the “Kafkaesque” nature of the case against his client. Defense attorneys elicited testimony about multiple errors in the complaint, as well as oddities such as the defendants accused of lying about their knowledge in August 2020 of a Senate report not released until September 2020.

FBI Agent Bryan Witt testified that agents never interviewed committee staff, and later discovered that the staff who responded to written questions about the alleged lies by Benavides and Floris were not necessarily present for all the interviews with them.

Witt also said he did not understand before this week that committees had partisan staff, and that only House Judiciary Committee GOP Majority Counsel Steve Castor responded to questions.

Only after investigators realized errors in the initial complaint did they conduct an interview with Castor, which Witt said occurred on Monday before the start of the sprawling hearing.

The defense also obtained a recording of an interview between Witt and investigators where they acknowledged a “f—up” in the complaint that they intended to correct.

Government attorneys objected to the scope of the hearing, arguing that the defendants should not be allowed to delve into possible political reasons for the case.

James Kirkpatrick, attorney for the Justice Department, argued that the pair took steps to downplay their knowledge of the investigations into Hunter Biden and that their attorneys are now trying to disguise those as innocent mistakes.

“Fool me two, three, four, five times — it is looking like less of a mistake,” Kirkpatrick said.

The DOJ announced the charges against Floris and Benavides on Friday, and they initially charged the pair with lying to Congress. The government attempted to file a superseding complaint against the pair Tuesday, replacing the initial charges with charges of false statements to Congress and adding obstruction or attempted obstruction of a congressional proceeding.

However, the DOJ filed that complaint without the signature of an attorney or approval of a magistrate judge, and Faruqui ordered that complaint struck from the case record.

Faruqui said he would not act as a “notary” for the federal government, and said that it was a fundamental constitutional principle that the government could not file criminal charges without a judicial signoff.

“Why today, on this one case, have you changed the entire history of how you charge cases?” Faruqui said. “It seems like you are afraid of me finding probable cause.”

Faruqui also criticized the government’s behavior more broadly in the case, saying the late-night unsigned complaint, the decision not to seek an indictment yet and the attempt to proceed with the charges without making a showing to a judge was making the case “a sideshow on top of a sideshow” that gave credence to the defense’s arguments about its partisan nature.

“Everything you are doing is making me more and more concerned there is something to that,” Faruqui said.

The pair worked for the FBI’s now-shuttered Foreign Influence Task Force, and their work drew Trump’s ire in part due to their alleged effort to tamp down on an intelligence report that suggested the Chinese government intended to interfere in the 2020 election on behalf of President Biden.

During a July 2026 primetime speech, Trump mentioned their work and called for them to be prosecuted. Witt testified in court this week that he received an assignment from Patel the next day to investigate Floris, Benavides and other members of the Foreign Influence Task Force.

Witt said he provided weekly updates to Patel and other senior leaders in the FBI, which was unusual. He also said he was concerned about the political nature of the case when he received the assignment.

While he said he had not called it a witch hunt, Witt said “people generally viewed it as that around the office.”

#6193. Democrats are the unwitting beneficiaries of Trump’s immigration policies

This article was originally published on The Conversation.

In a 2025 investigation, The New York Times reported that officials in President Joe Bidenâs administration, in the wake of Bidenâs 2020 election win, had viewed rising immigration as âa distractionâ best ignored so that the administration could concentrate political resources on more important economic matters.

Scott Shuchart, a Biden appointee who joined the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency in 2022, told the newspaper that the White House was âwishing the problem would go away so that they could focus on the things they cared about.â

But two years after Donald Trump leveraged voter dissatisfaction with the Biden administrationâs management of the U.S. southern border to win the 2024 election and enforce his immigration crackdown, the issue has suddenly become a secondary matter.

Amid the rising U.S. cost of living, a destabilizing war in Iran and a disrupted system of global commerce, the now-quiet border has relieved Democrats of their thorniest issue just in time for midterm elections.

For the past three decades, the Democratic Party and its candidates have struggled to develop and pass new immigration policies and communicate related political messages.

Bipartisan attempts at comprehensive immigration reform died on Capitol Hill in 2006, 2007 and 2013. Since then, a majority of Americans has trusted Republicans more with governing the issue. That has given the GOP an advantage when the salience of immigration policy has risen due to border crises and related high-profile events, even if that edge has recently narrowed.

In a February 2024 poll, 28% of U.S. respondents told Gallup that immigration was the countryâs most important problem â matching the largest share since tracking began in 1981. By May 2026, that figure was 8%, a staggering drop in such a short period.

In a different poll by The Economist/YouGov, the share of U.S. registered voters who identified immigration as the countryâs most important issue fell from 14% in October 2024 to 5% in September 2026.

Erik Iverson, a Republican Senate campaign pollster, recently told Axios that declining border crossings have reduced the urgency of immigration, depriving Republicans of an issue that previously energized voters and offered conservatives an advantage.

âYou become a victim of your own success,â he said.

But this success is dubious. President Trumpâs approval ratings on immigration are underwater.

In the RealClear Polling average from September to October 2026, his net approval was at negative 10.8%. In a recent Fox News poll, most Americans believe the Trump administration has âgone too farâ in enforcing immigration laws, including 60% of independents.

Despite Republicansâ insistence that the mass removal of undocumented immigrants and a halt to new migrants would raise wages and make housing more accessible, Americans are experiencing high inflation rates, slow gross domestic product growth and sour consumer sentiment.

Ominously for the White House, Trumpâs negative 10.8% net approval score on immigration is actually among his best. On inflation, the economy and foreign policy, his net approval rating is at negative 42.8%, negative 31.7% and negative 27.8%, respectively.

These dynamics bode well for Democratsâ midterm election prospects.

Republicans are now less concerned about immigration â what has been their greatest source of political energy and the leftâs greatest political liability â as both partiesâ voters are focused on other matters.

Despite the White Houseâs aggressive and frequently violent pursuit of undocumented immigrants, its proposal to end birthright citizenship, and its near closure of U.S. borders, even Democrats are no more likely to identify immigration as the countryâs top issue today than they were previously.

According to The Economist/YouGov polling cited earlier, 1% of Democrats named immigration as their top issue in September 2026. In October 2024, 3% said the same.

Remarkably, without Democratsâ endorsement of a single new immigration policy idea, independents now express greater trust in Democrats than Republicans on immigration, 41% to 27%, according to a September 2026 Marist survey.

Democratsâ sudden edge arises after a decade of trialing different approaches to counter the nativism and popular discomfort that Trump has harnessed.

Before Trumpâs 2016 election victory and immediately thereafter, Democratic leaders sought to ameliorate the image of foreigners in the U.S., by highlighting that immigrants start more businesses, file more patents and commit fewer crimes than native-born U.S. citizens on average.

During this period, Democrats commonly cited immigrantsâ acute vulnerability and their willingness and ability to fill critical low-skilled and high-skilled labor gaps. But the praise and pity produced resentment among many Americans who did not want an admissions system that elevated foreigners to a higher pedestal.

Toward the end of the first Trump administration, Democrats began citing the immense macroeconomic and fiscal benefits driven by immigrantsâ long-term settlement in the U.S.

Economists attribute to immigrants the bulk of U.S. population growth from 1990 to 2015. And economists have shown that continued immigration mitigates inflation and extends the solvency of Social Security and Medicare funds. Immigration also provides workers for industries like construction, agriculture, food production and healthcare.

However, the benefits of these relationships for average voters tend to be diffuse and realized in the medium-to-long run. That makes them hard to recognize.

After the global pandemic halted most human mobility in 2020, the Biden administration sought to avoid the immigration issue altogether. Itâs a strategy that Democrats have now carried over while the dynamics of being out of power still permit doing so.

Should Democrats win majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives in 2026, the issue of immigration is highly unlikely to be resolved. As a matter of constitutional oversight, Democrats plan to commence investigations into the Trump administrationâs abusive immigration enforcement tactics, questionable case adjudication and alleged corruption.

It will be almost impossible to pass meaningful immigration legislation in such an environment.

The Biden-era approach was a pivotal electoral liability in 2024. And the Obama administrationâs series of immigration executive actions instigated a tennis match of such orders between subsequent administrations ever since.

Democrats will soon feel some pressure to develop bipartisan approaches to immigration governance that ensure order at U.S. borders and a strategy for immigrant selection and integration that is designed with the national interest in mind.

Anything less, and the dysfunctional system â with its massive political risks â will return.ï»¿

Justin Gest, Professor of Policy and Government, George Mason University; Institute for Humane Studies

A few years ago, on a damp evening in late March in London, I learned the hard way that countries don’t all change their clocks for daylight saving time simultaneously. After ordering a glass of white wine at a cozy bar in Bermondsey, I mindlessly scrolled on my phone while the bartenders chatted about the clocks jumping forward that coming Sunday. I nearly spit out my Chablis.

Back home in New York City, I had already skipped ahead one hour on the second Sunday in March. As I frantically Googled, I learned that in the United Kingdom, the clocks go forward one hour on the last Sunday in March (and back one hour on the last Sunday in October).

Don’t be like me and lose two hours of sleep in one month. When you travel, remember the following to avoid daylight saving time-related snafus and other time zone mistakes — and if you're in the U.S., most states fell back one hour on Sunday, Nov. 1.

The U.K. isn’t the only country that changes its clocks on a different weekend than we do in the U.S. For example, most European countries follow the same calendar as the U.K., moving clocks forward one hour on the last Sunday in March and back one hour on the last Sunday in October.

Generally, when traveling in the spring and fall, it’s always best to check when the country you’re going to falls forward or backward — and also whether that country observes daylight saving time at all. In fact, according to the Pew Research Center, about 66% of the world doesn’t.

Though daylight saving time is commonly observed in North America and Europe, many non-European Union countries in Europe — including Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Georgia, Iceland, Russia and Turkey — stay on standard time year-round.

In 2023, Egypt became the only country in Africa to change its clocks when it reintroduced daylight saving time for the first time in seven years. Now, each year, its clocks move forward one hour on the last Friday in April and backward one hour on the last Thursday in October.

It’s also worth double-checking these things even if you're traveling within the U.S. In 48 states, daylight saving time runs from the second Sunday in March to the first Sunday in November. Arizona and Hawaii are the outliers that stay on standard time year-round. While it’s less of an issue on an island like Hawaii, Arizona shares enough borders with other states that do observe daylight saving time that it can be problematic.

“Always double-check timing when flying in/out and on road trips through the state,” Becky Blaine, TPG’s newsletter managing editor and former Arizona resident, said. Otherwise, you can risk missing a flight or a reservation.

To keep it simple, remember that Arizona is in the Pacific Daylight Time zone from mid-March to early November, and the rest of the year it’s in the same time zone as other states in Mountain Standard Time.

It’s a similar situation in Canada. Generally, Canada follows the same daylight saving schedule as the U.S., but most of Saskatchewan, the Yukon and some parts of Quebec and British Columbia stay on standard time year-round.

In Australia, daylight saving time starts the first Sunday in October and ends the first Sunday in April in the Australian Capital Territory, New South Wales, South Australia, Tasmania and Victoria; meanwhile, the Northern Territory, Queensland and Western Australia don’t observe it.

Outside of daylight saving time changes, there are some general time zone issues to be aware of while traveling.

In countries as large as the U.S., Canada and Australia, it’s easy to see why there are so many time zones. But Eric Rosen, TPG’s director of travel content, also pointed out that the airport in the Maldives is in a different time zone than some resorts in the tiny island nation.

Technically, the Maldives has only one official time zone: Maldives Time, which is five hours ahead of Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). However, some of the archipelago's private island resorts add an hour to Maldives Time to maximize their guests' evening light.

For example, The St. Regis Maldives Vommuli Resort sets its clock one hour ahead of the official clock to what it calls "Island Time," but also provides guests with butlers who coordinate transfers to and from the airport so nobody accidentally misses a flight.

Before you go to the Maldives, be sure to check if your resort also does this.

Due to its geographic location, the Canadian island of Newfoundland is 90 minutes ahead of Eastern Time instead of just 60 minutes ahead, as in the rest of Atlantic Canada. On a July trip, Nick Ewen, TPG’s editor-in-chief, found this challenging for calendar purposes.

While traveling in Newfoundland, he received an Outlook invitation to a 7:30 p.m. dinner meeting the following week and accepted it without much thought. However, the actual dinner back home in the U.S. started at 6 p.m. — a detail he completely missed until the reminder popped up 15 minutes before. At that point, he realized he would be late.

Other places offset from UTC by 30 minutes include India, Sri Lanka, Afghanistan, Iran and some states in Australia. Want to be confused even more? Nepal's time zone is offset by 45 minutes due to its geography.

Even when not dealing with half-hour time zones, it can be easy to make similar mistakes when adding events back home to your digital calendar while traveling in a different time zone.

"Last year, I brought my middle son to a birthday party. We were running a few minutes late, but when we arrived, it seemed like the party was almost over," Tarah Chieffi, a senior writer at TPG, said. "While the kids were eating cake, I double-checked my calendar to make sure we had gotten the time right, and it seemed like we had. But then I went to check the invitation, and we had, in fact, arrived one hour late."

Her mistake? When she entered the party into her calendar while traveling, her calendar app defaulted to the time zone she was in and showed her the incorrect time back home.

"Now, I always toggle the time zone to my home time zone if I enter appointments into my calendar while I'm traveling," she said.

"Outlook lets you have up to three time zones showing on the calendar," Madison Blancaflor, a managing editor at TPG, said.

Go to "Settings," then "Calendar," then "Time zones." Then, check the box for "Show second time zone in Day and Week view" underneath your default time zone. If you need a third one, you can also check that box.

It's also important to remember that it's possible to quickly encounter multiple time zones on cruises — especially on transoceanic cruises, where you'll change time zones daily or almost daily. And if you're on a cruise traversing the Pacific Ocean, you could lose an entire day if you cross the international date line, like Clint Henderson, TPG's principal spokesperson, did when he sailed from Seward, Alaska, to Tokyo last year.

Related: I made a rookie travel mistake that nearly cost me $4,000 — here's how I fixed it

Even on shorter cruises, check if you'll have to change time zones. When I was on a five-day Alaska cruise earlier this summer, I changed time zones twice as we moved in and out of Alaska Daylight Time on a round-trip sailing from Vancouver (which was one hour ahead, on Pacific Daylight Time).

Cabin stewards usually leave notes on your bed at turndown to remind you of upcoming time changes. Clint said he had to set his clocks back between one and two hours each night on his cruise. But you can't always rely on your cellphone to display the correct time when it’s in airplane mode and using satellite-based internet. Bring an analog watch or an alarm clock to ground you if you're unsure whether your device will update properly.

However, some cruise ships may ignore time changes at select ports. "I've had that happen on Royal Caribbean ships in the Caribbean, for example, to avoid the ship time changing three days in a row," said Christine Gallipeau, a senior editor on TPG's points and loyalty team. "So if you're doing shore excursions, make sure you know what time the ship is following, as it may not necessarily match the local time."

Related: Can a cruise help with jet lag? The answer might surprise you

When traveling, don’t assume every country or state follows the same daylight-saving-time rules and schedules as where you live, and be mindful of time zone anomalies. Losing or gaining an unexpected hour can lead to lost sleep, arriving late to an event and, worst of all, missed flights.

#6191. After Trump’s looming midterm loss, how ugly will it get?

Happy Halloween â and welcome back to the future.

My neighbor showed me his kidsâ Halloween costumes today; a vampire, a zombie and a clown. âTheyâre going as Stephen Miller, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Pete Hegseth,â he told me.

Laugh or cry, weâll be here all week. Try the veal.

I wonder what a Todd Blanche outfit looks like? The image of Frankensteinâs monster, for some reason, sticks in my mind.

Itâs time to sit back, relax and enjoy the elections â a midterm extravaganza featuring two flailing political parties jockeying for supremacy in a nation full of educated young adults working as cabbies and delivery drivers who aspire to be âinfluencersâ while their parents wonder how in the name of God theyâll be able to afford retirement.Â

To be able to handle that good news, maybe you can channel your inner Hunter S. Thompson, without resorting to dropping a couple of hits of acid or snorting lines of cocaine in Studio 54 while Donald Trump ogles the dancers in tight pants, female and male alike.

Then again, you might need a tall glass of Wild Turkey 101 on ice (Thompsonâs favorite) when you hear Trump say that Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola should be prosecuted because there are two Dan Sullivans running for office in Alaska, or declares that the country âwould be goneâ if he hadnât won the presidency two years ago.Â

Everything old is new again. At any rate, weâve seen this carnival roadshow before, though it seems a bit different this time. Trump has less energy as he flails about dancing to the Village People. He plays before smaller crowds every week. He seems to be on stage only to get laughs. âAm I right?â he whispered hoarsely with a big grin last Saturday night in Georgia, after mocking Democrats one more time. He apologized for his raspy voice and kept going with the low-energy insult comedy. His small crowd chortled and ate it up.

In the last week on the campaign trail, Trump has appeared at a livestock arena, a school gymnasium, a hockey rink and, on Thursday in Rock Hill, South Carolina, at a venue that holds just 1,200 people. He doesnât seem to care. Heâs on autopilot. The war in Iran? Heâs got nothing. The war in Ukraine? Nothing. Corruption, immigration, AI (sorry, never âSIâ), the economy and any other real-world issue? Heâs either got nothing, or itâs all nonsense weâve heard before: The Democrats, Joe and Kamala, and marauding bands of violent dark-skinned immigrants and communists are to blame. As for the economy, he tells us heâs doing great and making billions. We should all be happy.Â

In the last week on the campaign trail, Trump has appeared at a livestock arena, a school gymnasium, a hockey rink and, on Thursday in Rock Hill, South Carolina, at a venue that holds just 1,200 people. He doesnât seem to care. Heâs on autopilot.

Forget it. Heâs done with campaigning, quite literally. The White House confirmed Thursday that two campaign stops planned for Kansas and Iowa this weekend have been canceled. What happens next is what we need to watch. It must be the season of the witch. Or as Thompson himself told us, âWhen the going gets weird, the weird turn pro.â

Thompson was covering Richard Nixon when he penned that epigram, but it is equally applicable to covering the surreal spectacle of vampires, zombies, ghouls and degenerates awkwardly shuffling across the MAGA landscape. It certainly should be a factor in understanding what Trump does on Nov. 4 and afterward. Ask anyone, Republican or Democrat, and theyâll all say the same thing: Whatever happens is likely to be simultaneously annoying and frightening.Â

Trump has already filed suit against Alaskaâs election results, even though the election has yet to occur. In Missouri, the GOP lost three times trying to gerrymander districts in a case that went to the Supreme Court, all in hopes of gaining one seat in the House. That move may have backfired big time. Not only did Republicans fail to gain a guaranteed seat, but in Missouriâs Second District Democrat Fred Wellman is poised to pull off a miracle against Republican incumbent Rep. Ann Wagner (albeit with little support from party leaders in D.C.). Trump appears ready to file suit there as well. Some insiders say he might try to sue in every state where an incumbent Republican loses. Check your favorite gambling app for the over/under on that.

At the same time, thereâs a constant susurrus from Trump about âvoter fraudâ that surfaces wherever his candidates look to be failing. There are rumors of National Guard and ICE officers roaming the countryside on Election Day hunting and bagging anyone with a good tan who speaks something other than English. Long voting lines and randomly closed precincts are a given. A general feeling of chaos among the electorate, whipped into a frenzy by the president himself, is expected. Thereâs still stray talk about invoking the Insurrection Act and declaring martial law. Whatâs the over/under on that move?Â

Iâm actually tired of the talk. We all know Trump will not go gentle into that good night. If the GOP loses control of Congress, his administration will likely see more people convicted and jailed than Nixonâs during the Watergate weirdness that made Thompson âturn pro.â

On the other side of the aisle, the aging Democratic leadership looks as lost and confused as Trump. Some in the party want to remain silent, cross their fingers and hope for the best, fearful of Democratic infighting and hopeful that Trump is really on his last legs. Others want to defeat Trump then turn on the âestablishmentâ Democrats.

I donât want to listen to this from either side. After covering Trump for 10 years, he reminds me of my children during their pre-pubescence, always cocksure, arrogant and wrong. My children grew up to be adults. Trump never has. The same can be said for some of the more argumentative Democrats.

The Democrats, as is often the case, lack focus and leadership at the national level. The headless horsemen run amok, trying to scream âThe Trumps are coming!â while fighting with each other, even before they hold any power. It does not exactly inspire confidence. Younger voters find each party equally repellent, and for good reason. If Democrats win a majority in the House, as nearly everyone expects, and the Senate, as a growing number of Democrats have the audacity to hope, how long will it be before they slice each otherâs throats over their marginal political differences while what remains of the GOP looks on with glee?Â

Still, the Republican Party at this point looks like a horde of zombies led by Art the Clown. To extend the horror-movie metaphors even further, Trump is such a crude cartoon character that if he isnât the Terrifier then maybe heâs Pinhead from âHellraiser.âÂ

For lazy reporters, or those whoâve never covered another president, Trump makes the job easy. He doesnât hold news conferences. He has no policies. There are no long meetings with press secretaries. Come to think of it, thereâs no press secretary.

But our president can still generate media attention, even as his crowds continue to diminish. He may soon be reduced to appearing before middle school PTA meetings across the South, but heâll still be on TV. As one of the younger members of the White House Correspondentsâ Association recently said, in all earnestness, âWeâll miss him when heâs gone.â Some reporters even find his insults of the press amusing. I donât agree, but I admit that my experience is limited to the Ronald Reagan presidency â and every one since then.Â

Some of us were here before Trump, and will still be here when heâs gone. For lazy reporters, or those whoâve never covered another president, Trump makes the job easy. He doesnât hold real news conferences. He has no policies. We donât have directives to read or position papers to study. There are no long meetings with press secretaries. Come to think of it, thereâs no press secretary. Covering Trump is easier than covering a traffic accident, and twice as gory. Thatâs how he governs.Â

Itâs obvious to even the most casual political observer that Trumpâs campaign tactics are the signs of a desperate man with dwindling influence. After he lost control of Congress in the 2018 midterms, he purged his staff and yanked press passes from reporters. Some senior officials quit. Expect a repeat of all that, beginning next week. Only now most of my colleagues in the press pool will wag their tails and bark a bit before waiting for a presidential treat.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, unless he gets appointed as a senator from Tennessee, is most assuredly a goner. Even the Republicans in Congress dislike him, and Trump, who never accepts responsibility for anything, still needs a scapegoat for the war in Iran â the one he has claimed is over on more than a dozen occasions.Â

While Speaker of the House Mike Johnson says heâll do his job and seat every Democrat who wins in the midterms, Trump is eagerly searching for ways to stop that from happening. Some believe heâll try to stage another insurrection, while others believe heâll let government funding run out and spend the rest of his presidency presiding over a government shutdown, in effect dissolving Congress.

Whatever he does wonât work. His recent public appearances add up to a tell on how badly he will fail. High school basketball teams in Kentucky are filling gymnasiums better than this president.

White House pool reports from Trumpâs campaign stops no longer mention the venue capacity or attendance, but the empty seats in those modest arenas and his listless rhetoric, combined with ever-louder outbursts from protesters, are evidence enough that this guy isnât what he once was.

While Speaker of the House Mike Johnson says heâll do his job and seat every Democrat who wins in the midterms, Trump is eagerly searching for ways to stop that from happening.

Whether heâs complimenting another manâs (or womanâs) behind, berating reporters or making deals with Russia while screwing over former allies, his raging incompetence is still center stage at these increasingly feeble campaign events. We still canât look away.Â

I recently watched a documentary about the fall of the Bronze Age civilizations. It was an era of climate change, supply chain collapse, earthquakes, famine, disease, migration, drought and armed incursions and invasions. Stop me if youâve heard any of that before.

What worries one of the archaeologists in the documentary and causes him to lose sleep is how similar our world is to that one.

We are ripe for catastrophe, and poor leadership exacerbates the problems we currently face. âHow resilient will we be? How will we get back up?â the documentary asks. Those are excellent questions to ask now.

After the midterm elections are settled, we may learn some answers. If Hunter S. Thompson was right, maybe thereâs some hope. After all, Iâve never seen politics any weirder than this.Â

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only by Amanda Marcotte, also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

Trump looks done, in ways Iâve never seen him look done before. Iâve seen him stumble, fall and constantly deflect reality. Heâs always managed to survive those stumbles. Not now. The cancellations, his delusional ramblings, his anger and increasing desperation, the smaller crowds, the raspy voice combined with the collective shoulder-shrug I see from even his closest allies â countered by the quiet optimism of the Democrats and their muted sniping at each other â have created a stew of weirdness that Thompson might find eclipses the waning days of the Nixon administration.

All this leaves us pondering two questions: How far will Trump go to challenge the outcome of the midterms, and what will the Democrats do with power if they get it?Â

Trumpâs waning influence may ultimately be the deciding factor in both questions.

If Iâm wrong, Iâll admit it. But if the Democrats win both houses of Congress, I donât think Trump will do much of anything after the midterms. He will make lots of threats. But he has to deal with the zombies in his administration and all the fires they have started: wars, battles with immigrants, court cases, affordability issues, the economy, personal corruption, racism, misogyny, the destruction of healthcare and education and the existential problems brought about by ignoring climate change. Thatâs too much for almost any leader, and way above his level. For the next two years, weâre likely to see Trump in the White House on Tuesdays and Wednesdays and in Bedminster or Mar-a-Lago the rest of the week, somewhere on the back nine.Â

Meanwhile, we teeter on the brink, and any one of those issues I just mentioned could push us over the edge. During the Bronze Age, a natural climate disaster led to the decline of the culture. Today we can do that ourselves.Â

The week ahead will be challenging week, no matter what happens. I need to channel my inner Morgan Freeman, from the film âSe7enâ: âErnest Hemingway once wrote, âThe world is a fine place and worth fighting for.â I agree with the second part.â

Hyatt has filed an opposition with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office's Trademark Trial and Appeal Board to block Hilton from registering Select by Hilton, citing its own Hyatt Select registered trademark and two pending applications. Hyatt then filed a motion, with Hilton's consent, to suspend the case while the two sides negotiate, and spokespeople for both companies told Skift they "mutually agreed to suspend the action as we continue working toward an agreeable resolution." The two brands use the same word for different purposes: Hilton launched Select by Hilton in March 2026 as a "brand of brands" that brings established chains such as Yotel into its loyalty and distribution systems without acquiring them, while Hyatt introduced Hyatt Select in February 2025 as an upper-midscale conversion brand aimed at smaller markets. Trademark lawyer Josh Gerben, speaking from experience with similar cases rather than knowledge of the talks, said an opposition only decides federal registration rights, that litigation could cost $200,000 to $500,000 or more, and that Hyatt may be seeking something narrower than a ban on the word — such as limits on how prominently Hilton uses it. Gerben also noted the parties had about five months to resolve the matter and didn't, which he said suggests Hyatt has more than a passing concern.

#6189. I can’t stop making this cabbage

I have a very specific fantasy about the restaurant I would open, should someone ever hand me a set of keys and an unlimited supply of funds and optimism. It would be a little neighborhood bistro, the sort of place where the wine comes in mismatched stemless glasses thrifted from estate sales. The menus would be illustrated by hand, which sounds charming until youâve spent an entire afternoon trying to get the shading right on a watercolor artichoke. There would be personality wallpaper in the bathroom, icy sparkling cocktails, very good roast chicken and a bread service so generous it would probably make an accountant nervous.

Fortunately, I donât have to worry about razor-thin margins in a fantasy. But even if I did, I know one dish that would earn its place on the menu: cabbage.

Specifically, green cabbage roasted in miso butter, then showered with crispy, lemony panko breadcrumbs. Itâs inexpensive, uncomplicated and just a little chic. More importantly, I canât seem to stop making it.

The recipe began with one of my favorite ways to cook: playing matchmaker with ingredients. If Thing A already loves Thing B, and Thing B loves Thing C, perhaps A and C would get along, too. Thereâs a pleasing logic to it, like introducing two friends at a dinner party and watching them discover they have more in common than the host.

I already adored miso butter, with its salty, savory depth. And cabbage cooked in butter is a classic for good reason. Putting the two together was hardly a leap. I chopped up a head of green cabbage, coated it with the miso butter and let the oven do the rest. After about 30 minutes at 350 degrees, with a stir halfway through, the cabbage had softened into silky folds, with a little browning at the edges. The butter made it rich; the miso gave it a subtle funk.

My first instinct was to go the baked-macaroni-and-cheese route: lightly toast some panko, scatter it over the cabbage, then return the whole thing to the oven. In theory, a golden, crunchy topping. In practice, the crumbs more or less fused into a single crust over the slick cabbage beneath. Cutting through it was less delightful than Iâd imagined.

The fix was blessedly simple. I crisped the breadcrumbs separately in a pan with olive oil, red pepper flakes and the zest of an entire lemon, then spooned them over the cabbage just before serving. Now each forkful caught a little of everything: tender, almost creamy cabbage; browned edges; bright flecks of citrus; and individual crunchy crumbs that stayed crunchy.

That last part matters. The contrast is what makes this feel like a dish rather than a vegetable dutifully placed beside dinner.

And beside dinner it has appeared, repeatedly. With salmon and rice. With grilled chicken and sweet potato coins glossed with maple syrup and orange zest. With a skillet of white beans and sausage, plus sourdough for scooping. Different meals, same cabbage. At this point, Iâd be more surprised by a week without it.

Lately, Iâve been trying to make room for more vegetables in everyday cooking, ideally two kinds at dinner. Not as a grim exercise in virtue, but because I want the vegetables to be things I actually look forward to eating. That means finding a few sides that are so appealing, and so low-effort, that adding one more feels less like a chore and more like, âOh, hell, why not?â

Cabbage is particularly good at this. Itâs cheap, keeps beautifully in the refrigerator and demands almost no knife skills. You can even buy it pre-shredded. It sits in the oven while you make the rest of the meal, asking for little beyond a halfway stir. Low-maintenance, low-effort, high return.

I may never open that bistro, and perhaps thatâs just as well for the accountant and the watercolor artichokes. But on an ordinary weeknight, when dinner is nearly done and I find myself reaching for the cabbage again, I get a small piece of the fantasy anyway: something simple enough to make at home, and good enough that Iâd happily order it out.

1 medium head green cabbage, shredded (red works, too! Though it takes on a decidedly spooky dark purple color)

#6187. New York City, deliciously off-script

I ate lamb ribs sticky with tamarind and dates, watched fairy tales transformed into extravagant burlesque, learned to make stained glass and watched people take shots of alcohol poured directly from the head of a bluefin tuna during my latest trip to New York City. It wasn’t exactly a conventional sightseeing itinerary, but that’s increasingly how I like to experience the city.

I used to live in New York, and no matter how many times I return, it never fails to surprise, delight, frustrate and invigorate me. I spent another week revisiting favorites and adding to the list of must-visit places I might never get to. The possibilities seem endless, particularly when you’re willing to follow your curiosity. From unforgettable meals to unexpected experiences, here’s where mine took me this time — and where I’d happily go again.

One of my favorite things about eating in New York is how easily a casual lunch can become one of the most memorable meals of the trip. Take LAUT in Union Square, the first Malaysian restaurant in New York City to be awarded a Michelin star. While the establishment hasn’t retained it, if the bustling lunch crowd was any indication, it’s certainly a worthwhile stop. The menu draws from Singaporean, Thai and Malaysian cuisine, with fragrant curries, flaky roti, chewy noodles and wok-fried dishes.

We loved the fried butter garlic soft-shell crab with fragrant, crispy curry leaves. The roti canai was another standout, perfectly flaky and served with a spice-forward sauce you’ll want to eat with a spoon. Bone-in duck curry followed, braised in coconut milk with lime leaf and tomato, and served with rice. It had a stick-to-your-bones constitution, and you could easily get lost in the flavorful sauce.

Peruvian food is influenced by flavors from around the globe, with delicious peppers, lots of citrus and fresh ingredients as the stars of the show. At Mission Ceviche, also in Union Square, I found an excellent lunch menu offering a variety of ceviches — ceviche nikkei was my favorite! — and tiraditos, cravable mocktails and main dishes ranging from classics like lomo saltado to whole grilled branzino over a bright tomato chorrillana sauce. I could have easily downed several basil breeze mocktails.

Harlem is home to Red Rooster, co-founded by the acclaimed Marcus Samuelsson. Inspired by Black American, Southern and Caribbean cuisines, the restaurant serves as a gathering place with live music, good food and a lively atmosphere. The service was excellent despite the full restaurant and busy bar, and we ordered a variety of dishes for the three of us.

I loved fried chicken and this one was coated in a crispy shell while perfectly juicy inside, served with greens and unctuous mashed potatoes. Jerk wings were great, too, as well as the Uptown Guac, served with fried hushpuppies. Surprisingly, the highlight of our meal was dessert: a strawberry and mango salad with coconut sauce. So refreshing, and a perfect way to end the meal.

Of course, not every great food discovery requires a sit-down meal. Two small but mighty cafes in Greenwich Village made particularly memorable stops, each with a very different specialty.

Savory pastries meet halloumi from Cyprus at Hello Halloumi, a small bakery where the cheese is the star of the menu. Halloumi appears fried, baked into pastries, turned into grilled cheese, served as the meat in a “burger,” and featured in gyro wraps and bowls. The rose cloud matcha was delicious, and if you want something sweet, don’t miss the tahinopita, a cinnamon roll-style treat slathered in decadent tahini icing.

(Chaya Milchtein) Matcha and a Frenchie at Kawaii Cafe

Nearby, Kawaii Cafe is a little Vietnamese coffee shop with a French bulldog named Latte as its mascot that should be a required stop for any coffee or matcha lover. Kim, the owner, came to the United States from Vietnam and worked as a nail tech. Kawaii’s signature beverages hearken back to those days, when she’d talk to clients and hear all about their relationship problems. Situationship, Thirst Trap and What Are We are all handcrafted drinks inspired by those conversations.

Coffee beans are carefully sourced from Vietnam, cream toppings and jellies are made in-house, and vibrant green matcha from Shizuoka, Japan, makes for unforgettable combinations. The matcha was so good I came back twice!

For dinner, New York offers endless opportunities to get a little more adventurous. Some of my favorite dishes from this trip came from restaurants drawing on different culinary traditions and finding exciting ways to bring them together.

At Eyval in Bushwick, an Iranian restaurant that bills itself as “recreating traditional Iranian cooking for a contemporary audience,” the dining room was bustling and lively, with every table full when we arrived. The menu isn’t overly extensive, but every dish we ate balanced flavors, textures and ingredients superbly.

I could eat the citrus, date and cabbage salad every day and probably never get tired of it. The punchy, rich chile-tahini dressing balances perfectly with the sweet, chewy dates, bursts of orange and crunchy cabbage. Match made in heaven, really. Then there were fall-off-the-bone lamb ribs with a sticky tamarind-and-date sauce that you just have to lick your fingers after devouring, and a saffron half chicken, pressed and served over rice studded with barberries and pumpkin seeds. This restaurant will live rent-free in my brain for quite some time.

Marcus Samuelsson’s Hav & Mar offers another inventive approach to familiar ingredients. Born in Ethiopia and raised in Sweden, Samuelsson draws on both culinary traditions at this seafood-focused restaurant. The space is beautiful and lively, with mermaids on the walls and a central bar. The menu is spice-forward, with raw and cured dishes, small plates and a range of entrees.

We loved the crudo trio: tuna tartare with miso and injera, hamachi with gooseberries and crispy onions, and berbere-cured salmon, lox-style, in an orange broth. The highlight of our meal was a whole crispy-skin branzino served with fresh injera, shiro and plenty of herbs, while dry-aged lamb chops rounded out our order. My only regret is skipping the Hav bread basket, with teff biscuits, blue cornbread and injera crisps.

New York can also deliver an exceptional steak dinner, whether you’re drawn to Brazilian specialties or an old-school white-tablecloth institution.

The dimly lit Berimbau Brazilian Table in Midtown, from restaurateur Mario de Matos, was a delight, with a relatively small menu of Brazilian specialties. We started with the nearly obligatory pão de queijo, crispy, cheesy, chewy bread that’s naturally gluten-free and positively scrumptious.

The star of the menu is clear immediately: tableside-carved prime picanha, a treat for the eyes and certainly the taste buds. The massive 38-ounce portion sits on a bed of corn farofa, a textural delight, and is served with cheesy yuca purée, charred vegetables and salada vinagrete that adds a much-needed acidic punch. It technically serves three but is perfect for two, with plenty of leftovers. This might have been the best picanha I’ve ever had. The service, ambiance and lighting make it an excellent choice for a memorable meal.

Gallagher’s Steakhouse, on the other hand, is where you go for an old-school New York experience, complete with waiters in bow ties, dry-aged steaks and classic sides. Originally a speakeasy that opened during Prohibition, it changed hands several times and became a New York City institution.

The menu offers classics: a raw bar with delicious oysters (ask for horseradish, they have it!), Caesar salad, French onion soup and other starters. Steaks of all kinds, some dry-aged in the meat lockers you walk past as you’re seated, can be topped with blue cheese or served with bone marrow. I’d skip the latter, even as a bone marrow lover.

We opted for a well-aged, medium-rare T-bone steak cooked over hickory logs, with buttered corn and spinach served family-style. In the classic Gallagher’s way, the waiter fills your plate. Endearing or disconcerting? You decide. Save room for the New York cheesecake. It’s made in-house and was a surprising standout.

And for a completely different kind of fine dining, there’s Sushi Akira, where chef-owner Nikki Zheng is right at home behind the counter.

Sushi Akira specializes in Edomae-style sushi, using curing, marinating and dry aging to bring out the best texture and flavor of each ingredient without relying on heavy sauces. Chef Zheng is generous with her time, answering questions and explaining techniques and ingredients as she creates an 18-course omakase. Each carefully crafted piece of nigiri changes depending on what’s in season, and the meal unfolds in a choreographed dance for just 16 lucky diners.

Get the sake pairing if you’re imbibing, even if you don’t usually think of yourself as a sake drinker. The selections brilliantly complemented and enhanced each course and introduced me to combinations I wouldn’t have expected.

(Jodyann Morgan) Stripped jack nigiri at Sushi Akira

For a lively dinner with a group, I loved MangoSeed in Brooklyn’s Flatbush neighborhood. The playlist really set the mood. Billed as “Caribbean-inspired” and heavily influenced by Jamaican cuisine, the restaurant offers a fun atmosphere, hearty food and excellent service. My wife and I invited her mother, niece and nephew to join us, and despite the restaurant’s size, it fit our multigenerational group perfectly.

We really enjoyed the whole grilled fish with charred lemon and spicy jerk wings. Order a rum punch if you like a fruity drink that packs a punch, pun intended. A beloved favorite, the baked four-cheese mac and cheese was gooey and decadent. The rice and peas and oxtail didn’t quite live up to our high standards, but they rounded out the meal. And for dessert, the chocolate cake was moist and deeply chocolatey, a surprising standout for the entire group.

Of course, getting to and around New York City can be stressful. Between traffic and the sheer number of people, it can overwhelm even seasoned travelers. A couple of transportation services made my recent visits easier.

Having a professional driver from Gotham Ride Chauffeur Service pick you up at the airport can help a trip start off right. The company tracks your flight so the driver can meet you even if it’s delayed, and you’re greeted with cold beverages while you take a load off.

I’ve used the service on two trips, and both were a breeze, even when one of my flights was turned around midair and another was canceled as we were about to get into the car. Those are precisely the moments when having some help with the logistics makes a difference.

For getting around town, I’ve also been testing alternatives to the usual rideshare options. I lived in New York during the golden age of rideshare, when it was largely budget-friendly and so many new apps were popping up that the competition was fierce. In the years since, Uber and Lyft have become the primary choices, but whenever I return, I try to test-drive newer options.

Empower isn’t exactly traditional rideshare. The company bills itself as a software platform, allowing drivers to set their own rates and keep 100% of the fare revenue while paying a daily or monthly fee to use the service.

On my visits, drivers were available quickly, rates were reliably lower than the Uber fares I was comparing against, and service was what you’d expect. I plan to use the app again the next time I’m in New York City.

As much as I love eating my way through New York, every trip deserves a few experiences that don’t revolve entirely around a restaurant reservation. This time, that meant everything from burlesque and close-up magic to a four-hour stained-glass class and a very unusual encounter with a bluefin tuna.

For a night out with some genuine spectacle, Company XIV reimagines classic stories like “Little Red Riding Hood” as full-scale burlesque productions. Complete with live singing, expert choreography, ballet, aerial performances and costumes designed to be removed piece by piece, the shows are sensual and mesmerizing.

The theater is a magnificent setting for each performance, decked out in velvet and glitter, with chandeliers overhead. If you enjoy a really good performance art, you must catch a show at Théâtre XIV. Whether you’re with a lover or a group of friends, prepare to be dazzled!

(And if you’re peckish before or after the show, stop by Tortillería Mexicana Los Hermanos, just a three-minute walk away. The restaurant operates inside a tortilla factory that has been making tortillas in-house since 1998, and the food never disappoints. I always get the carnitas, perfectly crispy and deeply savory, served in fresh, warm tortillas.)

For another kind of performance, consider the tuna-cutting experience at Sushi by Bou. If your TikTok feed looks anything like mine, you’ve probably watched plenty of videos of live tuna cuttings. If omakase isn’t interactive or exciting enough for you, this is a chance to watch an entire bluefin tuna being carved, sliced and served in an endless parade of toro, akami and more.

Sushi by Bou curated a party-like atmosphere in a room full of eager sushi lovers. Libations flowing, delicious fatty tuna passed around, and alcohol poured directly into your mouth from the tuna head itself were some of the highlights. You can even scrape tuna directly off the ribs if you choose. It’s not exactly a typical sushi dinner, but that’s part of the fun.

For an experience that trades culinary spectacle for old-fashioned wonder, there’s Chamber Magic at the glitzy Lotte New York Palace.

Tune out everything and let yourself believe in magic — at least for an hour and 45 minutes. Magician Steve Cohen makes everyone feel like an important part of the show. Held on Friday and Saturday, with a cocktail-attire dress code, the performance brings together just 64 people to giggle, laugh and try to figure out how Cohen pours someone’s perfect cocktail from a teapot unprompted, among other magical acts. You’ll leave with a wide smile, enchanted by the experience.

Not all my favorite activities involve watching someone else demonstrate a skill, though. I love finding a creative experience while traveling, particularly when it means learning something new and bringing home a one-of-a-kind souvenir I made myself.

Craftsman Ave in Brooklyn offers classes for even the most adventurous crafter, including knife making, leatherwork, textiles and stained glass, which I chose. Its introduction to stained glass is a four-hour class that walks you through every step of making a wall hanging, from selecting your design to cutting the glass, soldering and finishing the piece.

My wife and I have taken many craft classes, but this one felt more advanced than anything we’d tried before, with experienced artists working alongside us. I definitely felt frustrated at times because it took me a while to grasp each step. But in the end, I was glad I took the class, even if my cat was more amateur than I’d hoped.

If you’re looking for a bite before or after class, stop by Sahadi’s at Industry City, just a few minutes away on foot. The longtime Lebanese grocer has been operating in New York since the late 1800s, and this location has a grab-and-go deli as well as seated lunch and dinner service.

Another New York experience worth considering is having something made specifically for you. Have you ever put on a suit and had it fit perfectly? Me neither! Nothing off the rack makes me feel like a million bucks.

That’s what makes Alan David Custom in Midtown such an interesting stop. The bespoke tailoring house crafts suits to your exact measurements and requirements, guiding you through the process from fabric selection to final fitting.

The fabric choices are endless, and every detail is dictated by you rather than a mass-market clothing producer: pocket or no pocket, type of stitching, exact fit, even the hemline for the style of shoes you actually wear. After the initial measurements, the company can ship a basted fitting and arrange a virtual fitting to finalize the details before sewing and sending the finished garment.

Whether you’re preparing for a big occasion or simply tired of wearing something that doesn’t quite fit, it’s a luxury experience that offers something more personal than an ordinary shopping trip.

After a full day of exploring, there’s something to be said for returning to a comfortable hotel, particularly one that feels a little different from the generic, nondescript rooms you can find almost anywhere.

The Kimberly Hotel has old-school charm and timeless elegance, with gracious, helpful service and a massive round fish tank in the lobby that you can get lost in. The hotel has 194 rooms, including one- and two-bedroom suites.

We stayed in a massive one-bedroom suite, even by regular standards, with a lounge area and kitchenette complete with a microwave and refrigerator that we put to good use. The bed was super comfortable, but the bathroom was tiny considering all the space. A balcony with Manhattan views was simply the pièce de résistance. Even if your room doesn’t have a balcony, you can get 360-degree views at the rooftop lounge, aptly called Upstairs at The Kimberly.

For a comfortable home base with minimal frills, Kimpton Ashbel New York Park Avenue fits the brief well.

The lobby is inspired by a living and dining room spread across two spaces, with the registration desk at the center. It’s designed to give you room to relax and connect, and it’s great for people-watching, although the hustle and bustle means it isn’t a place to go for peace and quiet.

Our room was surprisingly spacious for New York City, with a table, chairs and a jetted tub — which was quite difficult to climb into, if I’m honest. Kimpton Ashbel is also pet-friendly, with no deposit required and no weight, size or breed restrictions, a huge boon for travelers with pets.

My stained-glass cat didn’t turn out quite as I’d hoped, and there are still countless restaurants on my list I never managed to visit. But I came home with some excellent meals, a few wonderfully strange memories and plenty of reasons to return.

New York’s legal cannabis scene is flourishing, with countless dispensaries competing for your business. Each dispensary offers a different experience depending on your style and preferences.

Housing Works Cannabis Co. is both New York’s first legal recreational cannabis dispensary and one of a handful of nonprofit dispensaries. If the name sounds familiar, it’s because Housing Works has been serving homeless and low-income New Yorkers, particularly people living with HIV, in a variety of capacities for years. The dispensary, just a short walk from Union Square and the Village, puts all of its profits toward supporting that mission.

Then there’s The Daily Green in Times Square, impossible to miss beneath digital green billboards with cannabis displayed in bold newspaper type. The massive dispensary has a selection to match, with products ranging from pre-rolls and tinctures to topicals and vapes, including New York brands like ayrloom and national ones including STIIIZY and Dogwalker.

An interactive bud bar lets customers get a firsthand look at different cannabis varieties, with a terpene guide providing additional information. It’s a distinctly different experience from visiting a small neighborhood shop, and an interesting example of how cannabis has become part of the Times Square retail landscape.

On the Upper West Side, Superfly Dispensary offers another approach. The budtenders are knowledgeable, cannabis varieties are available to examine under magnification, and the selection intentionally includes LGBT- and Black-owned brands. Superfly also serves as a community hub, with weekly yoga and Pilates, disco nights, Halloween parties and brand activations. There’s something for people looking to connect and spend time with like-minded neighbors, not simply shop. Great choices include ayrloom’s Lychee Dream pre-rolls, Good Tide guava gummies and Sluggers Lemon Cherry Gelato vape.

#6185. Alaska Airlines to Lay Off 200 Employees as It Forecasts a Loss in 2026

Higher fuel costs have eaten into Alaska’s profits and now the carrier says it will cut 200 back office roles to help with cost control.

Alaska Airlines is laying off 200 employees as it grapples with high fuel costs and has lost $416 million in the past nine months of the year.

The cuts only impact back office roles, so pilots, flight attendants, ramp agents, and maintenance technicians are among those that won’t be affected, a spokesperson confirmed to Skift. In Washington state, 148 employees will be impacted and in Hawaii, 48.

Alaska Airlines is cutting about 200 back-office jobs as high fuel costs weigh on results, with losses of $416 million over the past nine months. The cuts hit non-contract roles only — 148 positions in Washington state and 48 in Hawaii — leaving pilots, flight attendants, ramp agents, and maintenance technicians untouched. Alaska said in a statement that volatile fuel costs and broader geopolitical pressures drove the decision, and that it had spent much of the last year controlling costs. The airline reported a third-quarter net loss of $147 million despite a 14% revenue increase to $14.3 billion, and expects to pay between $4.65 and $4.85 a gallon for jet fuel in the fourth quarter. It is forecasting an adjusted loss per share of $5 to $5.50 in 2026. Alaska's West Coast base leaves it exposed to some of the steepest fuel prices among U.S. carriers, because the region lacks direct pipelines and relies on imports. The cuts land while Alaska pursues an expensive growth plan built on the Hawaiian Airlines merger, including new routes to Europe and Asia, more business class seats, and a new premium economy cabin.

#6184. Patrick Stewart, the “Star Trek” captain who elevated television

Before the prestige drama era, people rarely associated nobility with the small screen. In old Hollywoodâs thinking, television was cinemaâs inferior cousin. Syndication ranked even lower. And syndicated science fiction shows? Total jokes.

Sir Patrick Stewart, who died Wednesday in Los Angeles at 86, changed these impressions when he accepted the seven-year mission of âStar Trek: The Next Generation.â As Jean-Luc Picard, the captain who inherited the helm of USS Enterprise from William Shatnerâs James T. Kirk, Stewart embodied franchise founder Gene Roddenberryâs humanist outlook.

Picard, the actorâs greatest TV legacy, is a paragon of grace: empathetic, dedicated to a mission of understanding and devoted to preserving what is best about Starfleet.Â  And Stewartâs shaping of the character ennobled television in ways cosmic and small.

By treating his Starfleet commander as if he were a Shakespearean protagonist, Stewart transformed a franchise at a crossroads into a fresh, thoughtful look at human possibility. This guiding principle traveled through âThe Next Generationâ and subsequent movies, along with the recent Paramount+ âStar Trekâ spinoff, âStar Trek: Picard.â

By the time Stewartâs final voyage with âStar Trekâ debuted in 2020, Picard was less of a Starfleet hero than a wise man exhausted by politics and cruelty. And âPicardâ was as much a response to Trumpian callousness as âThe Next Generationâ was to our cultureâs fatigue with materialism by 1987, when it premiered.

âIf the âTrekâ universe presented a leader like Picard, it may be because back then, we all thought we were just shy of getting to a better place with regard to how we treat each other,â I recalled in 2018. âOf thinking beyond ourselves, our immediate desires and thirst for gratification, and embracing our differences as strengths. It was a lovely illusion.â

When Stewart joined the Trek universe, he was largely unknown to Americans â save for the eagle-eyed nerds who recognized him, perhaps, from John Boormanâs âExcaliburâ or David Lynchâs âDune.âÂ  His Starfleet captain eschewed Captain Kirkâs swagger, though that didnât mean he was all business. Picard is a man given to philosophical debates and genteel pursuits like horseback riding and fencing. He isnât infallible, but he constantly demonstrates all the ways people could be better, not than others, but than we ourselves once were.

This is the essential definition of nobility, expanded upon over 178 episodes of âStar Trek: The Next Generation.â

Many factors contributed to that syndicated seriesâ success and Stewartâs resultant popularity as the man behind one of TVâs most beloved characters. âThe Next Generationâ ensemble featured some of TVâs most adored talent, including Jonathan Frakes and LeVar Burton, on a crew steered behind the scenes by Roddenberry himself. It went on to win 17 Emmys and a Peabody.

But Stewartâs gravitas, honed over many years of British stage performance, made Picard the showâs gravitational center, and he was proud of that. Long after TV catchphrases became associated with hackneyed scripting, Picard unironically claimed a few of the best, including âmake it soâ and âengage,â delivering them each time with an air of aristocratic confidence.

(Paramount Pictures/Getty Images) Patrick Stewart, left, and LeVar Burton in the 1998 film âStar Trek: Insurrection.â

Stewart came from humble origins, however: He was born on July 13, 1940, in a West Yorkshire industrial town, and raised in a house lacking an indoor toilet or running hot water.

âWhat identifies an individual as a king is how other people behave towards him,â says a quote attributed to the actor. âAll authority is assumed, and if other people donât accept your authority then you donât have it. Perhaps the critical thing to being a convincing figure of authority is actually not to try too hard.â

That understanding gives fresh insight into the passion he brought to his greatest starring roles and the smallest.

The authoritative voice we associate with Picard ordering his tea âEarl Grey, hot,â was fine-tuned over a career that began with training at the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, where he enrolled in 1957. Shedding his working-class Yorkshire accent during his studies, Stewartâs regal elocution won him his stage debut in 1959 in an adaptation of âTreasure Island.â From there, his career was largely defined by his 16 years with the Royal Shakespeare Company, where he started in 1966, before joining the Royal National Theatre in 1984.

As The Independent cited in a 2003 story, when a reporter once implied the two-time Laurence Olivier Award winner was slumming it by linking himself to the Trek universe, Stewart replied, âSitting in the Captainâs chair of the Enterprise is rather like sitting on the throne of England, though marginally more important.â

The Crown didnât take offense; Queen Elizabeth II conferred Stewartâs knighthood in 2010.

We can credit the actorâs innate emotional agility for his commitment to every part, or a versatility earned over decades of playing many major heroes and villains the Bard scribbled onto parchment. Whatever it was, Stewartâs charm was in his refusal to let snobbery dictate his life or career path. While most of his career was spent onstage, youâll find his name in the credits of many films and shows and hear his baritone in a slew of video games and animated work.

Although his association with âStar Trekâ and Picard came to define how people perceived him, Stewartâs merry attitude about his claim to fame let us appreciate his range. While his casting as the mutant telepath Professor Xavier in the âX-Menâ cinematic franchise resulted from his time in the starship captainâs chair, his multiple collaborations with âFamily Guyâ creator Seth MacFarlane showcased his playful side.

People who have never watched a single âStar Trekâ episode can easily pick out his voice from every other guest on âFamily Guyâ or know him as Stan Smithâs self-important CIA boss Avery Bullock on âAmerican Dad!â The sheer joy of watching Stewartâs comic turns in shows like âExtrasâ or hearing his voice in ludicrous contexts was magnified by the majesty he lent to his dramatic work. He owned his portrayal of Gurney Halleck in âDuneâ so completely that nobody blinked when he dashed into a battle scene bellowing mightily while clutching a pug, of all things.

But it was Picardâwho retired as an admiralâ that forever landed Stewart in our minds and hearts. He never minded that fact.

âHalfway through season 3 of âNext Generation,â I no longer knew where Jean-Luc started and Patrick Stewart left off,â he told reporters at a Television Critics Association press conference in 2020. âWe became melded, and he has never left me . . . He has always been there, and itâs a relationship that I am happy to continue with.â Thanks to his prolific presence in movies, shows and on screens large and small, we can keep that relationship alive too.
