#6155. The power of Latinas’ Trump regret could swing this election

This story was originally published by The 19th.

This story was originally reported by Mel Leonor Barclay of The 19th. Meet Mel and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy.

RIO GRANDE CITY, Texas — When Cynthia Villareal voted for President Donald Trump in 2024, she did so trusting his campaign promises of lower gas prices, border security and “assistance for the people — for the middle class.”

The 43-year-old mother of four turned out for Trump alongside a sizable majority of voters in heavily Latino Starr County, which hugs the border with Mexico and had reliably turned out for Democratic candidates for five generations.

Less than two years later, Villareal said the promise of her vote never materialized. “He said gas prices were gonna go down. They haven’t — they haven’t at all,” said Villareal, who drives around the Rio Grande Valley for her job supervising home health aides and feels every little surge. Villareal manages workers in a shortstaffed, tough profession where wages have simply not kept up with the cost of living. Many of her best workers, she said, are immigrants without permanent legal status experiencing the brunt of Trump’s immigration agenda.

“I mean, he didn’t mention that these ICE agents were just going to be picking up all of these hardworking employees, you know, that have no backgrounds,” Villareal said, referring to immigrants without a criminal record. “They’re leaving people without their family, basically, and then some of the people are even dying in there,” she said of immigration detention. “Like, who knows what they’re doing to these poor people?”

For Villareal, life is more expensive, and her job harder. “It’s just too much.”

Latina voters’ rightward shift was a crucial part of Trump’s reelection in 2024, and while more Latino men backed the president, Latinas actually made larger strides to the right in the last four presidential cycles.

Ahead of the midterms, Latinas are also registering higher levels of regret when thinking about their support for Trump, a dynamic that may decide the outcome of competitive races from Texas to Florida and beyond.

Voters like Villareal shed light on how Trump regret among this swingy and powerful group of voters — Latinas vote at higher rates than Latino men — may be the swell that breaks into a blue wave for Democrats this November.

“I do think the narrative of this election could be that Latina women, in particular, help decide who is in control of the House of Representatives and the balance of government. And I say that because of the shifts we’ve seen over time and the shifts back that we are seeing now among Latina women in particular,” said Stephanie Valencia, who studies Latino voters at Equis Research.

Latinos’ political power this cycle is spread across the midterms map. Latinos make up at least 15 percent of the population in six of the 17 most competitive congressional districts, as well as in 29 other districts considered broadly competitive, mostly in the Southwest, California and Florida. Latino voters could be the deciders in competitive races for the U.S. Senate in Texas and Florida. Also in Texas, Latinos could swing the most competitive governor’s race the state has seen in years and, in doing so, elect the first Latina to the state’s top job.

Start your day with essential news from Salon. Sign up for our free morning newsletter, Crash Course.

“Trump appealed to their pocketbooks and people were suffering here. I also think people were tired. We’ve been Democratic for over 100 years — why don’t we try something different?” said Cecilia Hernández, who founded the local political group Somos STARR this year in response to the big swings to the right she’s seen in her community.

In an interview at the office of her family’s trash collection business, Hernández said voters’ views are shifting this cycle.

“I think along with everything that’s happening with immigration and with the cost of living today, what I’ve been receiving a lot is, ‘I’m in the middle,’” Hernández said. “They don’t want to be seen as far right, and they don’t want to be seen as far left, either.”

Latinas stand out in just how much they are feeling the burn of rising costs. They report higher levels of financial stress and are less optimistic about the national economy, according to multiple surveys of Latino voters conducted over the past year.

An expansive survey of Latinos conducted in the spring and sponsored by UnidosUS, a Hispanic civil rights and advocacy organization, found that Latinas are more likely than Latino men to say that they have trouble meeting expenses — 23 percent of women vs. 17 percent of men. Men are much more likely to say they can meet their expenses and even have a little left over.

Thirty-eight percent of Latinas voted for Trump in 2024, versus half of Latino men, according to one high-quality analysis, driven by high costs and lack of confidence in the party in power on the economy. The UnidosUS survey of 3,000 Latino voters found that almost a third of Latinas who voted for Trump had regrets about their vote —  seven points more than Latino men.

Regret is most striking among young Latinas: 42 percent said they would not vote for him again, a 12-point gap with young Latino men. Latina voters are more likely to register and turn out to vote, and with Latino voters skewing younger, young Latinas wield outsize political power.

“Latina women have a large gender pay gap. We also have higher unemployment. We also generally have the responsibility of going to the supermarket and paying the grocery bills and understanding that eggs and and everything else is more expensive,” said Katharine Pichardo, the president and CEO of the Latino Victory Project, which backs progressive Democrats. Latinas are more likely to be closely involved in their kids’ education and doctors’ appointments, a frontline view on rising costs that Pichardo said shaped how they voted in 2024 and their views on that vote now.

Melissa Morales, the president of Somos Votantes, which does political outreach to Latinos on behalf of Democratic candidates, said Latinas started peeling away from Trump almost immediately in his second term, while Latino men started shifting in the latter part of 2025.

While Latinos, like voters overall, broadly rank the cost of living as their top issue, the disparate impact of the administration’s immigration policies on Latino communities is also registering among Latino voters.

A New York Times/Siena poll conducted in mid October found that only a third of Hispanic voters approve of the administration’s handling of immigration. UnidosUS’ survey found significant gender gaps between Latino men and women. While both groups rank the importance of the issue about the same, Latinas were more likely to oppose policies like ending birthright citizenship and more funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Latinas were also more likely to support banning ICE from sensitive locations like schools and hospitals and to support requiring warrants for enforcement at home or in a workplace.

Some of the most dramatic shifts toward Trump and Republicans in 2024 were logged in Texas’ Rio Grande Valley, where Villareal lives. A string of counties in this part of Texas saw double-digit shifts in Trump’s favor compared with the 2020 election, after significant shifts to the right from 2016 to 2020.

Latina voters in the Rio Grande Valley and around Texas will have a big impact on the Texas governor’s race, where Democrat Gina Hinojosa is locked in a dead heat with three-term Gov. Greg Abbott. Hinojosa describes herself as a populist who will tackle corruption and undue influence in government, which she ties to rising costs, weakened public schools and more.

Hinojosa rarely acknowledges the history-making potential of her campaign as a Latina in a state that has never elected a Latino to the governor’s mansion. She instead nods to it by saying that she’d be the first governor from the Rio Grande Valley, which for Texans may as well mean the same thing.

Hinojosa, who is bilingual, flexes her Spanglish easily on the stump, telling voters that the most important lesson she ever got came from her mother was the scolding, “No te dejes.” It doesn’t have a direct translation in English.

“The best thing I can come up with is, ‘Know your worth and defend it,’” Hinojosa said in an interview. Asked if the Spanish phrase was connecting with voters, Hinojosa said, “for sure with Latinos, and 1,000 percent with Latinas.”

“I’ve learned on the campaign trail that this is a saying that is mostly passed down through the women in the family,” she added. “And I think it’s because of this knowledge that women have for their daughters, grandmothers have for their granddaughters, that the world is tough, and we have to be strong.”

At campaign events in the Rio Grande Valley in September, several voters cited Hinojosa’s identity and approach to politics as a motivating factor.

Juanita Vallejo, 40, of Edinburg, Texas, said she sees Hinojosa as an “empowered woman,” and likes her firm stances in support of public schools and curtailing data centers.

“I don’t want to say it this way, but I’m going to say it — she wouldn’t kiss ass to Trump. I think she would stand up to what is right,” said Rosie Hernandez, 56 of McAllen.

Hinojosa is one of the breakout candidates of the cycle, but she has had to plead for funding from national Democrats hesitant to spend in Texas. Earlier this month, a group of influential Latinos in Democratic political circles put pressure on Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who chairs the Democratic Governors Association (DGA), to invest $10 million in the Texas governor’s race. The DGA decided to send $1 million.

Valencia, who signed onto the letter, said Democrats’ investment in Hinojosa’s race has larger implications for the party and sends a message to Latinos. “She’s a once-in-a-generation candidate from a state that is disproportionately Latino that has been the unicorn that Democrats have chased for decades,” Valencia said.

“To have such a young, dynamic, charismatic Latina candidate in this environment and to not back her is a statement in and of itself, and it says a lot about how certain national Democrats feel about Texas and how they feel about certain candidates.”

Hinojosa’s ability to build enthusiasm for her campaign after starting out with a low profile as a state legislator from Austin could bode well for one the biggest challenges when it comes to Latino voters: turning them out.

Latinos had the lowest turnout rates among the major racial and ethnic groups at 51 percent, compared with 71 percent among White voters and 60 percent among Black voters. Nearly 6 million eligible Latinas did not vote in 2024.

During a town hall in Houston with a local Latino influencer this month, Hinojosa mused about the event likely being the first time a candidate for governor hosts an event in Spanish. Before Hinojosa arrived on stage, the host ushered to the microphone a woman who identified herself as a 46-year-old Houston native who had never voted before. Holding a white and orange slip, she said she had registered to vote earlier that day. “Quiero cambio,” she said to cheers. “No more Trump.”

As both parties look ahead to the 2028 presidential election, they’ll have to contend with the fact that the Latino vote is a swing vote. Whatever gains Democrats make this cycle, they have a lot of ground to make up — especially with Latinas.

Nine days out from Election Day, Villareal said she is planning to vote for Democrats up and down the ballot. She described her vote this time as against Republicans — a register of regret — rather than about enthusiasm for the Democrats on the ticket.

“We have to trust somebody. We have to vote for somebody no matter what,” Villareal said.

“And obviously, the way things went in 2024 with Republicans, there wasn’t a change at all. It’s just been worse. So we’re gonna try and see.”

The top question for the GOP will be whether they continue to support current Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Speaker Mike Johnson if Democrats retake either chamber.

“Now, if we hold the majority or even hold [at] 50 and we remain the governing party, I think you have to give [Thune] an awful lot of credit for keeping it together,” he said of the possibility of a split chamber emerging.

A two-hour forum for candidates will take place the morning of Nov. 10, Politico first reported, followed by members casting their votes later that afternoon for the positions of leader, whip and conference chair.

While the floor vote for speaker doesn’t take place until January, if the GOP does retain control of the House, they would also nominate a speaker.

#6149. Right-wing media and the mystery of Texas’ transgender mailers

On Thursday night, the smear at the heart of the mysterious transgender mailers that have rocked the final weeks of the midterm elections in Texas completed its journey. What began as baseless social media whispers quickly ascended the ladder of conservative influence, jumped into mailboxes across the Lone Star State and ultimately into the comforting prime-time embrace of Fox News.

At a town hall in Fort Worth, a Texas mother of six named Rebekah Smith told Vice President JD Vance that her 11-year-old daughter had received a letter explaining how to transition without her parents ever knowing, and asked how Republicans would keep the government out of her family. “I don’t know who sent that letter to your child,” the vice president said, “but I think the person who sends a letter to an 11-year-old about gender transition, what I call that in my family is a pervert, and that person ought to go to prison.” Host Jesse Watters, never one to let a grievance go to waste, promised that Fox would investigate “this perverted letter.” Vance asked Smith to talk to his staff because he would “like the Department of Justice to investigate that” as well.

Watters rushed to promote the spectacle. “WHOA! Texas MOM tells JD Vance her DAUGHTER received a letter telling her TO TRANSITION TO A BOY,” he posted on X, followed by Vance’s promise. Missing from that framing was the question that should have governed the segment: Who actually sent the material?

Nobody on that stage mentioned that the pamphlet was a fake. Nobody mentioned that the real transgender advocacy group named inside it had disavowed the mailer. Nobody mentioned that sworn testimony filed that same week had tied the text messages that accompanied it to a national Republican organization. The vice president was asking federal prosecutors to chase a forgery that may well have originated in his own party’s orbit — and he was doing it on a network whose viewers had been marinating in that forgery for weeks.

The race between Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic challenger James Talarico has become a crucible for dark-money maneuvers. As polls show the Republican grip on the Lone Star State slipping, conservative campaigns and their surrogates have resorted to increasingly desperate tactics. In early October, for example, Talarico took a brief hiatus from the campaign trail to recover from a severe case of the flu. Rather than accepting a routine human illness, the right-wing echo chamber treated a temporary absence as evidence of mental illness. Within days, the fabricated scandal has collapsed — yet the machinery of right-wing media simply pivoted to amplifying a more insidious operation designed to trigger visceral outrage.

This second October surprise involved millions of unsolicited text messages and a wave of physical mailers sent to Texas households with materials that directed readers to the website of the Transgender Education Network of

It does not need to survive scrutiny. It just needs to circulate upward.

Texas while inserting provocative advice on child emancipation that the real organization says it never authored or authorized. By flooding the electorate with extreme material disguised as progressive advocacy, right-wing operatives appear to have sought to create a fake controversy that could be weaponized in attack ads and campaign speeches. Vance, for instance, told the Fox News audience that Talarico has “a weird fascination with trans kids,” and that “he’ll probably defend the right of the person sending the letter, not the right of the parent who is rightfully creeped out by this.” Vance claimed that Talarico “has actually called it abusive when parents try to prevent their children from transitioning” and that Paxton “has fought hard to prosecute those people, whereas James Talarico has fought hard to protect those people.” Even the distortion had been laundered by then — Talarico called denying a child’s gender identity abusive, a different claim from saying parents must permit medical transition, but at the top of the ladder the difference no longer exists.

That is how a smear works in the closed ecosystem of the American right. It does not need to survive scrutiny. It just needs to circulate upward. An anonymous account posts it; an influencer adopts it; a donor-funded outlet reports the influencer’s outrage as news; an elected official demands an investigation, and the demand becomes proof the story matters; cable news books the controversy; a vice president promises federal action. Each rung launders the one below it. The correction, when it comes, travels in the opposite direction and arrives nowhere.

The paper trail looks like what you would expect from a covert operation. Texas Transgender Student Union LLC was formed in Wyoming on Sept. 2 through a commercial registered agent that helps owners stay anonymous. After CBS News Texas visited the agent’s address in Sheridan, Wyoming, the agent announced it was resigning. The mailers listed a Houston-area post office box. The Texas Observer reported that the barcode on the envelopes traced to a mail-tracking company that has taken federal campaign money from only one group this year, the National Republican Congressional Committee. The committee said it had nothing to do with the mailers, and the company would not say who paid. CBS News Texas reported that the bulk-mail permit belongs to an Illinois printer owned by the Zerrusen family, who have given heavily to Republican PACs and been photographed with Donald Trump.

When the real Transgender Education Network of Texas filed a petition in Travis County court to unmask the perpetrators behind the impersonation campaign, the partisan safety nets of the Texas judiciary eventually snapped into action. A deposition of Infobip, the messaging company that delivered the texts, which a Travis County judge ordered made public, indicated that the texts were sent on behalf of the Republican Women’s Caucus Fund and a man named John Braun. But on Friday, the Texas Supreme Court, composed entirely of judges appointed by Republican Governor Greg Abbott, issued an administrative stay that blocked its release. Chris Hilton, an attorney who previously served under Paxton, defended him during his impeachment trial and was later pushed out of office amid sexual harassment allegations, argued on behalf of the company that the mailers were not political speech because they named no candidate or party.

Dirty tricks are an old tradition of American politics. This cycle, Republican PACs in Nevada mailed a flyer calling a nonpartisan candidate, Danielle Ford, the “AOC of Nevada,” hoping voters would mistake her for the actual Democratic nominee, Aaron Ford. This week also brought word that the group that funded Cornel West’s 2024 ballot drives raised every dollar through a dark-money network bankrolled by Elon Musk.

The president’s party whines about decoy candidates in Alaska while running them at home. Ratf**king is a long and proud Republican tradition, and the Texas operation fits inside perfectly.

Gulf events can still insure against cancellation but not against war. That is pushing organizers to postpone events or to take on the risk themselves. It’s a growing issue, and Saudi Arabia’s calendar has been paying the price.

Event organizers in the Gulf can still insure against cancellation for many reasons, such as bad weather, a declared period of national mourning, or an IT failure. What they increasingly can’t buy is protection if an event is canceled because of war or political violence, industry executives told Skift.

Standard event-cancellation policies exclude war and political violence, so organizers routinely have to buy that coverage as a separate layer. Since the U.S.-Iran war began in late February, it is something that has become very hard to find for Gulf events.

Only one insurer, possibly two on very limited terms, is currently willing to consider war exposure for events in the region, according to Panteha Peters, head of sports, entertainment, media and special risks at insurance broker Marsh Middle East and Africa. It does so case by case, and generally no earlier than about one week before the event.

Marsh said in May that political violence premiums in the Gulf have risen at least 20-fold since the war began, while capacity to write that cover shrank from about $1 billion to roughly $200 million. Saudi Arabia is the sharpest pressure point: Morningstar DBRS's Marcos Alvarez said the Houthi missile and drone campaign on Riyadh, Abha, and Dammam in October turned war from a theoretical exclusion into a live, priced peril, and a long list of events has slipped, including the Future Investment Initiative conference, the EU-Gulf summit, Intersec Saudi Arabia 2026, the Saudi Retail Forum, the 2027 Dakar Rally, the Saudi International golf tournament, the Red Sea Film Festival, and Riyadh Fashion Week. Pricing for standard cancellation cover has generally held stable this year, Gallagher's Yasmin Dacuycuy said, so the squeeze is concentrated in the war layer. Events that proceed are doing so with lower limits, more exclusions, and in some cases no cancellation insurance at all.

#6145. For under-50 Senate hopefuls, age isn’t just a number

“Young” is a relative term in the Senate.

A majority of members are older than the median retirement age in the U.S., and more sexagenarians are expected to land in the chamber next year. Of the potential newcomers heavily favored to win in Tuesday’s elections, five are in their 60s.

But youth may be a key factor in battleground races this cycle, as candidates look to paint themselves as change-makers and their opponents as hopelessly out of touch with what struggling families need. And that means a good chunk of the incoming freshman class could be under the age of 50.

Democrats, in particular, are eager to move past the recent angst in their party over age.

“Old age has become quite a big liability after seeing what happened in 2024 with [Joe] Biden running for reelection,” said Oscar Pocasangre, a senior data analyst for the Political Reform program at liberal think tank New America. “A lot of people were burned from that experience, and a lot of voters are seeking younger, fresher candidates. That, combined with a huge anti-establishment, anti-incumbent sentiment, has created almost a perfect opening.”

Ten nonincumbents under 50 are running across the 16 Senate races considered in play by Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales. Eight of them are Democrats.

Some are trying to make the most of double-digit age gaps, including 37-year-old James Talarico of Texas, who is 26 years younger than his GOP opponent, Ken Paxton. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, who turns 42 this weekend, is 21 years younger than rival Mike Rogers. And in New Hampshire, 46-year-old Chris Pappas is 16 years younger than John E. Sununu, who is seeking to reclaim the seat he held some two decades ago.

“It’s very clear voters are hungry for new voices at the table and for a new generation of leadership,” said Pappas, a fourth-term congressman. “The electorate is very unsettled. People are rejecting the status quo, and they want change, and that means they want people who are connected to the community, understand how tough it is out there, and are going to work to shake things up in Washington.”

Pappas is seen as a slight favorite to help his party retain the seat of retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, with Inside Elections rating his race Tilt Democratic.

Over the past four freshman classes, the average age of a newly elected senator has ranged from 50 to 58, and the new cohort is all but certain to fall in that ballpark again, according to a CQ Roll Call analysis. While “the Senate could be slightly younger” than before, Pocasangre cautions it won’t make a radical dent in the chamber’s overall average age, which stood at nearly 64 years at the beginning of this Congress.

But midterm voters often signal they want “something different, and that’s what a lot of these young candidates are offering and running on,” Pocasangre said.

The freshman class could also grow the ranks of a rare group in the Senate —  moms with school-aged children. According to Vote Mama Foundation, a nonprofit that aims to make it easier for mothers to run for office, just four women in that category are serving right now.

Among the Democrats hoping to join them is Annie Andrews, a 46-year-old pediatrician, who is making a serious bid in South Carolina against GOP Sen. Darline Graham. Inside Elections recently shifted the race rating from Lean Republican to Tilt Republican, and Graham took the fifth spot on CQ Roll Call’s latest list of the most-vulnerable senators.

Andrews cites her three children and affordability concerns for their future as her main inspiration to run in the ruby-red state, her campaign said.

Peggy Flanagan, Minnesota’s 47-year-old lieutenant governor who appears likely to keep the state’s open Senate seat in Democratic hands, similarly pointed to her kids.

“I have a lot of roles but being a mom is at the core of who I am — it influences all of my actions,” she said in a statement. “I think if we had more than four moms with kids under 18 serving in the United States Senate, this country would be in far better shape. We certainly wouldn’t have passed a bill that takes health care and food away from kids and families, and we’d have more support that helps everyone thrive like universal childcare and paid family leave.”

Others who may join the young-mom group include two House members who’re also the youngest GOP Senate nominees this cycle: Reps. Julia Letlow, 45, of Louisiana and Ashley Hinson, 43, of Iowa.

While Letlow seems likely to prevail, the Iowa race is rated a Toss-up, with the Democratic candidate, Josh Turek — also a young gun at age 47 — remaining neck-and-neck with Hinson in one of Democrats’ biggest pickup opportunities.

“Too many families have been priced out of the American dream because Washington has forgotten how hard people work just to get ahead,” Hinson said in a statement. “When I talk with younger Iowans, I share my plan to make that dream attainable again.”

“And as a mom, I especially love connecting with other moms across Iowa. We understand the challenges of raising kids today, and we’re fighting to make sure the next generation has every opportunity to succeed,” she added.

These potential future senators bring credibility if they can connect with voters’ struggles in ways older senators cannot, Pocasangre said. For example, Flanagan recently bought her first home and paid off her student loans during her tenure as lieutenant governor, two major issues for young voters in America.

Those are issues that N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas, a Democrat running a long-shot campaign for Oklahoma’s open seat against GOP Rep. Kevin Hern, said she understands firsthand as a younger millennial.

“My generation was told that if we went to school, worked hard, and did everything right, we’d be able to build a comfortable life,” Thomas said. “But many of us have experienced rising housing costs, student debt, expensive childcare, stagnant purchasing power, and healthcare that can feel financially out of reach.”

If Thomas, 31, were to succeed in her unlikely bid, she would become the youngest sitting senator, taking the title from Sen. Jon Ossoff, the 39-year-old from Georgia who is favored to fend off a challenge from GOP Rep. Mike Collins.

That title could also go to the 37-year-old Talarico, who major polls show is running ahead of Paxton, though often within the margin of error.

Arkansas Democrat Hallie Shoffner, 39, is also in the under-40 hopefuls club, though GOP Sen. Tom Cotton, only a decade her senior, is expected to easily turn back her challenge.

“What’s best for Arkansas should be intergenerational, but I do believe I bring more energy because I’m not yet 40. My perspective matters because I have an 8-year-old son and parents who are getting older,” she said in a statement. “It’s important to have younger representation because we think longer term out of necessity, not in theory.”

Another young Democrat is Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon, 42, who is running against appointed GOP Sen. Ashley Moody in a race Inside Elections rates as Likely Republican. Pocasangre said Nixon’s ground game helped her defeat a high-profile opponent in the primary and is something other young candidates are leaning on instead of “buying a blitz of ads for radio or TV.”

He pointed to the success of that strategy, coupled with a strong social media presence, for someone like New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

“I think it’s because they recognize people their age are not watching cable TV with ads,” he said “The way to reach these people, it’s either through short-form video, or actually finding them on the street and actually having conversations with them that feels more authentic than a TV ad.”

Those are things that Turek, a former Paralympian, has been highlighting during his campaign, often posting videos to social media of his door-to-door effort and what he calls “stair climbing,” pulling his wheelchair behind him.

And as party leaders in Washington and many Democrats across the country choose confronting corruption as their closing message, it helps to have candidates who aren’t entrenched.

“Younger candidates seem to have an easier time criticizing corruption in politics,” Pocasangre said, pointing to the effort to ban lawmakers from stock trading. “People who are new to politics are very quick to criticize it, but then people who’ve been in politics for a long time are more resistant, or try to deflect from that issue,” he said.

Pappas acknowledged that many voters are skeptical of politicians: People “don’t trust that elected officials are working in the public interest and see a president who’s $2 billion richer, who has brought the corruption out in the open.”

“Voters are really hungry to change the way Washington works, for tough new ethical reforms and to root out all the corruption, and that has to be a centerpiece of the next Congress, if we’re going to regain the confidence of the American people and fix a broken system,” he said.

Ryan Kelly, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari contributed to this report.

S&P and Fitch both described reduced marketing spend and agent commissions, weak direct sales, and outdated systems, with an EBITDA margin of 14% against more than 20% at competitors. Apollo set aside $50 million to upgrade operations. The family kept Red Carnation Hotels, which UK filings show had been funded by a loan of more than £50 million from Travcorp Financial Services at the Bank of England base rate — terms the hotel group's own audited accounts call below market. The London hotel group's losses widened from £1.6 million in 2023 to £7.2 million in 2025, while capital spending rose from £2 million to £7.6 million over the same period.

#6142. James O’Keefe election sting ends in his own felony voter fraud charges

Conservative activist James O’Keefe set out to expose alleged vulnerabilities in Minnesota’s election system. Now, he faces felony charges stemming from the undercover operation.

O’Keefe, formerly of Project Veritas and current CEO of the O’Keefe Media Group, and conservative influencer Cameron Higby were charged Wednesday with unlawful voting and identity theft after allegedly impersonating registered voters at Minneapolis polling places during the state’s Aug. 11 primary.

According to Hennepin County prosecutors, the men wore disguises, used fake accents and provided election workers with the names of registered voters without their knowledge or permission. They filmed the encounters and later posted videos claiming to expose weaknesses in Minnesota’s voter registration procedures.

The operation targeted the state’s *vouching* system, which allows registered voters to verify the residency of people seeking to register on Election Day. The process requires sworn statements and identifying information from prospective voters.

Neither O’Keefe nor Higby cast a ballot or signed the required vouching oath. Prosecutors contend that misrepresenting their identities while beginning the voting process was itself unlawful.

O’Keefe defended the operation as investigative journalism, calling the prosecution an attack on First Amendment rights. Higby also denied breaking the law, saying the pair intended to expose election vulnerabilities.

Start your day with essential news from Salon. Sign up for our free morning newsletter, Crash Course.

The charges are the latest controversy involving O’Keefe’s undercover tactics. In 2017, reporters at the Washington Post caught him trying to sell them a false story. In 2009, he collaborated on hidden-camera investigations targeting Planned Parenthood and gained national attention for videos involving the community organization ACORN. He later settled a lawsuit brought by a former ACORN employee for $100,000 without admitting wrongdoing.

But Minnesota officials say the latest operation demonstrated something different from what O’Keefe intended.

Election workers noticed suspicious behavior and reported it, prompting an investigation. Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said the state’s system for identifying and responding to potential misconduct functioned as intended. This vouching process itself accounted for fewer than 0.6% of votes cast in Minnesota’s 2024 general election, according to state election officials.

O’Keefe and Higby are scheduled to appear in court Nov. 16. Neither has been convicted.

#6131. Final rating changes: 63 races move toward Democrats, 1 toward Republicans

ANALYSIS — In the closing days of the midterm campaign, the fight for the House and Senate is taking place on traditionally Republican turf, including states and districts that would have been unthinkable Democratic targets at the beginning of the cycle.

In total, Inside Elections has made a total of 64 race rating changes this week – 45 in the House, nine in the Senate and 10 for governor. All but one of those contests shift in a direction more favorable to Democrats.

While President Donald Trump’s negative job approval rating is mostly to blame for Republican woes around the country, the rating changes don’t all fit a single mold. Some of the shifts are in swing districts, where it’s clearer that the Democratic nominee has at least a narrow advantage. But GOP candidates are struggling to pull away from their Democratic opponents in red districts and states as well.

Now, there’s a chance that the polls are underestimating Republican support or that GOP-leaning undecided voters will turn out and reluctantly support GOP candidates. But as I wrote two months ago, 2026 feels similar to 2006, when an unpopular Republican president and war in the Middle East created the conditions for a Democratic wave election. The final results could be remarkably the same. Twenty years ago, Democrats flipped both chambers, gaining six Senate seats and 30 House seats.

Democrats appear well on their way to winning the House majority. While they only need a net gain of three seats, Inside Elections’ latest projection is that the party will gain between 20 and 30 seats.

That’s the most bullish projection for Democrats at any point this cycle and a byproduct of the president’s standing and a shifting House battleground. In March 2025, when Inside Elections debuted its House ratings for the cycle, there were 64 races rated as competitive, including 30 Republican-held seats and 34 Democratic seats. Now the battleground has expanded and shifted into GOP territory, with 82 competitive races in all – 55 seats held by Republicans and 27 by Democrats.

In the latest batch of rating changes, 10 GOP-held districts have been added to the House battleground, with the races moving from Solid Republican to Likely Republican. They include Colorado’s 4th District (held by Rep. Lauren Boebert), Kansas’ 2nd (Derek Schmidt), New Jersey’s 2nd (Jeff Van Drew), North Carolina’s 3rd (Greg Murphy), North Carolina’s 9th (Richard Hudson, also the National Republican Congressional Committee chairman), North Carolina’s 13th (Brad Knott), Oklahoma’s 5th (Stephanie Bice), Washington’s 5th (Michael Baumgartner) and Tennessee’s open 9th. The race for Ohio’s 10th District, held by Rep. Michael R. Turner, jumped from Solid Republican all the way to Lean Republican.

Three Democratic-held districts moved off the battleground, going from Likely Democratic to Solid Democratic: California’s 45th (Derek Tran), Virginia’s 7th (Eugene Vindman) and New Hampshire’s 2nd (Maggie Goodlander). In different political circumstances, including if there had been an unpopular Democratic president in the White House, all three districts would have been hosting competitive races.

At the core of the battleground, a dozen races moved out of Toss-up status and are now rated Tilt Democratic: Arizona’s 6th District (held by Republican Rep. Juan Ciscomani), Colorado’s 8th (Republican Gabe Evans), Florida’s 14th (Democrat Kathy Castor), Florida’s 25th (Democrat Jared Moskowitz), North Carolina’s 1st (Democrat Don Davis), Ohio’s 7th (Republican Max Miller), Ohio’s 9th (Democrat Marcy Kaptur), Pennsylvania’s 10th (Republican Scott Perry), Texas’ 15th (Republican Monica De La Cruz), Virginia’s 2nd (Republican Jen Kiggans) and Wisconsin’s 3rd (Republican Derrick Van Orden) and North Carolina’s open 11th District.

And five House races shifted to Toss-up from Tilt Republican: Colorado’s 5th District (Republican Jeff Crank), Michigan’s 4th (Republican Bill Huizenga), Florida’s open 22nd, Kentucky’s open 6th and Montana’s open 1st.

While Republicans mostly drew the new congressional maps, Democratic prospects continue to improve in a handful of races in Ohio, Texas and North Carolina.

While both statewide races for governor and Senate in Ohio shifted from Toss-up to Tilt Democratic, a batch of Buckeye State House races moved toward Democrats as well: The races for Kaptur’s, Miller’s and Turner seats; the 1st District (Democrat Greg Landsman) moved from Tilt Democratic to Lean Democratic; and 15th District (held by Republican Mike Carey) moved from Likely Republican to Lean Republican.

In Texas, at least three of the seats Republicans were counting on winning through redistricting are not looking easy for them. The race for the open 9th District shifts from Likely Republican to Lean Republican, the 28th (Democrat Henry Cuellar) moves from Tilt Democratic to Lean Democratic, and the open 35th goes from Lean Republican to Toss-up.

And North Carolina is developing into a migraine for the GOP as well. Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper is running a strong Senate campaign, and GOP chances in certain House seats are diminishing. In addition to the newly added battleground races, the contests for the 1st and 11th districts are no longer Toss-ups and are now rated Tilt Democratic. CQ Roll Call’s Daniela Altimari was recently on the ground in the 3rd District.

The Senate landscape has changed as well, with the latest rating changes all favoring Democrats. The party needs to flip four seats for a Senate majority, and Inside Elections now projects Democrats to gain between four and six seats.

Two races moved out of Toss-up to Tilt Democratic: Ohio and Texas. Even though Texas Democrats haven’t won statewide in more than 30 years, state Rep. James Talarico has a serious chance to break that losing streak. Polls have shown him narrowly leading GOP nominee Ken Paxton for five months, despite hundreds of millions of dollars in spending against him. Paxton, the state attorney general who defeated GOP Sen. John Cornyn in the primary, could still pull this off, but Talarico has the edge.

Ohio is another extremely expensive race, and Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown is benefiting from a dramatically different political environment compared with two years ago when he lost reelection. Polling shows him with a narrow edge over appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted.

Senate Republicans are also at risk of losing the Iowa and Kansas seats, even though Trump won both states by double digits in 2024. The races could end up reverting to the states’ Republican roots, but for now, Democratic nominees Josh Turek in Iowa and Adam Hamilton in Kansas remain in the hunt. Both races shift from Tilt Republican to Toss-up.

It’s a somewhat similar story in Nebraska (Pete Ricketts) and South Carolina (Darline Graham), two typically Republican states that appear ripe for a Democratic takeover. Both of these races shift from Lean Republican to Tilt Republican. And there’s even enough data and party spending to warrant moving the races in Louisiana (Bill Cassidy’s open seat) and Mississippi (Cindy Hyde-Smith) out of Solid Republican to Likely Republican.

Overall, the latest changes are a continuation of a remarkable shift in the Senate battleground into GOP territory. In January 2025, Inside Elections rated just five Senate races as competitive: three seats held by Democrats (Georgia, Michigan and New Hampshire) and two by Republicans (Maine and North Carolina). Now there are a whopping 16 states on the Senate battleground, divided between 12 Republican-held seats and four by Democrats.

The four gubernatorial open races previously rated Toss-ups – Alaska, Georgia, Ohio and Wisconsin – have now shifted to Tilt Democratic.

In Nevada, Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo has had a consistent advantage over Democratic state Attorney General Aaron Ford, but the national environment could bring him down. That race shifts from Tilt Republican to Toss-up.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, who’s seeking a record fourth term, continues to be in a tight race against Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, proving that Republicans’ problems in the Lone Star State go beyond Paxton’s baggage. That contest moves from Lean Republican to Tilt Republican.

And GOP Sen. Marsha Blackburn appears to be in a surprisingly closer-than-expected race for governor in Tennessee, where a conservative independent candidate is drawing GOP support. Her race moves from Solid Republican to Likely Republican.

Oregon offers a glimmer of hope in what could otherwise be a rough night for Republicans. GOP state Sen. Christine Drazan narrowly lost the gubernatorial election four years ago, but she’s within striking distance in her rematch against unpopular Democratic Gov. Tina Kotek. Oregonians’ frustrations appear centered on the decades of Democratic control at the state level rather than Republican control at the federal level. The race shifts from Lean Democratic to Tilt Democratic.

Here’s the full list of the latest rating changes by Inside Elections:

Alabama’s 2nd District (Shomari Figures, D): from Lean Republican to Tilt Republican

Arizona’s 2nd District (Eli Crane, R): from Likely Republican to Lean Republican

#6129. The dark paradox of Israel’s election — and ours

Benjamin Netanyahu didnât win last weekâs election in Israel. But he didnât exactly lose it either. The real loser may have been Israelâs fragile democracy, already corrupted from within, perhaps past the point of no return, by Netanyahuâs decades-long death-grip on power.

On the eve of a momentous election in the United States, the parallels are both inexact and unavoidable. Israelis must now decide what kind of country they will have, or at least what kind they aspire to have. They must decide whose votes actually count, and whether some citizens are more equal than others.Â

Those same questions also confront Americans, both in this weekâs midterm elections and, in a more general sense, on the larger political and historical stage. No doubt it is tempting for liberals and progressives to express outrage at the blatant flaws and contradictions of Israeli democracy. But to invoke the Christian tradition here, it might be better to remove the plank from your own eye before trying to remove the speck from your brotherâs.Â

On the surface, the electoral arithmetic in Israel appears straightforward. Parties opposed to Netanyahuâs far-right government won 67 of the 120 seats in the Knesset, Israelâs parliament. So a majority coalition of anti-Netanyahu forces is clearly achievable, right? You would think so, except that 19 of those 67 seats were won by Israelâs âArab parties,â an all-time high, and that startling fact has thrown the entire political system into confusion.

Netanyahu and his allies have spent the last week airing groundless allegations that the election was fraudulent or rigged, a refrain that Americans are likely to hear a great deal in coming days. What the Zionist far right means is that too many Israeli Arabs â meaning the Palestinian population that remained in Israel after the state was created in 1948 â decided to vote this time, an outcome that no one expected, and that none of the parties representing the Jewish majority particularly wanted.Â

Now, in a masterstroke of historical or perhaps biblical irony, Israelâs Arab minority â which is not a monolithic group in political or cultural terms, and until now has never been electorally significant â holds the balance of power, and perhaps the nationâs future, in its hands.Â

In a masterstroke of historical or perhaps biblical irony, Israelâs Arab minority â which is not a monolithic group in political or cultural terms, and until now has never been electorally significant â holds the balance of power, and perhaps the nationâs future, in its hands.

Gadi Eisenkot, the former general who leads the centrist-Zionist opposition to Netanyahu, promised during the campaign not to form a government with Arab support. Over the last several nights, thousands of demonstrators in Tel Aviv and Jerusalem have urged him to do precisely that, since the only realistic alternative is the grim default setting of Israeli politics: another wobbly right-wing government headed by Netanyahu, which means more brutality and destruction in Gaza, more war with Iran and more settler violence in the West Bank.Â

As Gideon Levy of the left-leaning Israeli newspaper Haaretz explains it,Â

The future of Israel now depends on its Arab citizens and on the attitude of its Jewish citizens toward its Arab ones. Eighty years after the Nakba and the establishment of the Jewish state, Israeli Palestinians may determine its fate. Is there greater historical justice than that?

The electionâs unexpected results are âa cause for rejoicing,â Levy writes, in that they have presented Israelis with a clear choice âbetween a government led by Benjamin Netanyahu and a government that includes the Arab parties.â If the âchange blocâ within the Zionist majority cannot accept a coalition with Arab Israelis, he continues, âthey will make it clear that they are actually the same as Netanyahu, that they prefer even the devil Netanyahu over repressing their racism. â¦ [E]veryone will know that racism is the supreme value in this country, across the board, above any other value.â

That ferocious language certainly does not represent mainstream Israeli opinion, but itâs fair to say the strong emotion beneath Levyâs words is far more widely felt. I donât think itâs possible for a non-Jewish observer (such as myself), however well educated or sympathetic, to understand the anguish felt by Jewish people â wherever they live, and whatever their political views â at the enormous distance between what Israel originally represented to the world, or claimed to represent, and what it represents now.

Iâm old enough to remember when most American liberals and progressives viewed the state of Israel in overwhelmingly positive terms, as a locus of charismatic or heroic renewal for the people Hitler couldnât kill, infused with the spirit of European socialism and, not far below the surface, the collective guilt of the Holocaust. I grew up in one of the most left-liberal corners of America, surrounded by educated adults who supported the civil rights movement, opposed the Vietnam War, hated Richard Nixon and loved Israel. Golda Meir and Moshe Dayan were beloved celebrities; the Six-Day War of 1967 and the Yom Kippur War of 1973, as narrated by U.S. media, were straight-up battles between the forces of light and darkness.Â

That says more about the moral blindness or willful innocence of American liberalism, I must admit, than it says about Israel. In any event, when I saw Joe Bidenâs fateful bear hug with Netanyahu on the tarmac of Ben Gurion Airport in the aftermath of the dreadful Oct. 7 attack, I understood it. I recognized the country Biden was coming from, because I came from there too: It was the Democratic majority of the not-so-distant past, when Israel was embraced as a light to the nations and left-wing radicals who brought up the Palestinian cause were being unreasonable hotheads, if not openly antisemitic and a little bit Nazi.Â

What Israel has become during Netanyahuâs long and destructive reign is now clear to most of the world, and most of all to the many Jewish or Israeli critics who have been speaking difficult truths for many years, often at enormous personal cost. I am disinclined, however, to judge too harshly those who cling to the vision of Israel as an exceptional nation â one that has stumbled, perhaps, but may yet regain its true path.Â

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only by Amanda Marcotte, also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

Like I said earlier, we should mind the plank in our own eye first. Isnât that the same vision that many Americans still cling to? That somehow, on the other side of this dreadful phase of our history â yes, a full decade of Donald Trump, but Iâm afraid the damage goes back a lot further than that â the âindispensable nationâ variously articulated by Abraham Lincoln, John F. Kennedy and Barack Obama is still there, still retrievable, still bending its moral arc toward justice.

Americans and Israelis are conjoined by history, for better or worse, and now see each other as distorted reflections, through a glass darkly, as the King James Bible puts it. We face versions of the same decisions this week, about whose votes count and whether the highfalutin words of our constitution apply to everyone. About whether to see terror and tyranny for what they are, and turn the page.

from Andrew OâHehir on our bewildering world

#6126. The strange new math behind the price of your groceries

Walmart recently published a list of things it promises not to do to its customers.

“We price the product, not the person,” Walmart CEO John Furner announced in a September letter to customers. “Your income, shopping history, urgency or what we think you could pay won’t change the price,” he promised. Nor, he said, would the retailer’s AI shopping assistant, Sparky, use information customers shared to raise prices or conceal cheaper options.

This was nice to hear. I hadn’t previously considered that telling a computer I needed toilet paper might result in an emergency toilet-paper rate. There is something faintly unnerving about the specificity of a corporate reassurance, particularly when it introduces several possibilities you hadn’t thought to worry about.

It made me preemptively nostalgic for the little paper price tag beneath a box of cereal. There’s something reassuringly stupid about it. It tells you what the cereal costs. It doesn’t know how much money you make, whether you’re in a hurry or what the temperature is outside. Unless an employee comes along with a new sticker, the person reaching for the same box ten minutes later sees the same number. A modest achievement, perhaps, but one I’m growing increasingly fond of.

The appeal isn’t really the paper. It’s the transparency of the arrangement. As retailers gather more information about their customers and acquire increasingly sophisticated pricing tools, shoppers risk knowing less about why they’re paying what they’re paying. The problem isn’t simply higher grocery bills. It’s the possibility of a transaction in which one side can examine the other in exquisite detail, while the other can barely see the rules.

What prompted the letter from Furner is that Walmart is expanding its use of electronic shelf labels, little screens that let employees update prices digitally from a central computer instead of replacing stickers by hand. The change makes sense. Furner points out that updating paper tags is tedious work, and he’d rather employees spend their afternoons helping customers than tending to a small forest of adhesive rectangles. Digital labels can also help ensure the price on the shelf matches the price at checkout.

And electronic labels aren’t, in themselves, surge pricing. Walmart says it doesn’t use them to change prices according to who is shopping or the time of day. But efficiency is a different question from trust. Making a price easier to change isn’t necessarily a problem. Making it harder to understand how that price was reached might be.

Want more great food writing and recipes? Sign up for Salon’s free food newsletter, The Bite.

We’ve already accepted a surprisingly elaborate set of conditions for saving money on groceries. Download the app. Make an account. Remember the password. Clip the digital coupon before you leave home. After handing over our personal information and completing several minor administrative tasks, we’re permitted to save 75 cents on yogurt. The store, meanwhile, gets a rather detailed account of our preferences. What happens when that bargain runs in reverse?

Last December, Consumer Reports and Groundwork Collaborative found that shoppers using Instacart were sometimes shown different prices for identical groceries from the same store at the same time. At one Safeway in Washington, D.C., an 18-ounce box of Signature SELECT Corn Flakes appeared for $2.99, $3.49 and $3.69, depending on whose screen you were looking at.

Instacart said the shoppers were assigned to pricing experiments randomly, not sorted by income, demographics or browsing history. It ended the tests after the investigation. That distinction matters, especially because the research didn’t establish that anyone’s personal habits were being used against them. But it demonstrated how quietly prices can diverge when the shopper sees only the number assigned to her. You can’t question a difference you have no way of seeing.

I buy a lot of black beans. Enough, presumably, that a supermarket’s software could identify me as a woman with firm opinions about legumes. If that earns me a coupon, wonderful. I’m considerably less enthusiastic about the possibility of an algorithm deciding that my apparent dependence on black beans means I could stand to pay another 30 cents per can. It’s one thing to recognize a loyal customer. It’s another to recognize a captive audience.

Other pricing algorithms raise different questions (McDonald’s, for instance, faces a lawsuit alleging AI-assisted price coordination among franchises, which the company denies). Prices have always fluctuated; coupons have always rewarded some shoppers more than others. Nor should computers be banished from the business of deciding what things cost. But the supermarket is not an airline, and dinner should not require the same vigilance as booking a flight.

Walmart’s promise is worth taking seriously. The company has drawn a clear line around how it says it will use customer information, and that’s preferable to leaving shoppers guessing. But it’s a corporate commitment, not a rule every retailer must follow. And the fact that a supermarket now feels obliged to assure us it won’t charge extra because we seem hurried or financially comfortable suggests how strange our expectations have become.

Perhaps it’s naive to want a supermarket not to use what it knows about me against me. Still, I don’t need the price tag to know me. I need it to tell me what the cereal costs.

#6123. Fox News loses its grip on the culture wars

In any other election cycle, a viral Fox News gaffe would have registered only as a momentary laugh. Last week, reporter Lucas Tomlinson was covering a South Carolina rally for incumbent Republican Sen. Darline Graham, who is seeking to serve a full term following the death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham. In reality, the event was more about Donald Trump, who had flown to the Palmetto State to help shore up Graham’s candidacy, which increasingly appears to be at-risk. Spotting a middle-aged white man with a beard, Tomlinson assumed he was about to get some choice footage of a gushing Trump superfan. Instead, Tom Hoyle, with an admirable deadpan, joked that he had turned out for the rally because he was too young to have witnessed the 1978 Jonestown massacre, in which 918 followers of Rev. Jim Jones died after drinking a fruit drink laced with poison. “There’s nothing like seeing a cult right up front, man,” he added.

“All right, maybe this is not a Trump supporter,” Tomlinson said, scurrying away.

The surreal moment capped what has been a desultory midterm election season for Fox, a network that bills itself as “news” but has long been seen by fans and detractors alike as Republican propaganda. Despite their largely worshipful coverage of the president, Trump has been complaining that the network isn’t doing enough to salvage the campaigns of the GOP.

“FoxNews is spending far too much time putting on the OPPONENTS of Republican Party Candidates,” he recently posted on Truth Social, echoing his prior complaints that the network focuses too much on the Democrats running this cycle than on their Republican opponents.

Trump is not wrong about the coverage tilt. According to Media Matters, during this election cycle the network has mentioned the names of Democratic candidates at over three times the rate of Republicans. That disparity, though, doesn’t mean the coverage is sympathetic. To the contrary: Fox producers likely recognize that this year’s GOP field of candidates is deeply uninspiring. Some, such as Vivek Ramaswamy, who is running for governor of Ohio, and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is seeking a Senate seat, are so repulsive that even lifelong Republicans can’t pretend to like them.

This season, Democratic candidates are making more compelling TV, particularly the charismatic incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., Michigan’s Senate nominee Dr. Abdul El-Sayed and Texas state representative James Talarico, who is running against Paxton. The most Fox News can hope for is to hijack these candidates’ ability to command attention, and then use it to drive negative polarization with endless “who do these people think they are?” outrage. But then again, the network knows its audience.

As Salon’s Sophia Tesfaye recently noted, it’s not like Fox News knows what else to do. The hosts, she writes, have been grabbing wildly at straws, praying they can find any story to spark culture war hysteria that will distract voters from serious issues like inflation, the war with Iran or the metastasizing deportation crisis. The network tried to make hay out of the French riots, but even Fox viewers struggled to see why student protests in Paris matter to America. It attempted to pretend Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., was calling for mass arrests of young Republicans when she was asked during a recent appearance about holding the GOP accountable, but that never really caught on either. A last-minute gambit to feign outrage over Barack Obama’s recent joke comparing Trump’s White House decor to the Cheesecake Factory fizzled out as well, likely because it simply reminded people of how the current resident is defiling the People’s House.

Part of Fox’s problem is immediate. Many voters’ economic woes are sky-high, making it hard for culture war nonsense to feel relevant. But there’s also a longer-term problem for the network, which is that they don’t make as much sense as they used to.

Fox News has long existed to dress up gutter bigotries and far-right paranoia in the clothes of respectable news coverage, mostly through the use of dog whistles and innuendo. In the past, winks at some of the fouler ideas out there was enough to titillate the audience while keeping up the pretense of respectability. But now, that stuff seems dated and out of touch.

This is an era when, as Jamelle Bouie of New York Times said on YouTube, the actual president offers “Klansman-level racism” from the campaign stump, calling Black people “low IQ,” flinging a slur for transgender people at Democratic politicians and suggesting that El-Sayed’s Muslim faith makes him a terrorist. Right-wing social media, especially the Elon Musk-owned X, reads like Stormfront message boards from the 1990s, with Musk himself regularly promoting white nationalist ideas and memes. Former Fox hosts Megyn Kelly and Tucker Carlson offer their former employer stiff competition by being more dishonest and outrageous than the lawsuit-wary network can be, with segments suggesting only supermodel-hot women get raped or that Holocaust deniers have a point.

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only, written by Amanda Marcotte, now also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

But according to Salon’s Alex Galbraith, one Fox host seems to be getting sick of his network’s culture war strategy. Jesse Watters has complained openly on air about how bad the GOP is doing and how Fox coverage isn’t doing much to excite their audience. In one particularly telling segment, he lashed out about the relentless attention Fox News gives to non-stories from the WNBA, including hysteria over trans players, of which there are zero.

“I don’t want to push this story anymore!” Watters said. “I want to leave this story alone! I am no longer talking about the WNBA. As of now, I boycott this segment.”

Although his reasoning may differ, the host is right that the Fox fixation on the WNBA is stupid. The league has become such an obsession on the right because, plainly put, many male conservatives hate seeing female athletes perform feats they couldn’t even manage in their youth. They want to end professional women’s sports and return to the sexist delusion that all men are stronger and faster than all women. This much is evident in how real-life right-wingers behave toward the WNBA, such as going so far as to buy tickets so they can throw sex toys at the players.

Fox hosts are careful to never say outright that women shouldn’t play sports; that, as they well know, could alienate millions of Republican voters, especially women and fathers of female athletes who are more moderate on this issue. Instead, the network attempts to hijack the antipathy many conservatives feel toward female basketball players with their traditional wink-and-nudge coverage, pretending they want to “clean up” the sport. This preserves the illusion that the right doesn’t hate female athletes while portraying the players — the white ones at least — as fragile, helping to reassure an insecure male audience.

In the past, this kind of tap dance has worked. Now, as Watters implied, it’s floundering, feeling much too tepid when compared Fox’s online competitors and actual politicians flinging unprintable slurs. Watters suggested as much during another segment, when he argued that Republicans need more “fear porn” if they want to win.

His use of the word “porn” is telling. Watters was arguing that it doesn’t do to be coy any longer — that only the hard-core stuff will move the base. But for Fox News, that would come at the cost of losing advertising dollars and the eyeballs of less radical viewers. This is a true dilemma — and it’s one that couldn’t happen to a more deserving network.

Argument: Europe Was Never Meant to Be a ‘Regulatory Superpower’

Over the decades, the European Union has weathered recessions and revolutions, internal fissures and external threats. It has seen the Iron Curtain teeter and fall and watched as the world order shifted from bipolar to unipolar to something else entirely. Through it all, the EU has proved remarkably durable, but threats loom on the horizon.

The EU now faces a dizzying array of challenges. To the east, Russia’s grinding invasion of Ukraine strains European budgets, imperils fragile supply chains, and jeopardizes the longevity of the European project. Across the Atlantic, meanwhile, Washington has adopted a challenging stance on a variety of issues, placing mounting pressure on the trans-Atlantic relationship. And economic stagnation, soaring energy prices, and an ongoing migration crisis have further corroded European cohesion, contributing to widespread dissatisfaction and mounting distrust.

Over the decades, the European Union has weathered recessions and revolutions, internal fissures and external threats. It has seen the Iron Curtain teeter and fall and watched as the world order shifted from bipolar to unipolar to something else entirely. Through it all, the EU has proved remarkably durable, but threats loom on the horizon.

The EU now faces a dizzying array of challenges. To the east, Russia’s grinding invasion of Ukraine strains European budgets, imperils fragile supply chains, and jeopardizes the longevity of the European project. Across the Atlantic, meanwhile, Washington has adopted a challenging stance on a variety of issues, placing mounting pressure on the trans-Atlantic relationship. China’s use of predatory economics threatens the old continent’s export industry and its economic model. And economic stagnation, soaring energy prices, and an ongoing migration crisis have further corroded European cohesion, contributing to widespread dissatisfaction and mounting distrust.

These developments have left the EU in a precarious position. While the grouping was once a leading force in the global economy, decades of lax industrial policy and heavy regulations have eroded its influence. As recently as 1980, the 27 EU member states collectively accounted for approximately 34 percent of global GDP. Industrial output remains anemic, while the European tech sector continues to lag well behind foreign competitors, and productivity slows year on year.

In response, Brussels has fallen back on familiar logic. Rather than embracing uncertainty, the EU has sought to reassert control over it by turning once again to its vaunted regulatory ecosystem. For many European leaders, the continent’s strength lies not in military might or industrial productivity but in its ability to shape global rules and standards. The bloc has increasingly been described as a “regulatory superpower,” capable of projecting its normative power far beyond its borders. International trade expert Anu Bradford has dubbed this concept the “Brussels Effect,” arguing that regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation and the EU Artificial Intelligence Act have given the EU outsized influence over international economic standards. Advocates of this vision argue that for countries and companies interested in accessing the continent’s vast and wealthy internal market, adapting to European regulations is a small price to pay. European Commission Vice President Teresa Ribera went so far as to say these rules are “non-negotiable.”

But Robert Schuman and the EU’s founding fathers never intended to build a union focused on bringing companies to their knees—rather, they wanted to build one capable of standing up to foreign adversaries. The regulatory approach is outdated, too. Thankfully, the EU has another, even more potent tool in its arsenal: trade.

In its earliest incarnation—the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC)—the EU was almost exclusively an economic construct. The ECSC and its successor, the European Economic Community, were built primarily to amplify European economic influence by linking and coordinating the continent’s diverse economies. Individually, member states were relatively inconsequential; as a collective, they were a force to be reckoned with. But as the EU has matured, national leaders deprioritized competitiveness, and the bloc’s economic dynamism has dwindled. Many leading European firms have grown sclerotic with age, resting on historical legacies while foreign counterparts have surged ahead. And despite EU efforts to build a thriving start-up ecosystem, byzantine regulatory regimes and heavy tax burdens have continued to hamper growth. Brussels has lost its edge, and regulations are not the solution.

Meanwhile, the United States has abandoned global rules it deems obstacles to its own prosperity. It has replaced multilateral committees with bilateral dealmaking, de facto free trade with a realist-inspired industrial policy. U.S. tech firms have been empowered to act as implements of American power, becoming formidable international actors in their own right. Against this backdrop, the EU’s outdated commitment to red tape and regulations is potentially more of a burden than a boon.

According to the International Monetary Fund, red tape in the EU acts as a hidden tax, amounting to 44 percent on goods and up to 110 percent on services. Similarly, a recent report by the Information Technology & Innovation Foundation estimated that EU regulations have cost European businesses about $176 billion annually, equivalent to nearly 1 percent of collective GDP. Former Italian Prime Minister Mario Draghi railed against overzealous regulation in his 2024 report.

Organizations and governments do not have to choose between regulation and trade. In the age of AI, Europe’s regulatory skill could be an asset. But European states still have to choose what to prioritize and where to allocate finite political capital. Rather than doubling down on rule-making, Brussels should work to more effectively bring its vast economic resources to bear.

Indeed, it can be easy to overlook the EU’s massive economic footprint. Collectively, the bloc’s economy ranks as the world’s Its 27 member states boast a combined population of more than 450 million, accounting for approximately 5.5 percent of the global population. By international standards, EU citizens are exceedingly wealthy, controlling a total household income of some in 2024. This vast and affluent pool of consumers has made the EU an irresistible target for international trade partners.

By most metrics, the EU is the world’s largest trade power. Accounting for 16 percent of total world trade in goods and services, the bloc . Brussels currently maintains 45 trade agreements with more than 80 countries and territories from Mercosur to Indonesia. Collectively, these agreements encompass more than 2 billion people and a combined GDP in the tens of trillions of dollars. By some estimates, the EU’s trade network accounts for upwards of 52 percent of global trade.

Despite its immense economic importance, the EU has increasingly found itself on the outside looking in, particularly since the 2008 global financial crisis. To remedy this, European leaders have proposed a raft of reforms. A growing contingent has advocated for increased European defense integration, including massive investments in defense manufacturing and interoperability.

Some political leaders have argued that investing in the continent’s underdeveloped defense industrial base through an EU Defense Union can not only prepare Europe for conflict but also catalyze investment and create new jobs. This analysis is correct, but it is ultimately a long-term solution to an urgent, short-term problem. Reinvigorating Europe’s defense sector alone will not fix a stagnant economy. The political cost would be exceedingly high, while reactivating factories and building new armed forces could take well over a decade. The truth of the matter is that the EU was never intended to be a defense alliance, as failed negotiations on the subject in the 1950s and 1980s can attest.

The EU’s founders believed that by pooling together the industries of their individual countries, they could stand tall against foreign pressure, particularly from the Soviet Union. The European leaders of today should seize that same mentality to become a trade superpower, becoming a source of certainty, fair trade, and investment in an ever more uncertain and fractured world.

By signing new trade agreements with major economies in Africa and creating investment vehicles for infrastructure in emerging economies, Europe can become the world’s partner of choice. Importantly, the EU should promulgate a new trade architecture that seeks to a) connect opposing blocs; b) secure critical minerals and needed resources; c) invest in partners’ trade infrastructure; and d) expand trade agreements with existing partners and sign new ones. The EU free trade agreements with India and Mercosur, signed earlier this year, are two excellent steps in this direction.

This new strategy, however, should include distinct approaches for exports and imports.

The EU is heavily exposed to China for its rare-earth consumption, with Beijing supplying . To reduce this dependence, Brussels should proactively pursue bilateral mineral agreements with resource-rich nations, such as the Philippines, Indonesia, or Mexico. The goal should go beyond importing raw ore to be processed in Europe, to invest in those countries’ refining capacity. By doing so with dozens of mineral-rich countries, the EU could become the main trading house for critical minerals, leveraging a network of free trade agreements without parallel. By doing so, Brussels would develop significant influence in ensuring prices remain stable and advantageous to European interests. The Global Gateway, an EU program seeking to challenge China’s Belt and Road Initiative, is already poised to be the main vehicle for this proposal. To be clear, the EU should avoid any temptation to engage in predatory “resource colonialism.” Instead, this new strategy would treat resource-rich nations as equal partners, channeling investments into their territories to refine minerals there while granting market access in return.

On the export side, however, Europe still has great strengths to contribute to the global economy. Brussels would be wise to leverage them. The developing world has a growing need for readily available capital and credit from trustworthy institutions. Africa and Latin America have the highest percentages of unbanked populations in the world. European banks, many of which already have operations in these regions, should be empowered to expand operations, providing the capital that will unlock future prosperity. Through a combination of bilateral financing and capital deals with those countries, the agreement of standards under a new Basel agreement, and the creation of a Savings and Investments Union, the EU can strip away the red tape that currently holds these firms back. Doing so would bolster Europe’s banking sector while cementing its role as a financial powerhouse.

The same is true for chemicals, pharmaceutical ingredients, and heavy machinery. All of these industries are led by historic European firms, and they are the base of advanced industry, export capacity, and future prosperity. To maximize the effectiveness of its industrial champions, however, European capitals must first complete the Single Market and allow for the free movement of capital, investments, and banks.

Choosing this new path will require a shift in mentality in Brussels. For decades, policymakers have sought power in regulating the economy. Now, they must choose to lead it. Acting as a connector of parties and an economic gravitational pole, the EU can both gain a position of leadership and contribute to stabilizing this brave new world.

The plan will also need to be sold to the people of Europe, which won’t be easy as Euroskeptic movements surge in many EU member states. But carrying on the current path will only result in a weaker, less prosperous Europe. Regardless of ideology, European political leaders will have to explain to their voters that their national prosperity depends on Europe’s prosperity. On their own, European states are vulnerable and subject to external pressure. Together, they could be a colossus.

Eduardo Castellet Nogués is a research fellow at GLOBSEC, focusing on EU-U.S.-China relations and critical minerals.

Marshall Reid is the senior manager of U.S.-EU-Asia dynamics at the Bertelsmann Foundation.
