#6119. Democrat Haley Stevens endorses GOP Senate nominee in Michigan

Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost a Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed this summer, has endorsed his Republican rival, former Rep. Mike Rogers, a startling development in a race that could help decide control of the chamber.

“As you may have seen, our Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, Abdul, said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away. And he’s right. And that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers,” she said Sunday in a video posted to social media. “I don’t belong in Abdul’s campaign.”

Earlier in the day, Stevens attended a church service in downtown Detroit with Rogers, which was captured by local reporters.

An automated email response from Stevens’ Capitol Hill communications director on Sunday said he was no longer with her office as of Nov. 1.

Stevens’ appearance with Rogers, a former congressman, comes after a contentious few days that saw her fiancé, Jason Turkish, endorse Rogers and a planned Sunday event featuring Stevens and El-Sayed at another church fall through.

Stevens and El-Sayed, a former Wayne County health director, went through a divisive primary campaign, in which tensions flared over the topic of Israel and its war in Gaza. El-Sayed criticized Stevens’ support for funding Israel’s military and ultimately overcame millions of dollars in attack ads by the political arm of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee to win by less than a percentage point.

Stevens endorsed El-Sayed after the primary, but the tensions over Israel lingered and carried into the general election campaign. The Rogers campaign launched an effort to win over Stevens supporters. Some Jewish Democrats in Michigan have continued to express uneasiness with El-Sayed, saying his anti-Israel rhetoric risks fueling antisemitism.

But Democrats have also criticized Republican attacks on El-Sayed over his faith. At a rally in Michigan last month, President Donald Trump baselessly accused him of being a “jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member.” If elected, El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, would be the first Muslim senator.

Much of the current Democratic discord in Michigan centered around an ad from the progressive outside group Rebellion PAC, which tied U.S. financial support for Israel to the high cost of groceries. Jewish community leaders and others criticized the spot, saying it invoked antisemitic tropes.

After Turkish, who is Jewish, appeared at a Rogers event earlier this week, Stevens maintained that she would be supporting El-Sayed, saying hers was a “household divided.” But she called on El-Sayed to denounce the Rebellion PAC ad and to take down a campaign spot that featured conservative commentator Tucker Carlson.

That was followed by reporting that the pair would appear together this weekend. Stevens released a statement Friday stating that she would attend a church service in Detroit with South Carolina Rep. James E. Clyburn, the former No. 3 House Democrat, and El-Sayed. But she again called for her primary rival to disavow the Rebellion PAC ad and accused him of blaming Israel as “the reason Michigan cannot afford schools, health care, and child care.”

“If those words are wrong when a Political Action Committee supporting his campaign says them, then they are equally wrong when Abdul says them, and Abdul has said them from the start,” she said. “I therefore expect him to apologize for those statements as well.”

El-Sayed, whose campaign emphasized that the ad was “not affiliated in any way” with his campaign, stressed the stakes of the Senate race in a statement Friday, noting that “defeating [Donald] Trump’s hand-picked candidate, taking back the Senate, and defending our democracy” were top priorities.

“Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago,” he said. Politico reported Saturday that his campaign also asked Stevens to stay away from campaign events in the closing days of the race.

At a campaign stop Saturday, El-Sayed again distanced himself from the Rebellion PAC ad, saying, “I’ve already made it clear that that ad was not made by me, and I do not agree with the contents of that ad,” according to Spectrum News.

In her video Sunday, Stevens said she was “still a very proud Democrat” and “still very much [believes] in everything I voted for and said.”

But her endorsement of Rogers drew scorn from many in her party.

“Haley Stevens’ decision to campaign with Rogers — a man who has repeatedly sold out Michigan’s working class, wants to pass a national abortion ban, and has pledged to be a loyal vote for Trump’s agenda — shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about,” Curtis Hertel, the chair of the Michigan Democratic party, said in a statement.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, who endorsed Stevens during the primary, called her move a “despicable betrayal.”

“Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors,” the New York Democrat said on social media.

In a statement, Schumer also took aim at what he described as “the racist, Islamophobic, and over-the-top false attacks on Abdul by Republicans.”

“These attacks are evidence of the total bankruptcy of the Republican Party today, who resort to ugly and un-American fearmongering because they have nothing to offer on the problems that concern people today,” he said.

Coming out of the church service Sunday with Clyburn and Maryland Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, El-Sayed did not elaborate on Stevens’ decision to endorse Rogers.

“At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens,” he told reporters. “I think about the 9,999,998 people who are not those two, because, you know what, I’m just less interested in the politics of it all than I am in the policy of it all.”

Michigan Rep. Debbie Dingell, who reportedly also attended the church service, said voters in the state were talking about affordability, “not Congresswoman Stevens’ continued efforts to get attention.”

“If we are going to fight to improve the lives of working men and women in Michigan, we must stay focused on electing Democrats up and down the ballot, and that includes electing Abdul El-Sayed as Michigan’s next senator,” she said in a statement.

#6113. Is the UAE the Missing Link in the Fight Against the Houthis?

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Analysis: Is the UAE the Missing Link in the Fight Against the Houthis?

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Saudi Arabia has a growing list of problems in its escalating war against the Houthis in Yemen, which has entered one of its deadliest chapters since it began more than a decade ago.

The Iran-backed Houthis made major territorial gains along the Red Sea coast in a blistering offensive last month, and there’s been a sharp rise in deadly attacks on Saudi territory by the Houthis in recent weeks, including a strike on Oct. 10 on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport that killed at least 13 people and injured more than 300.

Saudi Arabia has a growing list of problems in its escalating war against the Houthis in Yemen, which has entered one of its deadliest chapters since it began more than a decade ago.

The Iran-backed Houthis made major territorial gains along the Red Sea coast in a blistering offensive last month, and there’s been a sharp rise in deadly attacks on Saudi territory by the Houthis in recent weeks, including a strike on Oct. 10 on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport that killed at least 13 people and injured more than 300.

Saudi Arabia has struggled to convince international partners to join the fight or offer support beyond defensive assistance—with powerful allies such as the United States refusing to intervene. The Saudi-backed coalition fighting to push back the Houthis on the ground in Yemen has also had mixed success.

A huge part of the problem in the fight is the lack of cohesion among anti-Houthi forces in southern Yemen, which is linked to tensions between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. A leading Yemen expert said that Riyadh and Abu Dhabi reconciling—and leveraging both the UAE’s military effectiveness and influence over anti-Houthi Yemeni factions—could be a gamechanger in the fight.

“It’s the most important thing that could happen to change the course of the battle on the ground,” said April Longley Alley, a senior fellow at The Washington Institute whose research focuses on Yemen and the Gulf. But it’s also a “complicated challenge to reconcile,” Alley said, due to “bitterness” between Riyadh and Abu Dhabi over what’s happened in Yemen, as well as tensions over Sudan and “wider regional competition.”

The war in Yemen began in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and overthrew the country’s government. In response, a Saudi-led coalition of Gulf countries, including the UAE, launched a military campaign against the group to try and restore the government. But although Riyadh and Abu Dhabi entered the conflict as allies, their regional ambitions have since driven a wedge between them.

Those tensions reached a boiling point last December, leading the UAE to disengage from Yemen. Analysts see this as among the many factors contributing to fragmentation among anti-Houthi forces.

“If there could be some kind of alignment between the Saudis and the Emiratis that brought the Emiratis back” in a way that helped reinforce the southern front and along the Red Sea coast, Alley said, then that would “probably be the best chance the Yemeni government and the Saudis have to really have a more effective counteroffensive.”

“To turn the tide on the ground, there needs to be more effective command-and-control systems to these local groups,” Alley said. The UAE could be essential in this regard, Alley said, because of their experience working with local forces in Yemen and the networks they still have.

Given that both countries view the Houthis as a threat, there have been some signs of rapprochement between Saudi Arabia and the UAE since full-scale war returned to Yemen.

Following recent discussions between the two, the UAE has reportedly agreed to resume funding for forces in southern Yemen. The latest known talks occurred on Oct. 18, when Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman met UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in Abu Dhabi. But details of progress and precisely what’s been agreed to are still hazy. The UAE’s Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment on this.

Differences remain on a range of issues, and further UAE involvement in Yemen is likely to depend, in part, on how Riyadh approaches questions over Yemen’s political future—including the aims of separatist groups with long-running ties to Abu Dhabi like the Southern Transitional Council (STC). Southern separatist forces have been allied with the UAE for years, and Abu Dhabi “would want their demands represented very clearly in a political settlement,” Alley said.

Abu Dhabi also has concerns about what role any group associated with the Muslim Brotherhood, such as the Islah party, will play.

Yemen was divided in two from 1967 to 1990, with the Yemen Arab Republic in the north and the People’s Democratic Republic of Yemen in the south. The STC has pushed for an independent state in southern Yemen with the borders prior to the unification of the country in 1990. Saudi Arabia, which wants a united Yemen, has opposed this.

The STC has a deeply complicated relationship with the Saudi-backed government in Yemen, largely because of its secessionist aims. It has been aligned with the Saudi-backed government in the past but has also fought against it—most notably in January, after the STC seized two provinces the month before. Riyadh saw this as a threat to its national security and helped government forces retake those areas. The group subsequently went through a contested dissolution, and the STC’s leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, fled to Abu Dhabi. The STC retains influence in southern Yemen despite the setbacks that it faced earlier this year.

Saudi Arabia also bombed a UAE arms shipment to Yemen in late December as it moved to reverse STC advances. This led Abu Dhabi to withdraw its forces from Yemen. Riyadh subsequently took up the mantle of restructuring anti-Houthi forces—and it has struggled to fill the void and unify rival militias after the UAE’s exit.

“Since Abu Dhabi left, there was a huge vacuum of deterrence against the Houthis and managing the situation, especially regarding the operational capabilities on the ground,” said Amr al-Bidh, a top STC official.

“We worked with the UAE for a long time in countering terrorism, fighting the Houthis, managing the areas in the south, doing all of the humanitarian work together. We’ve done a lot of work together, and we trust them,” Bidh said, describing the UAE as a “very efficient ally.”

But Bidh said that it remains unclear in what capacity the UAE would return to the conflict in Yemen. “Is it just financing as we’ve heard, or something more?” he said, adding that if Abu Dhabi does get directly involved again, it will “definitely help” politically and militarily in certain aspects.

The STC has signaled that it will not fight beyond the borders of old southern Yemen until Riyadh agrees to its call for an independence referendum.

“Our main concern is to defend our areas. Defending the south is our main objective here,” Bidh said.

The Saudi ambassador in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As things stand, it does not appear that Riyadh would be willing to make a grand compromise to bring the UAE back in. “It doesn’t seem like they’re there yet,” Alley said.

Given the stakes and how rapidly the situation is changing on the ground, however, the Saudi government may feel compelled to rethink its position.

When asked whether Yemen’s internationally recognized government would welcome more involvement from the UAE in the fight, Ambassador Marwan Ali Noman, political advisor to Yemeni Foreign Minister Afrah al-Zouba, said, “We welcome every step to have a united position in the region.”

“The Houthi threat is a threat to everyone,” Noman said, noting that Abu Dhabi was attacked by the Houthis in 2022. “But I’m not aware, of course, about the talks between the Saudis and the Emiratis.”

John Haltiwanger is a staff writer at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @jchaltiwanger.bsky.social X: @jchaltiwanger

#6111. Sen. Murphy ‘awake and alert’ after stroke

Sen. Christopher S. Murphy was hospitalized after having a stroke on Saturday, the Connecticut Democrat’s office said in a statement.

The 53-year-old started experiencing “numbness in his arm while at his son’s hockey game” and was “was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke,” Allison Herwitt, Murphy’s chief of staff, said Sunday.

“He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment,” Herwitt said. “The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery.”

Murphy is closing in on his second decade in Congress. He was first elected to the House in 2006, and, six years later, won election to the Senate, where he is currently in his third term. In recent weeks, the potential 2028 presidential contender has campaigned for Democrats across the country ahead of the midterm elections. Earlier this month, he also traveled to Qatar and Saudi Arabia.

Murphy is one of several senators who have experienced strokes in recent years.

Democratic Sens. Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland were hospitalized in 2022. Before his election to the Senate the same year, Pennsylvania Democrat John Fetterman had a stroke that led to speech and auditory issues.

#6108. No One Has a Plan for American Decline

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Argument: No One Has a Plan for American Decline

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

America’s geopolitical power is crumbling, and that shouldn’t be too much of a surprise. Hegemons, after all, rise and fall. Yet nobody in U.S. politics or punditry seems to actually want to talk about the consequences, especially for the American people. When it comes to decline, they either believe it won’t happen or won’t matter—in other words, that America can’t decline or that Americans will be just fine if it does.

Many in the neoconservative and traditionally conservative wings of the Republican Party believe that with the renewed application of its still considerable military and political power, America can remain the world’s dominant power for the foreseeable future. Republican restrainers, in turn, believe that if America forsakes dominance and conserves its power, global disorder can be kept at bay and the American people will be better for it. And while key figures in President Donald Trump’s orbit are all too worried about decline in racial or civilizational terms, they have their own dangerous and counterproductive ideas for how to reverse it.

America’s geopolitical power is crumbling, and that shouldn’t be too much of a surprise. Hegemons, after all, rise and fall. Yet nobody in U.S. politics or punditry seems to actually want to talk about the consequences, especially for the American people. When it comes to decline, they either believe it won’t happen or won’t matter—in other words, that America can’t decline or that Americans will be just fine if it does.

Many in the neoconservative and traditionally conservative wings of the Republican Party believe that with the renewed application of its still considerable military and political power, America can remain the world’s dominant power for the foreseeable future. Republican restrainers, in turn, believe that if America forsakes dominance and conserves its power, global disorder can be kept at bay and the American people will be better for it. And while key figures in President Donald Trump’s orbit are all too worried about decline in racial or civilizational terms, they have their own dangerous and counterproductive ideas for how to reverse it.

On the Democratic side, many in the more traditional, liberal internationalist wing of the party maintain, with more modesty than their neoconservative counterparts, that Washington can still lead the way in renewing a global order that will broadly serve U.S. interests. Finally, the progressive wing of the party is convinced that a more restrained foreign policy will bring peace to the world and prosperity to ordinary voters, with the only negative consequences borne by the billionaire class.

But what if everyone’s right about the wrong things? The worst possible outcome would be if the restrainers prove correct about the fact that sustaining America’s global preeminence is no longer possible, and the neocons and liberal internationalists prove right about all the bad results. What if ordinary Americans really did benefit from the unique international stature of the United States, and will sorely miss it when it’s gone?

A protester holding a cardboard sign that reads “People Over Billionaires” takes part in a national day of protest in New York on March 28. Jerome Gilles/NurPhoto via Getty Images

Much as Trump’s presidency has served as a catalyst for American decline, his open disdain for the U.S. foreign-policy consensus has catalyzed the debate over what went wrong and what comes next.

Committed champions of Washington’s traditional foreign policy lament that voters no longer seem to support American global leadership. On the other side, many progressives and pro-restraint conservatives have argued that, however duplicitously, Trump channeled the public’s justified anger over Washington’s failed commitment to global hegemony.

But there’s an alternative, more worrying, story about what Americans really gained from their country’s unprecedented geopolitical power and why they concluded these gains were no longer being realized.

Over the course of the Cold War, and all the more so immediately after, U.S. foreign policy largely delivered voters the benefits of hegemony—both material and psychological—without the cost of extensive foreign wars.

In both good ways and bad, U.S. power helped underpin an extraordinary expansion of global trade and industrialization from which America and Americans grew wealthy. Washington defended democratic stability in Europe through NATO and imposed autocratic stability through friendly dictators in the Middle East. It used its economic power to help allies industrialize on America’s terms and push recalcitrant governments to open their markets, while using military force to secure the freedom of the seas and prevent other governments from industrializing on their own terms.

Meanwhile, the dynamism and independence of American education, combined with massive military spending and an apocalyptic arms race, helped drive unprecedented scientific breakthroughs.

Partially as a result of all this, America’s real GDP has grown more than tenfold since 1945. These gains have not been shared equally by the country’s population. But the period of postwar prosperity and broad-based economic growth also helped maintain public support for expanded government programs and a strong social safety net.

President Joe Biden handed off a country that was in its strongest geopolitical position in decades.

He’s been one of the most consequential presidents in U.S. history—in all the wrong ways.

Meanwhile, Washington’s preponderance of power often enabled it to impose its will through pressure and proxy wars rather than direct military conflict. Other people paid the cost of American power, often in blood. While wars like Vietnam and Iraq took a violent toll on Americans, they took a far worse one on Vietnamese and Iraqis.

Now, however, that hegemony is waning—and so are the benefits. The financial gains from America’s position have increasingly accrued to a small and wealthy elite, while the prestige has accrued to a community that many Americans no longer identify with. As a result, voters now feel like they are paying the price of U.S. power without reaping its rewards.

Americans remain awkward about acknowledging the benefits of empire, and thus the price of losing it. Many neoconservatives and liberal internationalists are more comfortable discussing the freedom and prosperity American power brings the world. Trump and many others on the anti-internationalist right have taken the selfless side of this rhetoric at face value, suggesting that Americans are suckers for underwriting the world’s well-being free of charge.

Those on the left, by contrast, have been happy to highlight the material benefits of U.S. power. Progressive critiques have long reduced U.S. foreign policy to a neo-imperial bid for markets to exploit. But in this telling, the profits only ever accrued to big corporations, not ordinary Americans. Trump and the left might disagree on whether the plutocrats benefit from U.S. global hegemony, but they fundamentally agree that the rest of the country doesn’t. From this perspective, a more restrained foreign policy that accepts, even embraces, America’s smaller role in a more multipolar world brings considerable savings and no consequences.

Yet the reality may be this: During the heyday of postwar American foreign policy, the country’s role in the world really did bring widespread economic rewards to all Americans. But due to changes in the global order, there is no possible foreign policy that can bring these benefits back in the same way today. It is, at the very least, a possibility policymakers should be planning for.

U.S. President Donald Trump and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth step off Air Force One upon arrival at Dover Air Force Base in Delaware to attend a dignified transfer on March 18 for six U.S. military members who were killed in the Middle East. Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images

Mitigating the material consequences of American decline, however difficult, may still prove far easier than mitigating the psychological consequences. A lot of Americans derived a real sense of pride and security from their country’s preeminent position. Power conferred a sense of prestige, and also a sense of control over a chaotic world.

Since at least 1945, America’s national image has been wrapped up in its wealth and military might, but also, for Republicans and Democrats alike, its role as a respected leader, reliable ally, and generous benefactor. Trump rejected this tradition, but his presidency has been a continuous appeal to Americans’ deep desire for a lost feeling of power and control.

America’s victory in World War II offered the country a heady combination of both military glory and genuine respect. In the ensuing decades, ordinary Americans who traveled abroad, whether as service members, peace corps volunteers, government employees, tourists, or businesspeople—got to bathe in this. In politics, economics, and culture, Americans mattered more because America mattered. At the very least, they could safely assume that everyone in the world wanted to talk about American movies, American TV, and American music.

The country’s reputation became more controversial over time. But America, and by extension Americans abroad, still warranted a great deal of attention. Even people who never traveled saw their presidents and generals receive the world’s deference and were able to partake vicariously. But just as American power was peaking at the start of the new millennium, a mix of partisan culture war and racism changed the relationship between many Americans and their country’s international image. Unlike in the Cold War, the people representing America on TV, making foreign policy and talking about it, became both more liberal and less white than they’d been before.

This means that for Trump and his movement, responsible liberal internationalism delivered respect to the wrong people, and they no longer saw their country’s prestige as their own. Conservatives complained about President Barack Obama’s global “apology tour” while watching him receive the Nobel Peace Prize and international praise. Trump promised to fix this by, in David Frum’s words, “redistributing respect away from those who command too much (overeducated coastal elites) to those who don’t have enough (white Americans without advanced degrees who feel left behind).” Where once diplomats, aid workers, and journalists got careers that delivered a sense of stature, Trump would leave them crying outside of their offices, whether at the State Department, the U.S. Agency for International Development, or Voice of America.

To complete the redistribution, Trump’s policies would then bring a different set of psychological rewards to a different constituency. Instead of the “liberal-professional preference for restrained institutional blandness,” he offered “gilding,” “military fanfare,” and “inflated talk of seizure and possession.” This was a form of national strength Trump’s followers could partake in. Or, as the president himself said in explaining why he wanted to seize Greenland: “[W]hat I feel is psychologically needed for success.”

A U.S. flag hangs from a gas pump in Allagash, Maine, on Oct. 14. Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images

Over the course of the 20th century, Americans have gotten accustomed to global power and to exercising it on the cheap. No one has a plan for what happens when this is no longer possible.

When events ranging from terrorist attacks to foreign wars threaten their sense of security, voters expect their leaders to respond in a way that restores some sense of control. Thus, while Americans may have been genuinely sick of the Iraq War, and genuinely opposed to intervening in Syria, when the Islamic State started beheading people on TV, they demanded that Obama do something.

So far, Trump has been able to meet this expectation by spending down the military, diplomatic, and economic power that the U.S. accumulated through decades of responsible, or at least less reckless, policymaking. Flouting international law to bring Venezuela’s president to New York in shackles was a true testament to American military prowess. And the photos undoubtedly brought some viewers the same satisfaction Romans felt watching enemy leaders led by in a triumphal parade. But the Iran war quickly demonstrated the limits of Trump’s approach.

Already, Iran’s ability to defy Washington for eight months has had a direct economic impact on American citizens. And the White House, recognizing it has no good military route to victory, has been left to systematically lie about the number of casualties and the status of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz in order to counteract humiliating accusations of defeat.

Iran also shows why, after playing an outsized role in world affairs over the past decade, the United States cannot simply step back and leave others to reap the whirlwind. The end of the British Empire may have left behind civil wars that killed millions in Sudan and South Asia, but the impact on life in London was minimal. After decades of rapid globalization, though, the consequences for Washington are less likely to stay so safely at bay.

There is every reason to fear that in the coming decades, the world will be more violent, and this violence will make Americans less safe. It will also be less stable, and this will eat away at the sources of America’s wealth. A host of sober-minded foreign policies, coupled with sound economic leadership, can certainly mitigate the damage, but the country will still be less secure and less prosperous. This, in turn, will leave voters feeling even more powerless and aggrieved.

To be effective, a new foreign-policy agenda needs a plan for managing this, too. The restraint camp has embraced the belief that Americans are tired of forever wars and don’t want costly adventures abroad. But anyone who remembers the aftermath of 9/11 knows how quickly this can change in a moment of national anger and humiliation.

Restrainers are undoubtedly right that Washington would do better to accept the shift to a more multipolar world gracefully, rather than rage self-destructively against it. But they seem unduly confident that this process will be a win-win for America and the world, rather than a painful adjustment for everyone—including the American people.

Nick Danforth is a deputy editor at Foreign Policy. X: @NicholasDanfort

#6105. (Latin) America’s Pastime

The Milwaukee Brewers won the MLB World Series against the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday night after a five-game final matchup that gripped U.S. audiences. But beyond the excitement of the games, another story unfolded on the field. Some of the most compelling figures of the United States’ national pastime began their journeys thousands of miles away, in the neighborhoods and ballparks of Latin America.

Consider Milwaukee’s Jackson Chourio and William Contreras, both of whom are from Venezuela. Tampa Bay features Dominican stars Junior Caminero and Freddy Peralta, Cuban players Yandy Díaz and Victor Mesa Jr., and Mexico’s Jonathan Aranda. Their presence reflects how baseball has become one of the most enduring cultural and economic connections between the United States and Latin America, even at a time when those ties are being threatened by an administration that is deeply hostile to immigration.

The Milwaukee Brewers won the MLB World Series against the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday night after a five-game final matchup that gripped U.S. audiences. But beyond the excitement of the games, another story unfolded on the field. Some of the most compelling figures of the United States’ national pastime began their journeys thousands of miles away, in the neighborhoods and ballparks of Latin America.

Consider Milwaukee’s Jackson Chourio and William Contreras, both of whom are from Venezuela. Tampa Bay features Dominican stars Junior Caminero and Freddy Peralta, Cuban players Yandy Díaz and Victor Mesa Jr., and Mexico’s Jonathan Aranda. Their presence reflects how baseball has become one of the most enduring cultural and economic connections between the United States and Latin America, even at a time when those ties are being threatened by an administration that is deeply hostile to immigration.

Chourio’s journey began in Maracaibo, Venezuela. He started playing baseball in 2008, at the age of 4. He was encouraged by his father, a former player who shares his name. By age 12, Chourio believed that he could make a career out of baseball, and at 14, he was already attracting the attention of U.S. major-league scouts.

His athletic ability impressed Milwaukee’s staff, although he did not always perform well in early evaluations. At one showcase in 2018, he struck out in his first two times at bat before demonstrating the speed and hitting ability that convinced the scouts that they had discovered someone special.

The Brewers signed Chourio in January 2021, when he was just 16, paying him a $1.8 million signing bonus. He spent the next three seasons climbing through their minor-league system, beginning in the Dominican Republic and eventually playing for teams in North Carolina, Wisconsin, Mississippi, and Tennessee. He joined the major leagues in 2024, shortly after his 20th birthday. Today, he is one of the most recognizable athletes in Wisconsin.

Tampa Bay’s Caminero grew up in the Dominican Republic’s capital of Santo Domingo, less than 10 minutes from Quisqueya Juan Marichal stadium, where two of the country’s most celebrated professional teams play. Caminero was such an enthusiastic New York Yankees fan that, when his parents had another son, he persuaded them to name the boy Girardi, after Yankees manager Joe Girardi.

Caminero’s is a wonderfully Dominican baseball story and an equally revealing American one. He grew up following MLB, idolizing players who had already made the journey to the United States. As MLB’s account of his childhood makes clear, the U.S. game was woven into his family life long before he ever signed a professional contract. Yet he also grew up in a country with its own proud baseball traditions, professional teams, and devoted fans.

Dominican children shield their eyes while playing in San Pedro de Macoris, Dominican Republic, on Jan. 17, 1986.Manny Millan /Sports Illustrated via Getty Image

Latin America has made considerable contributions to U.S. baseball. According to MLB’s 2026 opening day statistics, 249 of the 948 players on major-league teams’ opening-day rosters were born outside the United States. The Dominican Republic led with 93 players, followed by Venezuela with 60 and Cuba with 20. Together, those three countries supplied nearly 70 percent of foreign-born players.

These figures reflect generations of shared history. Baseball spread through the Caribbean and parts of Latin America in the 19th and early 20th centuries, carried by travelers, students, workers, and commercial relationships. Over time, countries developed their own leagues, sporting traditions, and national heroes. What began as an American game became something distinctly Cuban, Dominican, Nicaraguan, Puerto Rican, and Venezuelan.

Baseball occupies a place in public life in these countries that outsiders can easily underestimate.

Migration, colonial history, and elite academies have redefined today’s national teams.

As the United States closes itself off from the world, its co-host is doing the opposite.

Festering battles on the international tennis circuit have finally burst into the open.

In Nicaragua, baseball heroes have become national figures. During the 1990s, when Nicaragua briefly transitioned to democracy, U.S. Ambassador John Maisto would go on live radio in Managua on Fridays at noon to discuss the local baseball teams. I served as a U.S. diplomat in the country and remember how those appearances made Maisto a local celebrity.

In 1998, the Nicaraguan government officially named the national stadium in the capital of Managua for Dennis Martínez, the first Nicaraguan to play in the U.S. major leagues. Martínez had pitched a perfect game in 1991, becoming the first pitcher born outside the United States to accomplish the feat. The stadium’s name was a fitting tribute to a national hero—and a reminder of the importance of baseball in the country’s collective imagination.

In Cuba, baseball has additional historical and political significance. It has remained a national passion through six decades of difficult relations with the United States. Fidel Castro himself was an avid fan—and he was falsely rumored to have been scouted by MLB prior to his revolutionary days. Yet for years, Cuban players have faced legal and political restrictions from both governments that prevent U.S. teams from recruiting them in the same way that they recruit players elsewhere in Latin America. Many have had to establish themselves outside Cuba before signing professional contracts.

Fidel Castro takes a cut at the plate during a sandlot baseball game in Cuba on March 10, 1961.Bettmann Archive/Getty Images

Venezuelan players face their own hurdles. U.S. teams once operated baseball academies throughout the country, but violence, economic instability, and political turmoil over the past decade led them to withdraw. But teams continued scouting promising Venezuelan players, often developing them through facilities in the Dominican Republic. Chourio’s career followed that route.

A 2018 agreement between MLB and Cuba’s baseball federation intended to provide a safer, legal route for Cuban players to sign with U.S. teams. But the U.S. government blocked it the following year. Still, the game itself remains a connection that political disagreements have not extinguished. Tampa Bay’s Díaz and Mesa are part of that continuing relationship.

If there were any doubts that baseball belongs as much to Latin America as it does to the United States, this year’s World Baseball Classic provided a convincing answer. In March, Venezuela defeated the United States for the title with a 3-2 win in Miami—its first championship in the tournament. The game was tied in the eighth inning after a two-run home run by U.S. star Bryce Harper, but Venezuelan hitter Eugenio Suárez delivered the winning run with a double in the ninth.

Venezuelan fans celebrate their national baseball team’s victory in the final of the 2026 World Baseball Classic against the United States, seen in Caracas on March 17. Juan Barreto/AFP via Getty Images

The celebration reflected something more profound than a sporting victory. For Venezuelans at home and throughout the diaspora, the championship offered an opportunity to unite around a common national identity, regardless of political and class differences.

Venezuela was not simply supplying players to MLB teams—it was defeating the United States at its own national pastime, under the Venezuelan flag, and before an international audience. The tournament demonstrated how far baseball has traveled from its U.S. origins, and how thoroughly Latin American countries have made it their own.

There is a substantial economic story behind the players on the World Series rosters. MLB’s international scouting and development system has created a remarkable market for athletic talent. U.S. clubs invest in training facilities and recruitment networks in other countries, while talented young players pursue opportunities that can transform their families’ circumstances. But not everyone enjoys the success that the likes of Chourio do.

A September ProPublica investigation examined the recruitment of young Dominican players and documented serious problems involving early informal agreements with players, financial intermediaries, and diversion of signing bonuses. ProPublica did not establish that MLB itself diverted the signing bonuses. The investigation concerned a network of private trainers, intermediaries, and lenders surrounding young Dominican players and their families.

According to MLB data cited in the investigation, fewer than 10 percent of Dominican prospects who sign professional contracts ever reach the U.S. major leagues. Those intermediary trainers and lenders may claim substantial portions of the money that young players expect to receive, while some children sacrifice years of education pursuing a professional career that might never materialize. Private trainers may have extensive relationships with MLB scouts, but that does not automatically make them employees, agents, or contractors of MLB organizations.

A fan waves the Puerto Rican flag before a game against Cuba at the World Baseball Classic in San Juan, Puerto Rico, on March 10, 2006. Al Bello/Getty Images

ProPublica’s findings do not diminish the achievements of Latin American baseball stars. They are a reminder that a system capable of producing enormous opportunity can also expose vulnerable young people to risk. The economic relationships between the United States and Latin America are often similarly complicated.

Baseball is not a substitute for diplomacy, trade agreements, or immigration policy. Nor should we exaggerate the ability of sports to overcome political disagreements. The economic interests of U.S. baseball franchises do not always coincide with those of the Latin American communities supplying their players.

Nevertheless, the game illustrates how deeply connected various cultures in the Western Hemisphere have become—independent of government action. Baseball is not simply entertainment imported from the United States: It belongs to the people who play it, follow it, and pass it from one generation to the next.

These connections are particularly visible in the way that U.S. fans embrace players from abroad. Brewers supporters need not know the details of Chourio’s childhood in Maracaibo to appreciate his performance in the outfield. Tampa Bay fans celebrate Caminero because of what he accomplishes at home plate. Yet behind those achievements are families, communities, and countries whose contributions have become indispensable to U.S. professional sport.

The World Series offers a particularly vivid reminder that—for all of the tensions between the United States and Latin American countries over issues such as immigration, trade, and security—there is something larger about the hemisphere that we all share.

Steven E. Hendrix is a former senior U.S. diplomat who served in leadership positions at the State Department and U.S. Agency for International Development. Bluesky: @hendrixse

#6103. Judge tosses DOJ lawsuit seeking to delay Alaska vote certification

A federal judge on Sunday tossed a lawsuit from the Trump administration that sought to delay the certification of the Alaska Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses.

Sullivan faces Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola and two other candidates in a contest that could help decide control of the Senate. One of those candidates is also named Dan Sullivan, which prompted the Trump administration to file its lawsuit, alleging that, under the state’s ranked choice system, voters may rank the challenger instead of the incumbent.

The complaint also asked the judge to allow a delay until an “investigation” into whether votes for the challenger, listed on the ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., should have gone to the senator, who is listed as Dan S. Sullivan.

But in her ruling Sunday, Judge Sharon L. Gleason of the U.S. District Court for the District of Alaska said the relief requested by the administration was “infeasible.”

“[Many] voters have already cast their ballots in the November 2026 general election. Those cast ballots have been commingled and cannot now be segregated or the identity of the person who cast each ballot ascertained,” she wrote.

Should the Trump administration appeal the ruling, it would go to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit.

The case started on Oct. 22, when the Trump administration filed the lawsuit, arguing that the courts should delay the certification of the Alaska Senate race if the incumbent Sullivan were to lose and the margin was less than the number of votes the second Sullivan received.

The Justice Department argued that voters could be confused by the presence of a namesake challenger on the state’s ballot and not cast their intended vote for the incumbent. Initially, the lawsuit was filed against the state, but Peltola and Democrats have intervened to argue that the case should be tossed.

Then last week, The New York Times reported that aides for Peltola were involved in the effort to recruit the second Sullivan to enter the Senate race. The DOJ filed an amended complaint accusing Peltola and Democrats of misleading the courts.

“Apparently emboldened by the success of their reported plot to deceive Alaskan voters, Alaskans For Mary and the [Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee] appear to have turned to misleading this Court,” the DOJ filing said.

Trump himself has accused Peltola of executing a “FRAUD ON THE AMERICAN PUBLIC” and called for both her and the second Sullivan to be removed from the Senate ballot. Under federal law, the state finalized its ballot more than a month ago.

Peltola and Democrats pushed back in their own filing Friday, calling the DOJ’s claims “nonsense.” They also said that they “lack knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief about the truth or falsity of the allegation concerning the purposes of Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy and therefore deny any allegation about those purposes.”

And on Saturday, the Republican-led Alaska state government called on Gleason to dismiss the lawsuit, saying that “the relief demanded is inappropriate and not even possible given Alaskan voters’ vital right to ballot secrecy.”

Earlier this year Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired school teacher, successfully sued in state court to be included on the ballot after election officials had previously removed his name. The state Supreme Court ruled that the second Sullivan was a valid candidate and should be included.

Under Alaska rules, voters can rank up to four candidates on the Senate ballot. If no one takes a majority of first-place votes, the candidate in last position is eliminated, with those votes assigned to the voters’ next choice. The process repeats until one candidate has a majority of the remaining votes.

Argument: A New War on Iran Would Deal a Death Blow to U.S. Leadership in the Mideast

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

If there’s one thing that’s clear in the aftermath of the Israeli election, it is that Benjamin Netanyahu will remain prime minister—for at least a few weeks and probably several months—while the political haggling is underway. And that means that the prospects of another U.S.-Israeli war with Iran are high. Netanyahu has been pushing for a new round for weeks, and the Trump administration has reportedly advised allies to expect a military campaign after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3. That campaign might be meant to force Iran back to the bargaining table—or to topple the regime. Either way, another war is unlikely to achieve even the most minimal U.S. and Israeli goals.

The United States is now locked in exactly the kind of protracted war scape in which decisive victory is close to impossible. Iran has long thrived in these environments. The U.S. blockade and episodic violence hurt Iran, to be sure, but the pain is not evenly distributed. It tends to reinforce rather than degrade regime control, strengthen the hand of hard-liners over any remaining moderates, and provide a ready-made excuse for collective suffering that might otherwise be blamed on the country’s leaders.

If there’s one thing that’s clear in the aftermath of the Israeli election, it is that Benjamin Netanyahu will remain prime minister—for at least a few weeks and probably several months—while the political haggling is underway. And that means that the prospects of another U.S.-Israeli war with Iran are high. Netanyahu has been pushing for a new round for weeks, and the Trump administration has reportedly advised allies to expect a military campaign after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3. That campaign might be meant to force Iran back to the bargaining table—or to topple the regime. Either way, another war is unlikely to achieve even the most minimal U.S. and Israeli goals.

The United States is now locked in exactly the kind of protracted war scape in which decisive victory is close to impossible. Iran has long thrived in these environments. The U.S. blockade and episodic violence hurt Iran, to be sure, but the pain is not evenly distributed. It tends to reinforce rather than degrade regime control, strengthen the hand of hard-liners over any remaining moderates, and provide a ready-made excuse for collective suffering that might otherwise be blamed on the country’s leaders.

Such a conflict will, by its nature, defy U.S. and Israeli hopes for a decisive blow. After the initial kinetic period, the hostilities will likely continue whether or not there is active shooting, forcing every affected actor to prepare as if violence could return at any moment. Talk of victory or defeat—whether for U.S. domestic political consumption or, worse, for the Pentagon’s actual war planning—has little meaning in a conflict that Iranians rightly expect to continue for many years to come. America’s regional allies that have to live in this environment can see this clearly and want none of it. That constant risk of a sudden eruption would deny the Gulf states the kind of stability and security they desperately need to get their economic projects back on track. And it would leave the door open to flare-ups elsewhere, such as the Houthi sweep down the Red Sea coast and seizure of the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint in September.

The suggestion to launch a renewed, intense military campaign represents a tacit recognition of U.S. failure. No amount of happy talk about the increased volume of oil flowing through the Strait of Hormuz and the mounting economic costs of the blockade on Iran can mask the new strategic reality. Iran has proved that it retains the capacity to close the strait when it wishes, and the Houthi advances in the Red Sea and effective targeting of Saudi Arabia have expanded Iran’s range of options. A diplomatic solution has been rendered largely impossible by the Trump administration’s constantly changing positions and incoherent messaging, which give Iran no reason to even consider a deal. From Tehran’s vantage point, any agreement would likely be broken before the ink was dry. Trump’s signature, as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has quipped, is written in pencil.

But if Iran can live with the state of potential war and episodic eruptions of violence, the Arab Gulf states cannot. Bahrain, Kuwait, and Qatar have no alternative shipping routes other than the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia, which for a time thought it could adapt by shifting its oil exports to the Red Sea, learned the hard way that it could not count on that option in the rapidly mutating conflict. The Houthi seizure of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and control over the Bab el-Mandeb and an Iraqi militia drone strike temporarily disabling the East-West pipeline put an end to that fantasy.

The escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities, and other targets, along with the Saudi inability to mount an effective military challenge to the new Houthi positions, have caught Riyadh in an untenable bind. The United States rather shockingly declined to come Riyadh’s assistance against the Houthis. That may be for the best. The large-scale international intervention against the Houthis proposed by the Saudi ambassador to the United States this week would simply pull the world deeper into an unwinnable war scape. Nor is the Mecca Pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan going to ride to a military rescue in Yemen. The three countries may have ratified the defense pact and floated intervention possibilities, but neither country is likely to provide the ground troops that would be needed.

Why staying the course is the most prudent of Washington’s three unsavory choices.

Some dramatic long-term consequences are just beginning to come into view.

To get out of this quagmire, Washington must decide what it wants.

But there could be a silver lining in this parade of failure. With no plausible military path to victory in Yemen or over Iran, Saudi Arabia has little stomach for renewed war and strong incentives to find a diplomatic way out of its predicament. The Saudis desperately need the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb reopened in a predictable and regulated way. They need an extended period of calm to reassure investors and tourists essential to economic transformation plans. That’s probably why a high-level Mecca Pact delegation visited Tehran this week and why other Gulf states have been urgently looking for a diplomatic path away from war. As Oman’s foreign minister recently noted, there is no security order in the Gulf without Iran and no alternative to a working relationship. That view seems increasingly prevalent in the Gulf—outside of Abu Dhabi—even as Washington prefers to dive deeper into its unwinnable war.

The current Iranian leadership does not think about this in terms of the resumption of war. It considers the war to be ongoing. While it would have little faith in any U.S. promises, it is conceivable that it might view Saudi-led outreach more positively, as a way to lock in its gains from the war and create a buffer against America’s more extreme options. The damage inflicted on Iran’s economy and infrastructure is real and will require massive rebuilding. There’s precedent. Following the conclusion of the horrifically destructive eight-year Iran-Iraq War and the death of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini in the late 1980s, the new leadership of Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani and Ali Khamenei chose to ratchet down revolutionary rhetoric and militant adventurism and create a period of calm to allow desperately needed economic reconstruction. Perhaps the new Revolutionary Guard-led Iran would do the same.

A de-escalatory deal between Iran and the Saudi-led bloc would pose a challenge to Israel and its allies in the region, primarily the United Arab Emirates, as well as to U.S. conceits about determining the terms of regional order. Netanyahu has been using apocalyptic language about the urgency of finishing the job. Indeed, a U.S.-Israeli attack might be motivated less by fear of Iranian escalation or nuclear progress than by fear of a new regional order consolidating in which Iran has reconciled with a Saudi coalition incorporating most of the major powers in the broadly defined region.

The Trump administration no doubt sees itself in an intractable situation from which it can still escalate to win. That is an illusion. Iran is once again perfectly capable of seeing the blow coming. It will not be taken by surprise and has already signaled its intentions to respond. The regime has strong grounds to believe that it (if not the Iranian people) will survive and prosper even under another round of intense military attack. The possible strike would simply accelerate the escalatory dynamics and reinforce emergent Arab convictions that the United States has become a destabilizing force and an unreliable partner that cannot be counted on to provide security or order. When the smoke once again clears, in Iran and in the countries that bore the costs of its retaliation, the renewed campaign may well prove to have been the final blow not to the Iranian regime but to U.S. leadership in the region.

Marc Lynch is a professor of political science and international affairs at the George Washington University and the director of the Project on Middle East Political Science. His most recent book is America’s Middle East: The Ruination of a Region. X: @abuaardvark

#6098. The Fog of Tech

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

Why the Future of War Can’t Escape the Past

At a time when debates about national security tend to be polarized along partisan and ideological lines, there is one thing analysts and policymakers across the political spectrum seem to agree on: the future of warfare will be determined by technology. Hypersonic missiles, quantum computing, drone swarms, and artificial intelligence have all been hailed as transformative technologies that will shape battlefields, remake strategies, and upend established military doctrines.

Without question, these technologies are already having a tremendous impact. In Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, Ukraine, and elsewhere, every party with the capacity to employ artificial intelligence and autonomous systems has done so—in the air, on land, and at sea, and at times in massive numbers. And there is also no question that in order to maintain its status as the world’s preeminent fighting force, the U.S. military must ensure that it has the most sophisticated and cutting-edge capabilities available. To continue developing and operationalizing these technologies, defense planners should prioritize scaling and integrating them and developing innovative operational concepts to employ them. The risk of being overtaken by rivals such as China is real.

But an equally significant risk exists: call it “the technology trap,” in which policymakers develop a misplaced sense of certainty about how innovations will change war and what warfare will look like in the future, while not paying enough attention to the unchanging fundamentals of war. An excessive focus on the role of technology would be shortsighted and lead militaries in dangerous directions, especially if planners are highly confident about how new capabilities will develop and make decisions in line with that confidence—which will almost certainly be misplaced.

For war planners, faith in technological answers can obscure the most fundamental questions: Who kills, who dies, and who decides? In the post–Cold War era, this myopia has contributed to dreadful outcomes in Afghanistan, Iraq, Ukraine, and Gaza. In the decade to come, as U.S.-Chinese tensions persist, the fog of tech could help pave the way for a disastrous great-power war. Policymakers should worry less about getting the right technology at the right time and more about how fixating on technology might make them lose sight of the essential elements of war and find comfort in false certainty.

More than 50 years ago, the military historian Michael Howard famously cautioned that future wars are unknowable. “I am tempted indeed to declare dogmatically that whatever doctrine the Armed Forces are working on now, they have got it wrong,” he wrote. “I am also tempted to declare that it does not matter that they have got it wrong. What does matter is their capacity to get it right quickly when the moment arrives.”

But Howard may have been a bit too sanguine about the costs of getting it wrong. For Americans, the paradigmatic example from recent history is how the U.S. military’s technological prowess in the 1990–91 Gulf War seemed to herald a new, high-tech American way of war that would guarantee victory in the post–Cold War era. Instead, Washington slowly and painfully learned that the technological advantages that beat Saddam Hussein’s regime could not defeat insurgencies in Afghanistan and Iraq during the post-9/11 wars.

Predicting the role of technology in future wars has become even harder today thanks to the speed, scale, and complexity of contemporary technological progress. In the past, transformative innovations tended to be expensive at their outset—in resources or personnel—or required specialized knowledge and skills accessible to only a few. Think of the combined power of the rifle, the railroad, and the telegraph in the nineteenth century, or fighter jets and nuclear weapons in the twentieth century. By contrast, many of today’s technologies have low barriers to entry: they are cheap to produce, and access to the knowledge necessary to make them has been democratized and globalized. Enemies today often face each other on more equal battlefields, making it trickier for war planners to understand when and for how long new tools will confer an outsize advantage.

Focusing too much on procuring the shiniest equipment also obscures the ways that high-end technology works in tandem with more basic tools. In the 2010s, defense planners failed to account for this dynamic when predicting future battlefields, which they believed would be dominated by sophisticated platforms. In 2017, a senior Pentagon official declared that the F-35 stealth fighter would be “a war winner.” The 2018 National Defense Strategy, drafted under the direction of Elbridge Colby, who now serves as undersecretary of defense, anticipated that a few primarily high-end capabilities—including advanced computing, artificial intelligence, robotics, hypersonics, and biotechnology—would “ensure we will be able to fight and win the wars of the future.”

Instead, what emerged were conflicts such as the war in Ukraine, which can be described as World War I meets World War III. Sophisticated Russian ballistic missiles wreak havoc on Ukrainian cities, as do precision-guided glide bombs delivered by fighter aircraft out of the range of air defenses. At the same time, however, highly lethal bombs are dropped by drones carried aloft by simple balloons, and one of the most effective antidrone defenses consists of fishermen’s nets (or similar netting) draped over security checkpoints, critical infrastructure, and, in the case of Izium, an entire small Ukrainian city. A sense of certainty that sophisticated tech would dominate battlefields represented a failure of imagination that has produced real-world consequences: a dozen years ago, few would have predicted that during a U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, cheap Iranian drones would assault soft targets in Gulf Arab states, as they have since February.

An obsession with technology can obscure the precept that war remains a human endeavor. As the military theorist Carl von Clausewitz said almost two centuries ago, “War is not the action of a living force upon a lifeless mass . . . but always the collision of two living forces.” Technology can inadvertently make war appear mechanical and sterile. But the nature of war has not changed. Its language is violence, and technology simply offers new and different ways to communicate. Therefore, the fundamental questions of war remain salient regardless of technological change: What are the ends (particularly with respect to politics), the ways, and the means?

Perhaps the most perilous time for leaders to be distracted by the allure of technology is when considering whether to go to war in the first place. They often mistakenly believe that technology will make doing so less costly in political terms, particularly if they assume innovations will help reduce casualties. A fixation on the tangible and quantifiable advantages technology confers can detract from vital debate and discussion of the broader consequences of resorting to violence. This dynamic likely influenced Russia’s decision to invade Ukraine. Putin and his advisers believed that the Russian military was sufficiently capable thanks to a massive technological reform effort that began in 2009. In the run-up to the 2022 full-scale invasion, Russian Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu proudly claimed that more than 70 percent of Russia’s military had advanced weapons. Within weeks of the invasion, it had become clear this had conferred little advantage on Moscow. The same goes for the U.S.-Israeli attempt to topple the Iranian regime in 2026, a decision shaped in part by the belief that the sophistication of the American military, particularly when compared with its opponent, made success almost inevitable. In the wake of U.S. strikes on Iran’s nuclear sites in 2025, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth declared that the attack showed Tehran that Washington’s military capabilities are “nearly unlimited.” In fact, the limits of those capabilities became glaringly obvious when the Iranian regime withstood the 2026 onslaught and even managed to close the Strait of Hormuz.

There are ways to avoid the technology trap. The first is to determine a clear goal before going to war. Planners must develop a theory of victory before a single shot is fired and then steadily put that theory into practice. These critical processes cannot be negated by or outsourced to technology. Before launching the 2026 war on Iran, the Trump administration failed to clearly articulate the operation’s goal, instead offering a shifting set of justifications and rationales and various descriptions of the desired end state. The hope seems to have been that technological wizardry would make it possible to achieve everything on a long wish list without having to prioritize or navigate tradeoffs.

To clarify goals, planners must identify what Clausewitz termed “the center of gravity” of a military operation: “the hub of all power and movement, on which everything depends.” This is where an opponent’s power originates, so it needs to be the focus of a military’s attention and resources. During the 1990–91 Gulf War, the commander of U.S. forces in the Middle East, General Norman Schwarzkopf, identified the center of gravity as Saddam Hussein’s command and control of his military. Accordingly, U.S. strategy focused on impeding Saddam’s ability to communicate with his troops and weakening the Iraqi military’s ability to execute orders—a state of affairs that helped convince Saddam to accept a cease-fire. Without this clarity about where to direct efforts and how to measure their impact, a military will struggle to achieve its ends. Early in the 2003 Iraq war, the U.S. military’s inability to identify the Iraqi population as the center of gravity—that is, failing to understand that the political and military leadership no longer wielded control—resulted in years of devastating losses by encouraging tactics that fomented anti-American sentiment, fueled an insurgency, and made it more difficult to establish a credible and functioning government.

Another way to avoid the technology trap is to conduct deliberate, impartial, and regular reviews of lessons learned during and between wars. Iran closely studied the attacks that Israel and the United States carried out on its nuclear sites in 2025. Recognizing that another war would likely pose an existential risk to the Islamic Republic regime, Iranian security officials engaged in a serious and intense effort to prepare. By devolving command and control at both the political and the military levels during the 2026 war, the regime has survived a lengthy onslaught. U.S. allies are, of course, equally capable of such adaptation. In recent years, NATO’s Joint Analysis and Lessons Learned Centre has maintained a team of researchers dedicated to studying the war in Ukraine, a smart way to institutionalize this task and a potential model to apply to other theaters.

The combination of a focus on strategic aims, preparation, and learning remains crucial for effective decision-making in war and cannot be replaced by technology. Similarly, the ways and means of warfare are influenced by technology but have not been fundamentally changed by it. Consider, first, the importance of coalitions and the difficulties of managing them. Going to war exposes the distinct and sometimes even opposing interests, objectives, and perspectives of allies. Planners can devise workarounds when they face disagreements in the heat of conflict, but those may be short-term fixes that mask strategic cleavages.

In early 2026, the United States and Israel launched the war on Iran relying solely on each other. Although the U.S. and Israeli militaries have never operated more closely together in the history of their relationship, their limited success calls into question the partnership’s strategic acumen, despite its remarkable technological capabilities. The two countries notably failed to bring in other partners in the region or in Europe. Early on, several U.S. allies and partners denied the American military access to their territory, bases, and airspace. Although U.S. defense planners have always understood that they might not receive such permissions—Turkey, for example, was unwilling to let the U.S. military invade Iraq from Turkish territory in 2003—the resistance this time was of a different quality and scale. Although most countries ultimately acquiesced, the ones that initially declined threw a wrench into U.S. defense planning, since the American way of war is predicated on an unparalleled global basing network. According to several media reports, Israel found ways around this challenge by setting up a military staging area in Iran during the 2025 war and one in Iraq in 2026. But the ad hoc nature of such creative approaches causes problems for military planning.

As the war has dragged on, the Arab Gulf states have not formally joined the U.S.-Israeli coalition, although at various times during the conflict, Bahrain, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates have used military force against Iran. Their willingness to use force was significant in and of itself, but it did not influence the battlefield, despite some of the sophisticated capabilities those countries possess. On the other side, Iran masterfully managed its proxy, the Lebanese militia Hezbollah, pulling it into the conflict and enabling Tehran to project power through relatively unsophisticated technologies such as rockets, mortars, and most notably, cheap drones that Hezbollah repeatedly deployed against Israeli soldiers in Lebanon and Israeli civilians inside Israel. Meanwhile, Russia also helped Iran target U.S. military facilities in the Gulf, resulting in devastating (though not determinative) consequences.

The complexities of coalition maintenance are on display in Europe, as well, where defense planners are wrestling with a security trilemma. First, they must figure out how to incorporate a highly capable and modernized Ukrainian military into continental defense planning. As Germany turbocharges investments in its military, Europe must also contend with a shift in its internal balance of military power—one with uneasy historical echoes. And, incredibly, during the past year, Europeans have had to consider the risk of aggression on the part of the United States, as President Donald Trump mused about securing U.S. control of Greenland. These three realities introduce a host of tradeoffs into European strategy, since prioritizing any one of them would likely make it harder to deal with the other two—and no technology offers a way out.

Technological determinism can also lead to faulty assumptions about casualties—both civilian and military. Today, target selection is increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence, and strikes are increasingly carried out by autonomous systems. Many have argued that these technological advances will improve targeting and better protect civilians. To date, however, it is unclear whether autonomous systems have delivered on this promise. During the war in Gaza, for example, Israeli military personnel have been able to rapidly approve targets generated by an artificial intelligence system called Lavender. But such systems reflect the rules of engagement set by decision-makers, and after Hamas’s October 7 attack on Israel in 2023, the Israeli military raised the level of civilian casualties it would accept when striking Hamas militants. Perhaps for that reason, researchers who conducted an experiment testing the decision-making of around 2,000 Israeli military personnel found that in hypothetical scenarios involving high levels of collateral damage, they demonstrated “algorithmic aversion” and a desire to rely more on human decision-making.

Ironically, civilians may become more vulnerable, not less, as new technologies make it harder to attack military personnel and targets, increasing the risk of collateral damage and even providing some parties with an incentive to deliberately attack civilians and soft targets. Many militaries, including the American one, increasingly employ technology to minimize the risks borne by their own forces. This desire for immaculate war is not new. Nearly 700,000 U.S. service members participated in the Gulf War in 1990–91, and contrary to expectations of a bloodbath, only 143 of them died, an outcome that bolstered arguments that technology had made it possible to carry out major military operations with minimal risk to American troops. Two years later, the Battle of Mogadishu undercut that view, as the U.S. military withdrew from Somalia after 18 service members died in a protracted fight with Somali militants armed with cheap and relatively low-tech weapons such as rifles, machine guns, and rocket-propelled grenades. Early in the present century, the rapid American overthrow of the Taliban in Afghanistan rekindled the dream of relatively bloodless warfare made possible by innovations. But the grinding fights that followed there and in Iraq once again poured cold water on the idea.

Technological hopes spring eternal, however, and the U.S. military once again seems to be planning operations that use high-tech tools to reduce risks to its personnel. In an operation carried out in Venezuela this past January, that meant employing special operations forces complemented by space-based and cyber platforms and more than 150 aircraft and drones—all to capture a single person, Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. In Iran, it has meant waging a war to transform conditions on the ground, but with attacks carried out primarily from the air and by sea.

To be sure, this approach is linked to the fact that the United States is not engaged in existential wars. And when the U.S. military has fought an adversary that perceives the conflict as existential, as in the Iranian case, American officials are often surprised that their adversaries refuse to back down and are willing to absorb staggering losses. Even if technology allows for fewer American casualties, that does not mean it should short-circuit robust political debate about whether to go to war. Casualties, after all, are hardly the only cost that contemporary warfare can impose. Even wars that produce relatively low casualties can destroy economies, bring down governments, and rip apart societies.

Countries that haven’t waged war in many decades, such as China, may be even more susceptible than the United States to the technology trap. Such countries might focus on acquiring innovative tools rather than preparing for adversaries that know how to integrate new technologies at scale. This may present some opportunities for Washington given its substantial recent experience in formulating concepts of operation tied to technological advancements. But countries such as China might be no less confident about their capabilities, even though they are significantly less experienced, which means the risks of miscalculation and escalation could easily increase.

Deep faith in new technologies could result in much smaller militaries, as machines replace human personnel. In the United States, this shift could widen the gap that already exists between ordinary Americans and those who serve, as even fewer Americans will have connections to—and therefore care about—how, when, where, and why Washington resorts to military force. This detachment of the military from the society it serves is corrosive to the institution itself and to democracy more broadly since it undermines the principle that war-making should reflect the will of the people. Countries that rely on conscription won’t face quite the same problem, but technological determinism will affect their relationships with their publics, as well: even if such countries need fewer citizens to serve, the technology trap could still reduce social cohesion by further marginalizing the sectors of society from which conscripts tend to be drawn.

Perhaps the most pernicious effect of the technology trap might be the way it could hollow out deterrence, as policymakers are tempted to adopt a myopic approach to the use of force shaped by deterministic views of technology’s impact on the battlefield. Deterrence requires an adversary to cogently read signals regarding capability and will. If both parties in a conflict have confidence in their own capabilities and in those of the other side, they may face increasing pressure to outdo each other in demonstrating a greater will to fight. Such a dynamic could result in a dangerous escalation spiral, particularly if it is paired with assumptions that technology will minimize the role and responsibilities of humans.

It is possible to escape the fog of tech. The most important thing for strategists and officials to grasp is that even though the means of warfighting will keep changing, the fundamental nature of war will not. There is not, and will never be, a shortcut—technological or otherwise—to answering the hard questions one must confront before sending troops to fight, kill, and die.

MARA KARLIN is Professor of Practice at the School of Advanced International Studies at Johns Hopkins University and a Visiting Fellow at the Brookings Institution. She served as U.S. Assistant Secretary of Defense for Strategy, Plans, and Capabilities during the Biden administration and in policy roles at the Pentagon during the Obama and George W. Bush administrations.

#6097. The EU and Canada Struggle to Define Their Relationship

World Brief: The EU and Canada Struggle to Define Their Relationship
