#6065. A Less-Is-More Strategy for America

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

BARRY R. POSEN is Ford International Professor of Political Science at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

The Folly of Expanding the Exhausted U.S. Military

On October 8, the USS Abraham Lincoln and its accompanying strike group returned to the United States after 320 days at sea. The deployment—a near record for the modern American military—had become controversial. As the group’s ships went month after month without a port call, conditions deteriorated precipitously. Sailors reported supply shortages, plumbing issues, and water contamination. Morale dropped markedly; eight sailors even tried to commit suicide. By the time the ships finally left the Middle East, their struggles had made headlines across the country.

The travails of the Lincoln are hardly the only story about the U.S. military to generate alarm since the war in Iran began last February. Military analysts have expressed concern about other carrier groups’ lengthy deployments. They have fretted about the Trump administration’s decision to pull soldiers and weapons stationed in the Indo-Pacific out of the region and position them in the Middle East. Perhaps most of all, they have worried as the United States drains its stockpile of sophisticated munitions.

These problems all share the same root cause: the U.S. military is not built for the near-constant use it has experienced for decades. Ever since the Cold War, American defense planners have structured the U.S. armed forces to be ready to fight two major conflicts simultaneously. In practice, that means Washington has constructed a force that is designed to win short, sharp wars. For that reason, the military does not have enough units, weapons, or personnel to handle never-ending conflicts and simultaneously use its forces around the world to coerce enemies and reassure partners.

American officials are now trying to modestly increase the size of the military. More important, they are hoping that huge infusions of money will increase the capability of the existing armed forces. But making these changes will be exceptionally challenging—and they are unnecessary. The United States is a highly secure country with many capable and wealthy partners. It does not need a defense apparatus capable of fighting everywhere all at once. Instead, it would be much better off focusing its attention on a smaller set of issues and scaling down accordingly.

The U.S. nonnuclear forces, which consume more than 80 percent of the defense budget, are structured and sized for particular contingencies—currently, a clash with China, Russia, or both nearly simultaneously. The military’s weapons are therefore designed for maximum lethality and survivability in what military planners expect to be an unbelievably dangerous environment. To that end, the Pentagon has emphasized purchasing precise, long-range, and stealthy weapons. These are supposed to kick open the doors of enemy defenses and allow other expensive advanced platforms, such as F-35 fighter jets or B-2 or B-21 bombers, to deliver large quantities of slightly less sophisticated but still quite lethal precision weapons.

Washington has never expected these wars to last long. Instead, it imagines that under the fierce pressure such conflicts would generate, the adversary will cry uncle or the war will escalate to nuclear threats or—worse yet—nuclear use. During the Cold War, for example, the United States and its allies planned for an extremely intense, roughly 30-day conflict against the Soviet Union. Today’s military planners have probably made similar assumptions about a war with Beijing or Moscow. Highly capable conventional forces and the risk of nuclear escalation, American thinking goes, should deter an attack. If deterrence fails, U.S. planners hope to stop an enemy in its tracks and create escalation risks so great that the adversary will realize its errors and try to reverse course.

But such thinking means that Washington does not have enough resources to sustain long, great-power conflicts. At $100 million each, the F-35 fighter aircraft, a mainstay of the air force, navy, and Marine Corps, is simply not designed for mass production. Neither are the long-range stand-off missiles that would be the preferred munitions in the early days of such a war. The U.S. military has developed sophisticated theater ballistic missile defenses, but their main purpose is to defend U.S. forces and essential military infrastructure—not towns, cities, and civilian industries. They can be used for this purpose under certain conditions, but doing so quickly exhausts the supply of missiles. In a war with China or Russia, civilians in local, allied countries will need to look after themselves.

These problems have become readily apparent in Washington’s war against Iran. The United States likely thought it could rapidly overpower the Islamic Republic—at best a middle power, albeit one with great ambitions. After all, under the right circumstances, the U.S. military handily overmatches these kinds of enemies, as it did Iraq in the 1990–91 Gulf War. But Washington’s enemies have smartened up since then. They no longer simply produce smaller and less capable versions of the great-power militaries that American forces are designed to deter and combat. Instead, they have prepared themselves to take a beating and keep on fighting, even if at modest levels of effectiveness.

Overly ambitious war plans and faulty policies are not the only reason the U.S. military is struggling. Politics is also creating difficulties. Because the American people hesitate to support wars abroad, U.S. politicians will do anything to avoid casualties. That means they take all the high-end weaponry that the military stockpiles to break down great-power defenses and instead spend it profligately on regional conflicts. Similarly, they deploy scarce air defense weapons to protect allies’ towns and cities, lest those allies consider finding new partners or decide to settle a war by compromising with their enemies.

U.S. policymakers also generally overuse the military. Politicians like to accompany diplomatic messaging with action, in part because they do not believe in diplomacy anymore, which pushes them to parade or use the armed forces far more often than is warranted. When asked to act, commanders usually salute and say yes. Others simply cannot sit still. Commanders, after all, took on their roles because they wanted to command something.

The result is a worn-down military. The defense press is full of stories about ships and aircraft that are not up to standard because they have been out too long, resulting in deferred maintenance. This, in turn, creates repair problems for other units. When a ship must stay in dry dock longer than usual to receive adequate repairs, other ships must wait longer for servicing—which means their needs also grow. Ultimately, the navy has fewer fully ready combat ships available in the event of a great-power challenge. The army has similar problems, with combat and support vehicles arriving at maintenance depots in unexpectedly poor condition. In the air force, the F-35’s “full mission capable rate,” which was never great, has deteriorated from 38 percent to 25 percent since 2021. And the overall readiness of air force aircraft has declined in recent years, in part simply because of overwork.

All the while, U.S. soldiers, sailors, pilots, and marines are constantly on guard, coercing and deterring U.S. enemies and reassuring allies. This, too, creates high levels of activity that can negatively affect retention. Although the military has generally been successful at retaining senior enlisted personnel in recent years, it may soon run into difficulty. Since 2024, navy warships have repeatedly gone to sea undercrewed. The ultimate result of this overuse is that the sharp edge of the military is dulled, and the steel blade is weakened.

U.S. defense officials are aware that they have a problem. Currently, they are trying to solve it by building a somewhat bigger and far more technologically capable military. Congress, for example, appears poised to increase the Pentagon’s so-called base budget—which encompasses what the Congressional Budget Office defines as the “enduring costs of manning, training, and equipping the military”—by over 25 percent, or to $1.1 trillion for the 2027 fiscal year. The Pentagon hopes to secure an additional $350 billion over the base budget in a subsequent bill. Defense officials also want to add over 40,000 new service members. But this is, at best, a personnel increase of three percent, which is much too small to fill the additional units needed to solve extant readiness problems. And the fancier weapons Congress hopes defense officials will buy cannot overcome the strain of constant deployments and repeated wars. The defense industrial base is barely keeping up with current demands, and recruiting large numbers of new service members would likely require offering much higher wages, which would then need to be extended to everyone else. Personnel costs would start consuming an ever-greater share of the defense budget. U.S. officials could instead opt for conscription, but that would produce a backlash.

There is, however, an alternative: scaling down. Instead of pretending that it must be able to fight two great-power wars at once, Washington should cut its policy coat to fit the available cloth. It should continue to build forces for major contingencies, such as deterring adventurism by China. But policymakers should agree to slow down other projects. Congress should task the Pentagon with reviewing the armed forces and come up with an activity budget, which would be based on an assessment of how much real military activity—flying hours, ship days at sea, training days in the field—can be undertaken without harming the readiness of the total force. It would then allocate that activity appropriately. Based on what they ought to know about the virtual attrition the military has suffered thanks to 30 years of hyperactivity, commanders should determine what level of exercises, forward deployments, and regional wars the military can actually support without doing damage to the capabilities it wishes to have ready every day to deter a great-power war and, if need be, wage one effectively. The U.S. Navy already knows the activity level that its fleet can support, which it has detailed in its Optimized Fleet Response Plan. But American presidents and defense secretaries have simply ignored this plan whenever they wanted to deploy more forces.

The activity budget should not be classified but instead should be public information, listed along with the dollar budget that the Pentagon publishes annually, voluminous summaries of which can be found at the Defense Department’s comptroller’s website. When politicians want to exceed the activity levels on which they have previously agreed, they should have to explain why and how they plan to repair the force after intense use. Commanders should think of this as an ethical issue. Every now and then, one should resign when overuse causes serious problems.

To help lighten its load, Washington will need to hand off some responsibilities to others. This should be feasible despite the need to manage Moscow’s aggressive impulses, which are the presumed cause of one of the contingencies—a war with Russia—that drives U.S. defense planning. The principal European states have more than enough economic and technological resources to deal with Russia on their own, if they so choose. The transatlantic bargain should thus be more forthright about the limited liability that the United States is prepared to assume for the continent’s defense.

The National Defense Strategy of the Trump administration is honest about this fact, but U.S. military activity levels and deployments in Europe suggest that the United States has not truly reduced its role in Europe’s defense. The supreme allied commander of NATO is still an American, when the position should be filled by a European. Tens of thousands of U.S. troops are still based all over Europe; many should come home. Pentagon websites and those of American commands in Europe feature laundry lists of exercises and maneuvers across the continent that involve not only forward-based U.S. forces but also rotating deployments of units based in the United States. These numbers, too, should diminish.

American officials may want to be able to solve most of their global security challenges by simply buying more forces. But a much better solution is for the United States to change its grand strategy and act with greater restraint. Washington simply does not have the will or the resources to provide for both Asia’s and Europe’s defense while fighting protracted conflicts elsewhere, most recently in the Middle East. Nor, for that matter, does it need to. The United States is inherently a very secure country. It is rich, endowed with bountiful natural resources, insulated by vast oceans, and blessed with relatively weak and pliant neighbors. Only huge changes in the political constellation of power in Asia, Europe, or the greater Middle East could seriously affect U.S. security.

Washington should buy sufficient military power and stock adequate reserves of raw materials to ensure against such changes. But in general, it can afford to be less proactive. A change in grand strategy might even allow the United States to cut the defense budget. If concerns about the ballooning U.S. deficits are correct, then the Pentagon will need to help pay the bills to set things right.

The Arab Monarchies Must Help Washington and Tehran Save Face

#6063. How Israel’s Coalition Wrangling Could Play Out

Q&A: How Israel’s Coalition Wrangling Could Play Out

Israel’s elections on Tuesday have delivered a parliament with no clear path to a new government. Incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party has won 27 out of 120 available seats in the Knesset, leaving his right-wing coalition short of the seats needed for a majority, and opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party has won 21 seats, also leaving it unable to form a government unless it joins forces with the surging Arab parties that his allies have previously refused to join forces with.

What happens next, and what will coalition bargaining reveal about where Israeli society stands, three years on from the devastating Hamas attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, and the deadly regional wars that followed? On the latest episode of FP Live, I spoke with Dahlia Scheindlin, an Israeli pollster and political scientist who is a columnist for Haaretz. The full interview is available on the video box atop this page, or on the FP Live podcast on Spotify, YouTube, or Apple. What follows here is a lightly edited transcript.

Israel’s elections on Tuesday have delivered a parliament with no clear path to a new government. Incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party has won 27 out of 120 available seats in the Knesset, leaving his right-wing coalition short of the seats needed for a majority, and opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party has won 21 seats, also leaving it unable to form a government unless it joins forces with the surging Arab parties that his allies have previously refused to join forces with.

What happens next, and what will coalition bargaining reveal about where Israeli society stands, three years on from the devastating Hamas attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, and the deadly regional wars that followed? On the latest episode of FP Live, I spoke with Dahlia Scheindlin, an Israeli pollster and political scientist who is a columnist for Haaretz. The full interview is available on the video box atop this page, or on the FP Live podcast on Spotify, YouTube, or Apple. What follows here is a lightly edited transcript.

Ravi Agrawal: Dahlia, you’ve covered so many elections in Israel. Why was this particular election seen as so important for the country’s future?

Dahlia Scheindlin: We definitely had record turnout, which means that the vast majority of the voters saw it that way.

I don’t think I’ve ever seen two major blocs of voters as polarized. The opposition parties won a clear majority of 67 out of 120 parliamentary seats. This is getting a bit lost in international coverage. The opposition parties have a majority, and they share the sense that the country is heading for a disaster. They believe that Netanyahu was deeply committed to his alliance with his ultranationalist, extremist, religious fundamentalist political partners, and that they had sacrificed the best interests of the country for an attack on the Israeli judiciary that was unpopular among the majority from the start of 2023.

It sparked such a social backlash that it left Israel open to attack—the worst attack in Israel’s history, obviously—and then the government refused to take responsibility for it. And the issue of the government refusing to establish an independent commission of inquiry into what happened on Oct. 7, 2023, was among the most animating issues for the opposition voters.

Those who support Netanyahu see Israel as having been attacked on numerous fronts. They believe that only Netanyahu has the kind of political savvy and international clout to be able to resist pressure to end the wars that they believe are a matter of survival. When they think about Oct. 7, they think of how close Israel was to existential destruction. In their minds, Netanyahu is the prime minister who managed to marshal Israel’s closest ally, the United States, to join Israel in its war against Iran. They believe that Israel must continue on that path. They also believe Israel must never give up any control over the West Bank or Gaza, or leave its positions in Lebanon and Syria, and that these are a matter of survival.

RA: You suggested the international media is missing the headline here. But isn’t it true that Netanyahu is better placed than we expected?

DS: First of all, I’m looking at the data. Mr. Netanyahu and the parties that are loyal to him did not achieve a majority of the votes. Netanyahu’s loyalist parties won 44 percent of the vote; 56 percent wanted Netanyahu out.

The problem is that the opposition is composed of many fragmented political parties. If the opposition can’t form an alternative, then it doesn’t really matter. The biggest elephant in the room here is that the Zionist parties of the opposition—parties representing mostly Jewish citizens of Israel—have stated time and again that they do not want to build a coalition with parties representing mostly Arab or Palestinian Israeli citizens. But ultimately, it is a completely self-imposed constraint—and, frankly, it’s racist.

RA: So Israel has a parliamentary system with many parties, and we’re now going to enter a period of coalition wrangling. But it’s also interesting to me that this election had at least some element of the personality contest that comes with a presidential system. So you’ve mentioned Netanyahu; the other figure everyone was talking about was Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party.

DS: The fact that he’s a former IDF (Israel Defense Forces) chief of staff puts him in the highest level of esteem among most Jewish Israelis. There is a constituency of people who are in the center but lean right, who prioritize security issues and believe that Israel needs to be militarily strong and a Jewish state. But beyond that, they’re not extremists; they want a liberal society that separates religion from the state and ensures the separation of powers. They’re not happy with Netanyahu’s leadership, which has tried to consolidate power in the executive. And that group has supported somebody like Eisenkot time and again.

RA: Give us some insight into how the coalition wrangling works out. Now that we know a couple of the main characters, could Eisenkot cobble together some of these other opposition parties, plus the Arab parties, and maybe try to form a government, or is Netanyahu the one who has the best shot at trying to do so? How does this all work?

DS: The various scenarios for how to reach a government are manifold, and they are all uncertain. One scenario is that nobody can build a government, and Israel goes into another election, which is the precedent we had from 2019 through 2022, when we held five election cycles for this very reason.

Another scenario is that there is a minority government, which is legal as long as it’s sworn in with more votes than those against it. It is inherently unstable, because there is a majority of parliamentary seats who could vote to disband the Knesset and call new elections. There is also a possibility—and not an unlikely one—that, for example, Netanyahu is asked to form the government by the president, and somebody from the Zionist opposition parties defects to his side.

Most Israeli parties are amalgamated factions of smaller parties. There’s a lot of speculation about a unity government between Likud and the mainstream Zionist parties, with bargaining over who would be prime minister when. That is very complex, legally and politically. Netanyahu would want to be first in any rotation; the opposition parties would not want to accept that. If he goes second in a rotation, he’s in trouble because he is legally not supposed to be serving as a regular minister since he is under indictment for three counts of corruption and has been standing trial for the last six years. But you can see how many options are on the table. None of them are great ones.

Main opposition parties fail to muster majority.

Early results indicate deadlock in parliamentary elections.

RA: It does seem like Israel is generally becoming more right-wing, more focused on its security at the cost of soft power. Netanyahu has frequently said he’s happy to turn Israel into Sparta. And it seems like what is so striking from everything you’ve said so far is that Netanyahu won a fair number of seats, and despite the opposition’s performance, he is still somewhat popular. Clearly, the differences between him and the potential opposition are not that great on some key issues on security. So what does this mean for Israel’s overall trajectory, no matter who actually forms a government after this?

DS: It’s a good observation about hard power versus soft power. Israel is a militarist society and has placed so much emphasis on the image of the omnipotent army, but of course, it was no less invested in its global image over the decades and prided itself on being part of the family of democratic nations in the West.

But in recent years, the country has unapologetically moved away from its liberal trajectory. Across the board, Israelis increasingly think that the entire world is against them, that the whole world is inherently anti-Israel and antisemitic no matter what Israel does. That goes beyond the right wing. The backlash against Israel in the immediate days after Oct. 7 was proof of concept to those who already felt that way and also really scared a lot of Israelis who didn’t necessarily think that way.

RA: But Dahlia, since you speak to so many voters and have your pulse on how Israelis think, can you play out that school of thought of feeling like everyone’s against you, of feeling that much of the region and the world is antisemitic? Where does that lead? What is the logical conclusion of that feeling?

DS: Netanyahu told us where that will lead just a day or two before the election. He said that in light of the possibility that Israel will be facing more sweeping sanctions—even more than it already is—it would have to build a separate economy that is free of the global system, and that Israel can just do that based on cryptocurrency. Nobody took it very well. But again, he maximized his vote. Netanyahu’s supporters are not deterred; they think that Israel has always been a resilient country, so they’re not as worried, whereas the Israelis who didn’t vote for the government are terrified at the idea of being shut out of the world that they want to be part of. They see themselves with a more globalist orientation.

RA: How much do regular Israelis reckon with the change in attitude toward Israel in the United States, as more and more Americans seem to be openly discussing a changing U.S.-Israeli relationship, in part because of Israel’s politics over the last few years, and in particular over Gaza and U.S. military support for Israel in that war. It doesn’t seem like this has been a change election on that front.

DS: The majority of Israelis believed it was a change election, just not in the ways the international community was looking for. I’ve never seen a bigger gap between how outsiders view Israel and how Israelis are talking about their country since Oct. 7. It’s natural that from the outside, people don’t always see the inside of any country, but I do think the gap has gotten so much bigger.

For Israelis, American attitudes are a background issue. It occasionally makes a headline when a new Pew or Gallup survey comes out showing the erosion of Israel’s position. But again, that’s when the majority of Israeli Jews return to the idea that people were probably always against Israel, and that certainly in America, they have that “woke disease” that has poisoned the public mind toward Israel and has nothing to do with Israel’s policies—even those who are critical of Israel’s policy at home. When they hear that kind of criticism from abroad, they get defensive.

People who are already opposed to the government will say that this is another thing they think is problematic or that they’re worried about. But it’s not the number one most urgent issue for them. There is an awareness of the possibility of a change in America following the midterms and an awareness of where the Democratic Party is going. But I think the presidential election and the possibility of a change of administration is too abstract for Israelis right now.

It was always a profound and frankly incomprehensible mistake to think that you could just hold people under a hostile and violent military occupation. The day-to-day reality of Palestinians is so bad that there would always be some sort of escalation. I know of no national movement seeking self-determination that has ever given up on their self-determination, no matter how good their quality of life. Palestinians have neither.

That’s the delusion in every unresolved ethno-nationalist territorial conflict, especially when the gap is so huge and one side enjoys full sovereignty—complete international integration and great economic indicators—while the other side has none of those things, nor national self-determination. There’s no reality in which that would ever go away or fail to escalate. The longer it goes on, the more extreme the escalations become.

So it’s not just bad for Israel’s foreign relations or image. Primarily, it’s bad for the Palestinians who continue living under this hostile and very violent regime, and of course for Gaza, the vast destruction of which is incomprehensible at this point. But it’s bad for Israel, too. Israel’s democracy cannot really ever be fulfilled. These are the same state institutions who are ultimately implicated in that regime, and this is what ultimately fed into the chaos that we saw in 2023.

It is also the source of the deepest divisions within Israel over the very nature of its regime, which is what was at stake in 2023 and what so many Israelis thought was at stake in this election, even if they didn’t make the connection that it’s fundamentally connected with occupation and Palestinians.

Ravi Agrawal is the editor in chief of Foreign Policy. X: @RaviReports

#6061. 'Toxic cocktail' of renter protections destroyed $39M affordable housing investment as Dem cities follow suit

Rental Housing Association of Washington Executive Director Sean Flynn discusses a Seattle landlord's constitutional challenge to city rental laws, the impact on affordable housing and the ruling's potential national implications.

Seattle's effort to protect renters allegedly helped destroy a $39 million investment meant to provide affordable housing, sending a 254-unit apartment complex that served lower-income residents into receivership. Now, its owners have scored a court victory in a battle that could influence similar fights in Philadelphia and other Democrat-led cities.

The Washington Court of Appeals ruled Monday that GRE Downtowner LLC, the company behind Seattle's 254-unit Addison on Fourth affordable housing development, can proceed with claims that the city's sweeping rental regulations amounted to an unconstitutional taking of private property. GRE alleges the restrictions, including an ordinance requiring landlords to accommodate certain additional occupants without their consent, sent rent collections plummeting, triggered millions in losses and ultimately made the once-viable affordable housing investment financially unsustainable.

The development operated under the federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credit program, which offers tax incentives to private investors in exchange for providing rent-restricted apartments to lower-income residents. Sean Flynn, executive director of the Rental Housing Association of Washington, explained that while such developments typically generate relatively modest profits, the federal tax credits make them financially attractive to investors, helping bring private money into affordable housing projects that might otherwise struggle to get built.

Flynn, who is working with GRE Downtowner in its case against the City of Seattle, told Fox News Digital that the city's successive ordinances targeting landlords ultimately created a "toxic cocktail of legislation" that took a functioning affordable housing property and "destroyed it."

PROPERTY OWNER ADVOCACY GROUPS PUSH BACK ON MAMDANI'S 'RENTAL RIPOFF REPORT,' PUBLIC DATABASE OF LANDLORDS

A photo of a housing development in the state of Washington. (Wolfgang Kaehler/LightRocket via Getty Images)

According to court filings, GRE's investment initially proved financially viable, with the property generating positive cash flow from 2015 through 2018. But as Seattle enacted a series of ordinances restricting criminal-background checks, expanding tenants' ability to bring additional occupants into their apartments, limiting certain evictions and requiring relocation assistance following qualifying rent increases, GRE alleges its rent collections collapsed from 93.9% in 2018 to just 44.1% in 2023, contributing to nearly $5.8 million in cumulative operating losses.

The financial deterioration ultimately culminated in a federal judge appointing a receiver in January 2026 to take control of the property following a mortgage default.

"The policies they're passing are detrimental to the folks they're actually trying to help," Flynn warned, arguing that excessive restrictions on landlords ultimately hurt renters by discouraging housing investment. "No one will invest to build more housing if they believe that the government can come in and effectuate a taking – to take the property out from under them – and they have no legal recourse."

OREGON DEMOCRATS PROPOSE 'RIGHT TO REST ACT' DECRIMINALIZING PUBLIC CAMPING AS HOMELESS CRISIS SURGES

Sean Flynn is a Seattle-based real estate attorney and the president and executive director of the Rental Housing Association of Washington (RHAWA). (Fox News Digital)

"What this decision says is, 'Government, you can regulate, you can regulate to your heart's content,'" Flynn added. "But if your regulations amount to the point of which you take my real property, I'm allowed to sue you for it."

Ilya Somin, a George Mason University law professor specializing in constitutional law and property rights, told Fox News Digital that the ruling is more consequential than a routine procedural decision but cautioned against overstating its broader impact.

"This is only moderately significant, but it's more significant than just a routine legal decision that only affects the people immediately involved," Somin said, explaining that courts in other states could consider the Washington ruling when weighing similar constitutional challenges. He also said the case could theoretically go to the U.S. Supreme Court, but said that was fairly unlikely.

Seattle is hardly alone in imposing sweeping restrictions on landlords. San Francisco has long enforced rent controls and limits on evictions, and New York City expanded eviction protections in 2024 under the state's Good Cause Eviction law, limiting landlords' ability to remove certain tenants or refuse lease renewals while allowing renters to challenge excessive rent increases. Portland, Oregon, limits landlords' use of criminal histories when screening prospective tenants and requires relocation payments following certain rent increases of 10% or more. Philadelphia has also adopted restrictions involving criminal-history screening. These policies reflect a broader push to strengthen renters' rights in major Democrat-led cities, even as property owners raise concerns about the consequences of increasingly restrictive housing regulations.

OBAMA-ERA MANDATE SLASHED AFTER BEING BLAMED FOR 'SKYROCKETING' HOUSING COSTS

The owners have scored a court victory in a battle that could influence similar fights in New York and other Democrat-led cities. (Getty Images)

Flynn warned that the consequences of Seattle's housing policies extend well beyond Addison on Fourth, arguing that mounting restrictions have driven developers and smaller landlords away from Seattle — a city once bustling with residential construction.

"Once upon a time in Seattle, you could stand from my office and you could see crane after crane after crane building housing," Flynn said. "They're gone, and they're not coming back."

Flynn argued that the resulting decline in investment ultimately hurts ordinary renters, leaving them with fewer housing options and higher costs.

"When you take the investment incentive out of providing a product, you get worse products at a higher cost," he said. "Investors listen and they vote with their feet. And as a result, there's less housing and the housing that is available is of lesser quality."

NYC RENT BOARD DISSENTER WARNS MAMDANI-BACKED FREEZE COULD HURT AFFORDABLE HOUSING OVER TIME: 'SLOW BURN'

GRE's lawsuit seeks compensation under a legal principle known as inverse condemnation, which allows property owners to pursue payment when they believe government actions have effectively taken or damaged their property without providing just compensation. GRE argues that Seattle's ordinances, individually and collectively, went so far in restricting its property rights that the city should be held financially responsible for the resulting losses.

The Seattle City Attorney's Office told Fox News Digital that officials are reviewing the appellate ruling and weighing their next steps. "We haven't made a decision on an appeal yet," chief of staff Dan Nolte said in an email Thursday.

Housing in front of the Atlanta skyline in Georgia on Nov. 13, 2022. (Elijah Nouvelage/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"I believe the plaintiffs in this case deserve to win at least on that roommate provision," Somin told Fox News Digital, referring to Seattle's restrictions on landlords' ability to exclude certain additional occupants from rental properties.

Somin pointed to the Supreme Court's 6-3 decision in Cedar Point Nursery v. Hassid , which ruled that a California regulation requiring agricultural employers to allow union organizers onto their private property constituted a physical taking under the Fifth Amendment. He argued that Seattle's Roommate Ordinance raises a similar constitutional question because it requires landlords to accommodate additional occupants with whom they never entered into a rental agreement.

"I think the strongest per se argument is simply an argument against this provision of the ordinance, which says they have to take these people who they never made any contract with at all, never screened, and so on," Somin said. "The additional requirement to let them on their land is going beyond what's in the contract, and the same thing you know would apply here in the Seattle case."

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

With just days to go until the U.S. midterm elections, many Europeans and Canadians are watching closely to see if Democrats will retake Congress and perhaps begin to rein in U.S. President Donald Trump for his final two years in office.

Canadians, who have been on the receiving end of some of Trump’s harshest trade actions, are so hungry for news about the U.S. midterms that they are searching for information at a higher rate than even Americans, according to Google search trends.

With just days to go until the U.S. midterm elections, many Europeans and Canadians are watching closely to see if Democrats will retake Congress and perhaps begin to rein in U.S. President Donald Trump for his final two years in office.

Canadians, who have been on the receiving end of some of Trump’s harshest trade actions, are so hungry for news about the U.S. midterms that they are searching for information at a higher rate than even Americans, according to Google search trends.

“Normal, average Canadians know so much more about the United States and care so much more about the United States,” said retired Royal Canadian Air Force Maj. Gen. Scott Clancy, a former director of operations for the North American Aerospace Defense Command. “Whereas Canada doesn’t even come into the daily [consideration] for the vast, vast majority of Americans in any given day.”

Europeans are also gripped by midterm fever. After Canada and the United States, midterm election information searches were the highest in Denmark, Qatar, and Norway—three countries that have also been rocked by Trump’s foreign-policy actions, from his aggressive claims on Greenland to the war against Iran.

Damian Murphy, the senior vice president for national security and international policy at the liberal Center for American Progress think tank, said that European officials he’s met with lately are “laser-focused on the midterms.” Murphy said he has been struck by the granular level of knowledge his European interlocutors have shown for the state of play of individual House races.

“What I’ve been telling them is that you shouldn’t have super high expectations for what any Congress can affirmatively do,” Murphy said. “In our system, the executive has a lot of power when it comes to the conduct of foreign policy. But what is important is the political message that it will send to the rest of the world: that the American people repudiate all of this—ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement], the Iran war, the treatment of allies.”

Other foreign observers have cautioned against high expectations of a U.S. reversion to pre-Trump foreign policies even if Democrats win control of Congress.

“Let us not overestimate the consequences of a defeat for the Trump administration in the midterm elections,” said former French Ambassador to the United States Gérard Araud in a recent post on X. “An American president holds considerable powers, particularly in foreign policy, and Trump can rely on the Supreme Court to bypass Congress.”

The experiences of Trump’s surprise 2016 and 2024 presidential election wins also continue to act as ballast against runaway hopes of a blue tidal wave.

“My philosophy of life is to have low expectations, and I apply that to the midterms as well. My mission is to stamp out any glimmer of hope of a return to normalcy after the midterms,” said one European diplomat, who requested anonymity to give an unvarnished take on the U.S. political situation.

One outcome with a strong chance of occurring in November, though, is a vote on impeaching U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over allegations of violating war powers and war crimes laws. A vote on the defense chief’s impeachment is likely to happen the week after the midterms.

Even if Republicans find the votes to protect Hegseth in the impeachment vote, a new impeachment inquiry may be launched in January if Democrats win control of the House, as is predicted.

Like the midterms, Canadians are likely to closely follow any impeachment process against Hegseth.

The former Fox News host “deeply offended” many Canadians this fall, Clancy said, when he separately appeared to disparage Canadian troop cadets and denigrated the contributions of NATO allied troops who joined the U.S.-led mission in Afghanistan.

“Personal friends of mine perished during that conflict,” Clancy said.

#6056. Brazil’s Economic Impasse

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

MONICA DE BOLLE is Senior Fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, an Adjunct Professor at Georgetown University, and a co-author of The New Economic Nationalism.

Neither Lula nor Bolsonaro Can Solve the Country’s Problems

On October 5, the day after the first round of Brazil’s general elections, the country’s financial markets were euphoric. Brazil is struggling with high debt and low growth, and investors are eager for leaders to reduce budget deficits, deregulate, cut taxes, and perhaps even privatize state assets. After nearly four years under the left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, who has been slow to implement such measures, investors hope a right-wing government will create opportunities for bold reform.

Rule by the right might be exactly what Brazil gets. The far-right Liberal Party made substantial gains in the legislature, becoming the single largest party in both the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies. Its presidential candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the notorious former President Jair Bolsonaro, led the aging incumbent, Lula, by nearly two percentage points in the first round of voting. Lula has shown himself capable of impressive political comebacks, but Flávio Bolsonaro is still the favorite in the runoff vote scheduled for October 25.

Even if Bolsonaro wins, however, the prospects for the Brazilian economy are dim. The policies he has put forward are nothing close to the substantial fiscal consolidation program that will be necessary to bring down debt and stimulate private investment, and his determination to weaken Brazil’s political institutions creates the kind of uncertainty that scares investors away. Economic growth has been sluggish under Lula, whose administration has struggled to relieve the high debt burdens afflicting the public sector and households. What would truly doom the country to economic crisis, however, is the kind of authoritarian-inspired politics that a Bolsonaro government could usher in.

Brazil is in serious economic trouble. The country’s sovereign debt ratio has ballooned to 83 percent of GDP, fiscal deficits leave no room for additional government spending, and high interest rates are hurting consumers and investors. Meanwhile, the Iran war has raised the price of fuel and other goods, weighing on household balance sheets already strained by high debt and leaving many Brazilians desperate for leaders who can alleviate their daily hardships.

This predicament is years in the making. Before Jair Bolsonaro was elected in 2018, his predecessor, President Michel Temer, enacted a cap on public spending to contain Brazil’s runaway fiscal problems. Temer introduced the cap as a constitutional amendment to prevent future governments from changing the spending ceiling to suit their needs. Yet Jair Bolsonaro raised the cap several times anyway, which required convincing Congress to amend the constitution. In return, the executive branch effectively ceded control of the budgetary process to the legislature.

Lula therefore inherited a system in which he had little room for fiscal adjustment, and he made few attempts to fix the problem during his term. The result was high budget deficits and persistent inflation, which forced the central bank to raise interest rates substantially. In turn, high interest rates damaged household balance sheets and lowered overall investment and growth.

If Lula were reelected, he would find it incredibly difficult to introduce new fiscal reforms and other measures to support growth. He promised to reduce spending and has proposed a comprehensive overhaul of Brazil’s tax system, which would help increase the budget surplus and reduce public debt. Yet Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party and its allies now hold a majority of seats in the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies, allowing them to block any legislation Lula might pursue.

Yet it is overly optimistic, if not completely unrealistic, to expect that Bolsonaro would fare better. Neither candidate has provided much detail during the campaign about what he would do to fix the economy. Bolsonaro has instead spoken often about “institutional reforms,” which he has said would include amending Brazil’s 38-year-old constitution to make existing labor and environmental regulations more flexible, among other changes; meddling with the Supreme Court; and granting amnesty to his father, who is serving a prison sentence for leading a 2023 coup attempt. Those steps are likely to drive away investors because stable institutions are necessary for an economy to function well. A government that undermines the judicial system and the constitution will compromise the integrity of its economic policies, no matter what those policies are or how good the reputations of the officials making them may be.

Gathering support for such an overhaul of the country’s political institutions, moreover, would require compromises that could worsen Brazil’s economic troubles. To secure enough votes in Congress to advance Bolsonaro’s priorities—for example, two-thirds of the Senate would need to approve the removal of a Supreme Court justice, and three-fifths of both houses must approve a constitutional amendment—the government would have to bring legislators outside its coalition on board. Those politicians would almost certainly demand substantial funds for their constituencies in exchange for their support, adding to the budget deficit.

Bolsonaro’s far-right movement will also be focused on holding together its recently formed coalition of governors, mayors, and voters. Much of its constituency is lower-middle-class Brazilians who rose out of poverty during the boom years two decades ago, while Lula was serving his first two terms in office. After seeing their income growth stagnate in the years since, these voters have turned to the Liberal Party, but their loyalty is new. Most are self-employed and face economic precarity. Both Bolsonaro and Lula are now trying to appeal to these voters by promising initiatives that boost income and offer household debt relief, but delivering such programs—if it is even possible—would only exacerbate Brazil’s economic woes.

What Bolsonaro has shared about his economic policies does not inspire much confidence, either. His party has said it would reduce government spending by $40 billion, or 1.5 percent of GDP, and deliver primary budget surpluses—a measure of the budget balance that does not include interest payments. But it has not explained how it would accomplish this, nor has Bolsonaro elaborated on his vague plans for controlling the rise in public debt. Ultimately, it is unlikely that Bolsonaro can deliver on any of these promises, especially if he keeps his pledge not to cut pensions and key social programs.

Part of the problem is that the Liberal Party’s economic program lacks a viable plan for reducing costs. It proposes eliminating at least ten government ministries but has no estimate of the resulting cost savings. When Jair Bolsonaro took similar steps after he assumed office in 2019, removing cabinet positions and laying off public servants, those moves had little effect on fiscal outcomes. Other promised measures include reducing Brazil’s value-added tax, phasing out a tax on financial transactions, lowering taxes on electricity and fuel, spending $180 billion on infrastructure over four years, and building 2.5 million new homes. None of them would fix Brazil’s fiscal problems; they would only make those problems worse.

The same goes for the rest of Flávio Bolsonaro’s tax plan. His economic advisers have said they intend to reverse every tax created or raised under Lula’s finance minister, Fernando Haddad. Haddad’s tax increases were intended to shift the tax burden to high-income brackets, raise government revenue, and reduce inequalities in the tax system. These taxes have contributed to a modest increase in revenue but fell short of delivering budgetary surpluses. Bolsonaro has argued that the measures are impeding investment because they tax higher income brackets more heavily, but there is no evidence to support this idea. Instead, repealing all these tax increases would worsen Brazil’s fiscal situation. A simple calculation shows that Brazil needs to increase its primary budget balance by about six percent of GDP, either through increased revenue or decreased spending (or both), to keep its debt from rising further. That adjustment would have to be spread over at least three years, giving indebted households and firms time to change their consumption and investment patterns, to avoid a recession. Slashing taxes, however, would reduce government revenues, raising the debt.

Brazil’s high interest rates are another constraint. The central bank’s current rate is 13.75 percent, astronomical by Latin American standards, dictating interest rates everywhere in the economy. Public debt service payments alone consume some 8.7 percent of GDP. Bolsonaro would not be able to lower interest rates significantly without sparking a recession, so he would face the same problem that has plagued Lula during his latest term—few good options for containing a rapidly growing debt.

Neither Lula nor Bolsonaro is well positioned to solve Brazil’s economic problems. A decisive turn toward illiberalism under Bolsonaro, however, would all but assure economic disaster.

Flávio Bolsonaro has never disavowed his father’s championing of Brazil’s dictatorship, which lasted from 1964 to 1985, and his Liberal Party traces its lineage to the party that sustained the military regime. Moreover, he has pledged to release his father and his father’s associates who are in prison for staging an insurrection and a coup attempt in 2023. Flávio’s brother Eduardo Bolsonaro, a former member of Brazil’s Congress who would likely play a significant role in his brother’s government, has openly expressed his admiration for Viktor Orban’s illiberal regime in Hungary, claiming a desire to learn the “best practices” of a movement that rewrote Hungary’s constitution, reshaped its courts, silenced its press, and deployed other overtly authoritarian tactics. And the substantial far-right bloc in Brazil’s Congress supports policies to undermine institutions, including by impeaching members of the Supreme Court—a step these parties advocated even before corruption allegations emerged against several of the court’s justices. (Flávio Bolsonaro is also under investigation for his involvement in the same corruption scandal.)

Although Brazil is not at risk of returning to military rule, the former authoritarian regime serves as a warning of what could happen if a Bolsonaro administration follows its illiberal inclinations to their logical conclusion. During those two decades of military dictatorship, Brazil spent at unsustainable levels, mostly funding state enterprises, to preserve the regime’s hold on power. The country defaulted on its public debt, endured corrosive hyperinflation, and saw income inequality skyrocket. Six economic stabilization plans failed and growth stagnated. Brazil is not alone in this experience. No Latin American country that swung from democracy to authoritarian rule in the past century has benefited economically from the shift. Countries elsewhere in the world that prospered after such a transition, including some in East Asia, became less authoritarian during their economic ascent.

Brazil’s rightward shift fits a regional pattern. The common thread that unites Brazil with Argentina, Chile, and Colombia is the crude libertarian worldview that each of their far-right movements espouse. All of them talk about citizens becoming entrepreneurs free of the state. They tell voters who have unstable employment and little economic security that their policies will bring prosperity. But their populism rarely wins the confidence of investors. Like its peers, when the Brazilian far right says it can overcome the country’s substantial problems with institutional demolition and a threadbare economic agenda, what it really offers is empty promises.

#6054. The Gulf Isn’t Ready for a Renewed Iran War

Analysis: The Gulf Isn’t Ready for a Renewed Iran War

By the narrow measure of barrels shipped, the Persian Gulf has weathered eight months of war better than most energy analysts expected. Oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes averaged more than 24 million barrels a day in the week ending Oct. 18, above the prewar level of 23.3 million, according to the ship-tracking firm Kpler. JPMorgan analysts wrote last week that energy markets are “converging on a forever conflict” and that view has encouraged a belief in the Trump administration that the region can absorb another round of fighting.

That view confuses how much oil and gas are still flowing from the Gulf with the state of the plants and terminals that move it. Since the war began on Feb. 28, Iranian missiles and drones have damaged refineries, liquefied natural gas (LNG) trains, and export terminals across the Gulf, and the Houthis have opened a second front in the Red Sea. Much of what has been lost will take years to rebuild. The cost will fall mostly on importers in Asia, Europe, and the developing world that built their energy systems around reliable Gulf supply.

By the narrow measure of barrels shipped, the Persian Gulf has weathered eight months of war better than most energy analysts expected. Oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes averaged more than 24 million barrels a day in the week ending Oct. 18, above the prewar level of 23.3 million, according to the ship-tracking firm Kpler. JPMorgan analysts wrote last week that energy markets are “converging on a forever conflict” and that view has encouraged a belief in the Trump administration that the region can absorb another round of fighting.

That view confuses how much oil and gas are still flowing from the Gulf with the state of the plants and terminals that move it. Since the war began on Feb. 28, Iranian missiles and drones have damaged refineries, liquefied natural gas (LNG) trains, and export terminals across the Gulf, and the Houthis have opened a second front in the Red Sea. Much of what has been lost will take years to rebuild. The cost will fall mostly on importers in Asia, Europe, and the developing world that built their energy systems around reliable Gulf supply.

U.S. and Israeli planners have drawn up options for a short, intensive campaign against Iran’s nuclear facilities, missile and drone arsenals, and energy infrastructure after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, the New York Times reported last week. President Trump has not approved it. This week, the Wall Street Journal reported that Washington has told Gulf governments to prepare for such an offensive. Iranian officials have responded by naming Saudi oil facilities, Gulf data centers, and undersea cables as targets. The next round would likely concentrate on the assets and importers that Gulf states can least afford to lose.

The Gulf’s reputation as a dependable supplier rests on decades of investment as much as on geology. After the 1973 oil embargo, consumer nations created the International Energy Agency (IEA), and the 1980 Carter Doctrine committed the United States to keeping the Gulf open by force. After the 1991 Gulf War and the 2003 invasion of Iraq, Gulf states invested in redundancy. Saudi Arabia expanded the East-West pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, the United Arab Emirates built a pipeline to Fujairah to bypass Hormuz, and Riyadh kept spare production capacity in reserve. All of this assumed that U.S. power would protect the region’s infrastructure or at least deter attacks on it. This year’s fighting has overturned that assumption.

A recent Reuters investigation documented at least 135 Iranian drone and missile attacks on at least 84 infrastructure sites across seven Gulf states since the war’s start. Iranian-linked strikes damaged five of Saudi Arabia’s nine largest refineries and both export manifolds at Fujairah, the UAE’s main terminal outside Hormuz. At Qatar’s Ras Laffan, the world’s largest LNG complex, strikes on the cold boxes that house liquefaction equipment took out two LNG trains representing about 17 percent of Qatar’s export capacity. QatarEnergy expects repairs to take three to five years and to cost an estimated $20 billion in annual revenue. Since much of this equipment is custom-built, the losses will outlast any cease-fire or peace agreement with Iran.

Proponents of a renewed campaign point to U.S. and Gulf air defenses, which by most measures have performed well. The UAE reported intercepting 132 of the 137 ballistic missiles fired at it on the first day of the war. The Jewish Institute for National Security of America (JINSA) estimated in March that more than 90 percent of Iranian projectiles had been intercepted across the theater. Interception rates, however, are the wrong measure for energy infrastructure. A refinery or LNG complex does not need to be hit repeatedly to be taken offline; it needs to lose only one critical component. On March 18, Qatar’s Defense Ministry said its forces intercepted four of the five ballistic missiles Iran fired at Ras Laffan. That attack took out the two trains cited above. An 80 percent interception rate still produced a loss of LNG supply that will last for years. The Financial Times reported that the missiles were maneuverable enough to evade Patriot batteries.

A second round would also begin from a weaker defensive position. JINSA estimated that by late March, Bahrain had used up to 87 percent of its Patriot interceptors and the UAE and Kuwait roughly 75 percent. Even if defenses performed better next time, a handful of missiles reaching a gas train, a pumping station, or a terminal manifold could remove capacity the market cannot replace for years. For planners, the share of Iranian missiles stopped should matter less than what the few that get through will hit.

Neither appealing to Washington nor diversifying security partners nor back-channeling with Tehran is insulating the region from the consequences of war.

Meanwhile, since declaring a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia on July 20, the Houthis have struck Saudi Aramco’s 400,000-barrel-a-day Jizan refinery three times, forcing it offline for repairs in August. Drone strikes on East-West pipeline infrastructure in September led Riyadh to shut the line for 11 days, halting loadings at Yanbu. The group claimed new attacks on the pipeline’s pumping stations on Oct. 24 and Oct. 26, which Saudi Arabia has not confirmed. The pipeline built to cope with a Hormuz closure has become one of the most exposed parts of the Saudi export system.

Asia, which received nearly nine-tenths of the crude shipped through Hormuz before the war, has borne the brunt. In March, Bangladesh closed its universities early, rationed fuel at the pump, and diverted gas from four of its five state fertilizer plants to keep the grid running. Pakistan imposed a four-day workweek and closed schools. India limited households to one subsidized cooking-gas cylinder every 25 days as crowds besieged dealers. The Philippines declared a national energy emergency, and in May rotating blackouts left nearly 2 million people on Luzon without power. By September, Bangladeshi garment exporters reported canceled orders and idled production lines, hospitals in Sylhet were losing power almost hourly, and some families in Dhaka waited until midnight for enough gas pressure to cook dinner. Europe’s exposure runs mainly through refined products; European diesel premiums hit records in September.

Iranian strikes on Saudi oil facilities, combined with the Houthi campaign, would place both Saudi export routes under simultaneous attack while the region’s other bypasses are already degraded. Recovery timelines would lengthen toward a decade, and the Saudi spare capacity that has absorbed supply shocks since the 1990s would erode. Buyers and sellers are already adjusting in ways a second round would make permanent. On Oct. 22, QatarEnergy signed a deal to buy up to 4 million metric tons a year of U.S. LNG from Cheniere through 2054, supply that does not pass through Hormuz. If fighting resumes, Gulf producers may find that the market share they cede to the United States, to coal, and to other suppliers does not return.

The alternative to another round is a negotiated settlement in which both sides give ground, and the outlines of one are already visible. Qatari mediators delivered a draft agreement to Tehran on Oct. 25 that reportedly sets out a seven-day sequence of reciprocal confidence-building steps, backed by several guarantor states. A senior Iranian official dismissed it as “not an offer,” but Tehran is expected to respond this week. Washington has moved from demanding an end to Iranian enrichment to seeking a “meaningful” reduction, while Tehran’s priorities are relief from the U.S. naval blockade and oil sanctions. A deal that trades verifiable limits on enrichment and an unconditional reopening of Hormuz for phased relief on the blockade and sanctions would require each side to accept terms it has so far resisted.

Those concessions carry political costs, but they are cheaper than the alternative. The U.S. military’s costs had reached $47.1 billion by mid-October, according to U.S. Central Command, $29 billion of it for replacing expended munitions. A short campaign would not repair Ras Laffan or restore Saudi spare capacity, and it would invite exactly the retaliation that air defenses cannot fully stop.

Gulf producers spent five decades persuading the world that their supply could withstand regional wars. Eight months of fighting on two fronts have badly weakened that case. A negotiated end to the war would give the region time to rebuild it. Another round, on top of the Saudi-Houthi war, would leave damage to infrastructure and to importers’ confidence that markets are likely to carry for a generation.

Amir Handjani is a board member at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft and a partner at KARV, a strategic advisory firm based in New York. X: @ahandjani

#6053. A look inside the Somali mall where Omar reappeared after DC raid raises more failed assimilation concerns

Fox News Digital was given permission to film inside the Karmel Mall of Somalia in Minneapolis, which the owner says is the largest Somali mall in the world.

MINNEAPOLIS — The day after Rep. Ilhan Omar's first public appearance since the raid on her home, Fox News Digital was given a tour of the mall where she reemerged in her home state.

The footage provides a glimpse inside an enclave within America that is dominated by Somalis and Somali culture, and gives a peak into the community that Omar represents in the U.S. House of Representatives.

The mall isn't just a place for people to buy clothing, food and receive services, but is a "community hub" of mostly women entrepreneurs, as described by a female shop owner.

"We're here today at Karmel Mall with brother Basim, to kind of browse through this amazing community corridor that is full of amazing women," she told Fox News Digital, referring to the Karmel Mall of Somalia's owner, Basim Sabri, who provided the tour.

'RADICAL LEFT LUNATIC' JUDGE TRUMP WANTED IMPEACHED TAKES UP ILHAN OMAR WARRANT FIGHT

Rep. Ilhan Omar and Karmel Mall of Somalia owner Basim Sabri inside the dining area in the mall. (Rashid Umar Abbasi/Fox News Digital)

Sabri, a Gaza-born immigrant, came to the United States to study in Minneapolis. During that time, he became a real-estate investor and steadily grew his business. Now, he owns a vast real estate empire, which includes the mall and several apartment complexes in the area that house Somalis. He has political ties at all levels of local and state politics, and is friends with Omar. He also knew the Somali-born congresswoman's father.

Fox News Digital interviewed him separately, days before the official tour of the mall.

For most inside, English is the mall's second language. It's packed with stores offering electronic SIM cards to call overseas, foreign money exchanges and travel agencies arranging trips to the Middle East and East Africa. Vendors also sell gold, fragrances and traditional Somali fashion items, mostly for women.

There are Somali barber shops, cafes, traditional Somali food vendors and henna tattoo shops. Sabri gave conflicting figures on the exact number of stores, once saying 900, and later 750.

SOMALIS IN MINNESOTA UNLEASH FURY ON TRUMP AFTER FEDS RAID ILHAN OMAR'S DC HOME

It sports a food court with a giant Somali flag painted on the ceiling, as well as Somali, Palestinian and American flags hanging from the walls. Many politicians use that space for press conferences, Sabri explained.

It's also where Omar ate lunch with friends, supporters and state Attorney General Keith Ellison during Fox News Digital's foray into the mall when the lawmaker reemerged after casting an early ballot in her own re-election.

Women selling clothes inside the Karmel Mall of Somalia in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Rashid Umar Abbasi/Fox News Digital)

Karmel Mall also has an Islamic weekend school for children, where they're taught the Quran and engage in recreational activities.

While the mall isn't strictly for Somalis, few outside the Somali community were present when Fox News Digital toured. Fox News Digital was initially bucked by security upon attempting to enter and film inside the mall without Sabri's permission.

The owner banned Democratic Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey from the premises in February 2024 after he vetoed an Israel-Gaza ceasefire resolution passed by the City Council.

OMAR’S MIDTERM RIVAL EXPOSES 'VICIOUS' SOMALI GANGS AMID IMMIGRATION PROBE INTO EMBATTLED REP

"It is kind of an incubator setting where many businesses start in here, and then many succeed and grow and move somewhere else, to a bigger space," Sabri explained to Fox News Digital.

He claims that the mall is a space where Somalis learn to integrate into the community.

A woman receives a henna tattoo inside the Karmel Mall of Somalia in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Rashid Umar Abbasi/Fox News Digital)

"You can see [the] Somalis not only integrating in the community, but also prospering," he said. "Somalis are very smart business individuals."

But the mall's very name — the Karmel Mall of Somalia — along with the overwhelmingly Somali culture inside, raise questions about whether the group is actually assimilating into American society.

WORKING-CLASS AMERICANS SAY THEIR TOWN IS THE NEXT DEARBORN — AND THEY'VE HAD ENOUGH

Steven Camarota is the director for research at the Center for Immigration Studies (CIS). He pointed Fox News Digital to a CIS report published in December of last year that describes Somalis as a "struggling group."

The report shows that more than half of children who live in the homes of Somali-born immigrants in Minnesota live in poverty, compared to only 8% of children living in homes of native-born Minnesotans. Among Somali-born immigrants who have lived in the United States for more than a decade, half cannot speak English "very well." The report says that 89% of Somali households receive some form of welfare, and 39% don't have high school diplomas, compared to only 8% of the native population.

A sign for the Karmel Mall of Somalia in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Peter D'Abrosca/Fox News Digital)

Camarota argued that across America, assimilation among various foreign-born groups, including Somalis, has dropped, though today's immigration numbers are about the same as they were during America's first great wave of immigration.

In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, immigrations from across the world flooded the United States. During that time, immigrants comprised about 15% of America's population, on par with today's numbers. After World War I, restrictive immigration policies that lasted until the 1960s took effect. In more recent history, immigration has ramped up to the tune of one million legal immigrants per year entering the United States, Camarota said.

MINNESOTA SENATE HOPEFUL WARNS THREAT LEVEL RISING AMID RASH OF SOMALI GANG CRIME, TERROR PLOT

"So, there are three big things about modern immigration that you can argue greatly hinder assimilation, and it has much less to do with the immigrants, and a lot more to do with just modern conditions," he told Fox News Digital. "The first is technology. You can fly home and visit home for the holidays if you want. In a way that just wouldn't have been possible in 1900, and in terms of costs."

Women working inside the Karmel Mall of Somalia in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Rashid Umar Abbasi/Fox News Digital)

Camarota noted that the internet allows people access to constant news from home, and the constant ability to stay connected with family and friends via phone and video calls.

"So this technology, travel and communications is fundamentally different today than in the past. And that likely means that the connection with the home country doesn't become as attenuated as quickly as it would have," he said.

The attitudes of those who Camarota characterizes as "elites," in academia, government, media and other institutions, have also changed. He said there are now dueling theories about what exactly America is that could be contributing to a lack of assimilation.

FORMER MN STATE TROOPER TEARS INTO DEMS AS SOMALI GANG VIOLENCE TERRORIZES MINNESOTA: ‘WHERE IS ILHAN OMAR?’

"So is America essentially a magnificent historical project of democracy and equality and republican government, or is it essentially — most of that's a sham and it's really a racist, sexist, homophobic [and] classist society?" he said. "The immigrants are arriving in a country in many ways that received both those messages, and so this elite attitude which permeates down is just so different than the world of the last great wave of immigration and almost certainly matters a great deal."

A barbershop inside the Karmel Mall of Somalia in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Rashid Umar Abbasi/Fox News Digital)

Essentially, Camarota argued, if immigrants adopt the narrative that America is a fundamentally flawed nation, there is little reason for them to assimilate.

"The word assimilation itself is seen as a bad word in many circles. The idea that immigrants are supposed to shed their old culture and become American is now seen as a kind of, for some — I don't want to say universally for all — but some fraction of it at least, as an undesirable Anglo conformity," he continued.

"We are living in a country that can't really agree itself about its own history, let alone agree on what it wants from the immigrants."

The third important fact to assimilation in Camarota's mind is the sheer number of immigrants coming to the United States.

ALARMING FRAUD TREND PUTS SMALL-TOWN MOSQUE WITH INDUSTRY AND FOREIGN GOVT TIES IN FOCUS: ‘OUR MOTHERLAND NOW’

"The last point is numbers," he said. "So, we're at a record high now, right? Fifteen percent of the population is foreign born. It's matched the levels of between 1890 and 1910... during the last peak of the last great wave. But the one question then has to be asked, what happened then?"

He said the immigration restriction of the mid-20th century necessarily resulted in assimilation, as immigrants could not endlessly build enclaves for more and more foreign-born residents, as is happening today.

"I think it's pretty clear it likely played a very big role in facilitating the assimilation of the immigrants," he said, suggesting that a similar immigration restriction could have the same effect if implemented now.

A sign for the Karmel Mall of Somalia in Minneapolis on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. (Peter D'Abrosca/Fox News Digital)

In 2005, he was sentenced to 33 months in federal prison for bribing a local Minneapolis public official. He told Fox News Digital in the first interview about his time in prison, which included a brief stay at the infamous Federal Correctional Institution, Leavenworth in Kansas, in colorful detail.

In that interview, he also insisted that the mall is for everyone.

"But my experience is that Somalis are very, very intelligent and extremely hard-working people," he said.

"So, I would invite anybody to come into the mall, and know that there are many people doing a great job and making a good living, and learning the American dream, and doing business, and opening businesses that eventually tend to be very successful for them."

Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.
