#6027. How to Secure the Straits

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

DANA STROUL is Director of Research at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. She served as U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for the Middle East from February 2021 to December 2023.

Why Iran and the Houthis Keep Winning the Waterways

Over the past month, Iran has made its most intense attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz since the United States and Israel declared war, in February. More than 100 drone and missile launches into the strait have been recorded since the war began; in October alone, a container ship and a bulk vessel sank in the waterway. Meanwhile, in the Red Sea, Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have sustained their campaign to throttle seaborne trade as they target Saudi Arabia more directly, seizing new territory along the Bab el Mandeb Strait.

These dual maritime crises form part of the same strategic problem—one that, despite its new intensity, has existed for years. In 2019, Iran attacked shipping across the Gulf in response to the first Trump administration’s maximum-pressure sanctions campaign; in 2023, the Houthis launched assaults in the Red Sea following Hamas’s October 7 massacre in Israel. After each of these campaigns, the United States and its partners established maritime coalitions to protect these vital seaborne trade routes. The efforts helped secure the waterways, but they never fundamentally persuaded Iran and its proxies that asymmetric attacks on shipping were an ineffective way to project power. On the contrary, such tactics have only become more appealing to Tehran.

Even now, some shipping persists through both waterways. On October 15, Lloyd’s List Intelligence reported that transit through the Bab el Mandeb Strait was up modestly from August. U.S. naval patrols—as well as creative logistical adaptation by Gulf states, including ship-to-ship transfers, have allowed some oil to move through Hormuz. But shipping still remains throttled, and international actors have not yet found a way to update their deterrence playbook. In 2019 and 2023–24, U.S., European, and Middle Eastern navies formed separate, overlapping defensive maritime coalitions to escort vessels, collect intelligence on evolving threats, and intercept missile and drone attacks. In the United States’ case in 2024, a separate multinational coalition also conducted offensive strikes in Yemen to undermine Houthi maritime capabilities. Today, governments are falling back on the same instinct—to join forces, but not all their forces. The British and the French have proposed a multinational maritime defense coalition to secure the Strait of Hormuz once the war ends, while Saudi Arabia is planning, but has not yet deployed, its own alliance to protect the Red Sea. Neither project includes the United States, which has deployed nearly one-third of its naval warships to the Middle East in an attempt to reestablish freedom of navigation, enforce a naval blockade against Iran, and support U.S. attacks on Iran.

Multiple short-term, insufficiently coordinated defensive missions organized around voluntary contributions can buy down marginal risk for shippers in the near-term but they cannot deliver long-term deterrence. Separate missions embolden Iranian and Houthi leaders, who will interpret them as half-measures that are easily strained by resource scarcity, an inability to adapt quickly to evolving threats, and the absence of real-time intelligence sharing across the two chokepoints. As crises in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea become more linked amid an expanding regional war, replicating the patchwork maritime strategy that never fully worked would be a serious mistake. What is needed instead is a single, sustained multinational effort to secure both waterways that combines American military capabilities with the imprimatur of a unified coalition of Asian, European, and Middle Eastern countries. Otherwise, Iran and the Houthis will again learn that threatening global commerce in maritime chokepoints is a strategy worth repeating.

The maritime coalitions now taking shape share a troubling precedent. Twice before, international actors have mounted similar efforts, and their mixed results show why even effective defensive operations fail to prevent renewed attacks in Middle Eastern waterways. In mid-2019, after the first Trump administration launched its “maximum pressure” sanctions campaign against Iran, Tehran attacked tankers off the coast of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and in the Gulf of Oman and seized a British-flagged oil tanker from international waters in the Strait of Hormuz. Insurance premiums spiked tenfold, and freight rates for crude-oil-carrying tankers jumped nearly 40 percent. In response, Washington established the International Maritime Security Construct (IMSC), headquartered in Bahrain; the mission sought to maintain naval vessels across key waterways in the Middle East to deter Iran and collect intelligence on Iranian maritime activities to share with commercial shippers.

By the end of 2019, Albania, Australia, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and the United Kingdom had joined the IMSC. But despite Washington’s efforts to expand the coalition further, most European countries abstained from joining. They were frustrated with the Trump administration’s withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear deal with Tehran and wary that joining the IMSC—with its focus on confronting Iran—would be seen by Tehran as aggressive or an endorsement of Washington’s maximum pressure campaign. Instead, eight European countries joined a French-led mission called European Maritime Awareness in the Strait of Hormuz (EMASoH), which emphasized de-escalation, surveillance, and encouraging regional dialogue with Iran.

Four years later, when the Houthis began to threaten shipping in the Red Sea—spiking maritime insurance rates and forcing vessels to detour around the Cape of Good Hope—the United States and Europe once again organized separate responses. In December 2023, the United States launched Operational Prosperity Guardian (OPG), a naval coalition soon joined by more than 20 countries. The mission maintained four to eight warships in the Red Sea area at any given time and successfully shot down Houthi drones and missiles; within its first month, its leaders said it had facilitated safe transit for more than a thousand commercial vessels. The European Union formed its own, substantially smaller defensive maritime operation that escorted European commercial vessels through the southern Red Sea and also intercepted Houthi drone and missile attacks.

In both crises, the United States, Europe, and the Gulf states broadly agreed that Iranian and Houthi threats to freedom of navigation required a response. Because freedom of navigation was viewed as a fundamental principle of the global order, assembling large groups committed to upholding this pillar was intended to demonstrate international resolve and isolate the bad actor. But disagreement over how to confront the challenge diluted the missions. Many governments declined to join offensive strikes or coalitions explicitly directed at a state. Political divides further splintered the response, as Europe sought to put distance between itself and the United States’ Iran strategy.The 2019–24 missions achieved important tactical successes by improving maritime awareness, intercepting some attacks, and stopping a complete shutdown of shipping. But the lack of a long-term, coordinated strategy for ending Iran’s aggression weakened the response. The missions never fully persuaded shippers that these waterways were safe—especially the Red Sea—or prevented Iran and the Houthis from eventually returning to their efforts to exploit the chokepoints. According to a 2021 assessment by the Dutch government, the Netherlands assumed that Iran could differentiate between the European maritime mission and the American-led one and would be less aggressive toward European vessels, underscoring Tehran’s ability to exploit the gaps between overlapping operations and the need for a unified front.

The lessons from these missions matter enormously today. After years of shadow warfare, the United States and Israel have now fought Iran directly. In 2025, the United States and Israel also launched separate months-long campaigns against the Houthis in Yemen, following a decadelong Saudi-led effort to dislodge the rebel group. These campaigns badly battered Iran and the Houthis. But they also gave them a chance to hone their asymmetric tactics. Having survived wars intended to collapse their regimes, Iran and the Houthis have emerged more willing to hold global commerce at risk and impose costs on actors not directly involved in the wars against them. Both have learned that they do not need to fully close maritime chokepoints. Simply threatening them can change decision-making in the halls of power.

Nobody wants tolls or unilaterally imposed service payments on these waterways, proposals that Iran has tabled. Instead, to try to deal with the crises, there has been a flowering of disjointed maritime coalition planning efforts. The British-French plan resembles previous European maritime efforts, proposing a defensive multinational mission to escort vessels. It excludes the United States and will not activate until the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran ends for good—a condition that essentially guarantees its uselessness in the near term. Houthi aggression, meanwhile, has sent Saudi Arabia scrambling to secure Red Sea transit, which is increasingly vital given disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. In late July, Riyadh announced the formation of its own defensive maritime coalition with 14 countries from across Africa and the Middle East, as well as Bangladesh and Pakistan, which will be distinct from both European efforts on Hormuz and the U.S. mission. The United States has put up its own military effort to secure Gulf waterways focused on escorting vessels through Omani waters and actively defending commercial shippers from daily Iranian attacks. Concurrently, the U.S. Navy is enforcing a naval blockade against Iranian ports and disabling tankers that ignore its warnings.

The European and Saudi plans are already behind the curve of events. Leaders across Europe and the Middle East want to differentiate their defensive maritime missions from U.S. and Israeli offensive campaigns against Iran in order to prevent escalation and protect their own forces. But the European and Saudi efforts have not moved beyond planning. The U.S. mission, for its part, is active in the wartime waterways of the Middle East and has for now successfully restored much of the prewar crude oil flows out of the region amid Iranian attacks. But eventually, the U.S. Navy will struggle to maintain its large presence in the Middle East given competing priorities and the wear and tear of continuous deployment. Iranian leaders are gambling that they can outlast the United States in will and capability, while driving wedges between Washington and its long-standing partners in Asia, Europe, and the Middle East, who have yet to meaningfully defend maritime transit. These coalitions will all fail to deter Iran and the Houthis for good if they do not coordinate with each other.

Without American naval capabilities and intelligence, maritime missions to secure these waterways simply cannot succeed given the scope and scale of the threat. (In 2019, the European mission was only able to field a maximum of three warships and a single patrol aircraft, compared with the United States’ dozen ships; the United States’ 2023–24 OPG mission was able to respond thanks to its naval bases nearby in Bahrain.) Yet U.S. naval superiority itself is insufficient. Iran and the Houthis have seen this rush to uncoordinated maritime coalitions before, and they know how to exploit the political and operational gaps. Truly isolating Iran is the best way to win concessions from its leaders. Both it and the Houthis have little reason to abandon their tactics if governments cannot agree on how to confront them.

European and Saudi leaders need to merge their maritime planning efforts and invite the United States to join. Whatever serious disagreements they have with Washington about its military actions in Iran must be set aside when it comes to confronting the throttling of international waterways. An Arab- and European-led command structure, supported by American military capabilities, would demonstrate broad international opposition to maritime aggression while distinguishing the mission from the U.S.-Israeli war on Iranian territory.

For now, the United States should be prepared to contribute significant military capacity and operational support, given the extensive deployments it already has in the Middle East. Its partners across Asia, Europe, and the Middle East should redirect the resources they pledged to the European and Saudi missions to a broader coalition that includes the United States. And Washington must lean into a role as military integrator, smoothing out communication and coordination at sea for navies not used to dynamic multimember missions. In particular, the United States and Israel must share real-time intelligence about the evolving nature of Iranian and Houthi targeting capabilities and weapons, so that maritime coalition members can get ahead of the innovation curve.

In the near term, the United States should commit to operational flexibility, seconding any offensive strikes to a separate chain of command. Leaders in Tehran will take notice of a unified international response to Iranian and Houthi maritime aggression and will think twice before attacking a mission made up of dozens of navies all working together. In return, Washington must accept that its partners would be joining a defensive maritime mission—not enforcing the naval blockade or entering the war against Iran. In 2024, Washington took care to differentiate its role in the OPG defensive Red Sea mission from the separate multinational offensive strikes it undertook against the Houthis. The U.S. government should replicate that model today.

Other militaries, including Israel’s, should contribute intelligence, sea drones and other unmanned capabilities,maintenance and logistical support, and personnel. In return for the United States serving as the mission’s backbone, European, Middle Eastern, and Asian partners should commit to gradually expanding their own naval capabilities and assets so the coalition becomes a long-term investment with equitably shared burdens. Joint messaging—regular coordinated statements and outreach to commercial shippers to counter Iranian and Houthi disinformation—will be vital, as well as collaborative innovation. Iran and the Houthis adapt rapidly; it will be easier for coalition countries’ defense industries to stay ahead of them if they work together.

Military efforts to date have failed to compel either Iran or the Houthis to change course at sea. In fact, Iranian and Houthi leaders believe that they have more to gain from escalation, as evidenced by their statements and continued attacks. Countries everywhere are suffering for it. In October, the World Bank projected that Gulf economies would contract by 4.3 percent in 2026, thanks in no small part to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian attacks on energy infrastructure. In June, the International Monetary Fund estimated that the war in Iran could reduce growth in the euro area by 0.5 percentage points in 2026.

A unified Middle East maritime coalition on its own would neither reverse these trends nor fully restore freedom of navigation. But it would be an important first step in denying Tehran opportunities to drive wedges between long-standing allies and partners. If, instead, the current trajectory of political discord, piecemeal missions, and short-term adaptation by commercial shippers continues, Iran and the Houthis will learn that they can exploit divisions among foreign governments, selectively escalating maritime threats to extract concessions. And other U.S. adversaries will learn the same lesson—that economic disruption is an extraordinarily effective weapon when the world lacks the will to defend its commons.

How the Iran War Will Transform America’s Military Role

The Arab Monarchies Must Help Washington and Tehran Save Face

How Military Partnerships Make Washington Vulnerable to Its Adversaries

Sam Mullins, Michael Mayo, and Niel Kaneshiro

The Folly of Expanding the Exhausted U.S. Military

#6026. Is Netflix’s ‘The New Stanford Prison Experiment’ for Real?

Review: Is Netflix’s ‘The New Stanford Prison Experiment’ for Real?

I had to chuckle when I got the email. A PR blast announced “Netflix presents The New Stanford Prison Experiment.” Was this an attempt to one-up the satirically dystopian phrases in David Foster Wallace’s Infinite Jest? A “yes, and” to Wallace’s “Year of the Depend Adult Undergarment”? Alas, no. And for the streaming service that only became more ubiquitous after the global success of the gleefully sadistic Squid Game, it seemed apt.

The phrase “Stanford prison experiment,” like Lord of the Flies, is pretty much synonymous with violence, anarchy, and the bleakest confirmation of man’s inhumanity to man. Do we really need a “new” one?

I had to chuckle when I got the email. A PR blast announced “Netflix presents The New Stanford Prison Experiment.” Was this an attempt to one-up the satirically dystopian phrases in David Foster Wallace’s Infinite Jest? A “yes, and” to Wallace’s “Year of the Depend Adult Undergarment”? Alas, no. And for the streaming service that only became more ubiquitous after the global success of the gleefully sadistic Squid Game, it seemed apt.

The phrase “Stanford prison experiment,” like Lord of the Flies, is pretty much synonymous with violence, anarchy, and the bleakest confirmation of man’s inhumanity to man. Do we really need a “new” one?

Chances are you know about the original Stanford prison experiment. In August 1971, with the campus on break, a psychology professor at Stanford University named Philip Zimbardo offered a paying gig to students willing to run through an unusual and morally questionable exercise. The basement of a university building was made up to resemble a prison. Twenty-four students (all male, all white except for one Asian-American; “good boys,” Zimbardo called them) were randomly split into groups of inmates or guards and given appropriate uniforms. For two weeks, the professor thought, he would take notes on how unchecked power in an enclosed system would reveal itself. The experiment, funded by the U.S. Office of Naval Research, ended after six days, and that’s only because Zimbardo’s girlfriend stopped by and said, “Holy crap, what the hell is happening here?!”

Stanford professor Philip Zimbardo discusses the Stanford prison experiment on Aug. 20, 1971.Duke Downey/San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images

At least that’s the lore. Zimbardo—a wonderful self-promoter later taken to wearing t-shirts with the letter Z resembling Superman’s logo—seemed eager not just to lean into his experiment’s findings, but to allow that he, too, lost his ethical mooring, suggesting that all closed institutions are incubators of depersonalization and madness.

You can watch this all play out in a pretty good fictionalized version of the experiment produced in 2015 called The Stanford Prison Experiment, adapted from Zimbardo’s 2007 book The Lucifer Experiment. In it, Billy Crudup plays Zimbardo, Michael Angarano plays a guard nicknamed John Wayne, and Ezra Miller and Tye Sheridan play the inmates who suffered the most, eventually quitting.

Indeed, the fact that the experiment went haywire and needed to be canceled surely aided in spreading its premise—that merely donning the costume of guard or inmate in a sealed-off environment would radically alter someone’s personality, and rather quickly. These findings, plus the inherent “wait, they let students do this?” question, made Zimbardo a notable and sought-after voice on cable news during the Abu Ghraib scandal.

But recent research and a three-part 2024 documentary that aired on the National Geographic channel, The Stanford Prison Experiment: Unlocking the Truth, offers firsthand testimony from the participants that they were coaxed to behave in ways that would conform to the experiment’s thesis. John Wayne, for example, wasn’t really a skull-cracking bully as the film clips suggest, but a pot-smoking theater kid who wanted to please his director. One of the kids who quit wasn’t on the verge of psychological collapse; he just thought the experiment was annoying and was told the only way to get out of it was to pretend he was losing it.

All these decades later, it’s hard to know which version is accurate. (As with so much in life, it is likely somewhere in between.) But the suspicion surrounding Zimbardo’s data is, I suppose, reason enough to call for a redo.

The punchline, of course, is that however bogus the original may actually be, this new iteration is a hundred times more manufactured.

Trymaine Lee and host Alison Wood Brooks in The New Stanford Prison Experiment.Netflix

Enter television producers Jane Lipsitz and Dan Cutforth, whose previous work includes competition shows like Project Runway, Top Chef, Nailed It!, and my personal favorite, the ongoing Is it Cake? franchise, which has somehow managed to stretch the act of wondering whether something is cake for three seasons plus five holiday-themed specials. With that eternal question still lingering, they decided it was time to turn their reality TV lens to issues of crime and punishment. (One wonders how Rodion Raskolnikov’s life would have been different had he had access to fondant.)

“Does power corrupt?” is the big question laid out in the first of six episodes in The New Stanford Prison Experiment. Our host—the Ryan Seacrest of this affair—is Alison Wood Brooks, an associate professor of business administration at Harvard University and a behavioral scientist, and she assures us this experiment will answer this question once and for all. Her two associates offering color commentary are Trymaine Lee, a Pulitzer-winning journalist and author, and Michael Cantrell, a retired federal corrections officer and podcaster.

In a decommissioned wing of an actual county correctional facility in Georgia, the trio sit before a bank of monitors from their panopticon’s perch, which naturally includes a whiteboard featuring circled names, flowchart markings, and vague phrases like “test ourselves.” They observe the activity of the show’s willing participants as though they were Harry Lime on a Ferris wheel, strikingly detached from humanity.

And who are the participants? Unlike Zimbardo’s crew—kids looking for a summer gig—these are adults with a full understanding of what they are doing. If there is a financial incentive, it is never mentioned. What is mentioned is that everyone involved considers this is a test of their character, and that the experiment may lead to an important conclusion. What’s more, the show has intentionally kept the pool of applicants diverse in age, race, and class—CEOs and bartenders walk side by side in their civilian clothes before the selection begins.

Contestants wait to join the experiment in The New Stanford Prison Experiment.Netflix

The original experiment left who would be an inmate versus a guard completely up to chance. Not so here. The producers have predetermined this, but the audience isn’t privy to how they made their decisions. (The three women are guards because someone must have wisely realized that mixing genders in a locked-down 24-hour quasi-jail was something no insurance company would cover.)

But there’s an elephant in the room. Unpleasant though this may be, no one is actually incarcerated or in anything resembling danger. There are cameras everywhere, and all anyone needs to do is say the safe word (“pineapple”) and they are free to go.

Also, all of the inmates have clearly been encouraged to give periodic first-person addresses (cleverly shot through glass to resemble a visiting room)—a very common reality show trope to add narration and assist in the editing process. Annoyingly, while watching the finished product, we have no idea how scripted these moments are, or when during production they were recorded. Also, everyone, from all walks of life, uses Instagram-friendly therapy speak phrases. Great for marketing clips.

This is the perfect project for the creator of ‘Adolescence.’

Vince Gilligan’s “Pluribus” asks whether an AI-led society would really be that bad.

Over time, some personalities begin to shine. One of the younger inmates, Pete, who has a Jesse Eisenberg-like quality, is a fifth-grade social studies teacher who feels compelled to instigate and push back against authority. His reasoning is hazy, but he seems to be working toward some poorly defined, somewhat utopian ideal. (The show works mostly in soundbites, not thorough arguments.) He quickly finds some teammates in the art of pushing back, one specifically who seems even more eager to be a thorn in the guards’ side, even though Pete is quietly calling the shots.

The guards, meanwhile, are split into a night and day shift, and an alpha male soon finds himself the unelected leader of each. On night shift, there is Chris, an entrepreneur with a coaching business and an intense desire to be liked. He enforces rules but does it with a smile. On the day shift, there’s Chet, a supervisor on an oil rig, who seems more than eager to carry the metaphorical big stick.

The guards get printed memos (not unlike directives from the Gamemakers in The Hunger Games) with certain tasks and directives. They are to vote for a head guard among them on their shifts (in one case reversing what seemed like natural selection) then each shift must elect what is effectively a shop steward from among the inmates. As the choices are made, our three observers titter and murmur in fascination.

Things move along largely as expected. There is discord. Much of this is due, so the experts conclude, from too much individuality, which is anathema in a prison. Chris and Chet have different styles, and this imbalance causes a rupture. When penalties (such as removing a common clock) aren’t enforced, it creates a mess.

On the seventh day of the show, longer than the original experiment ever went, there comes a new twist. Some of the guards and inmates are directed to trade places. Wouldn’t you know it, the troublemakers are now wearing the badges. How will this change things?

Naturally, the show milks this reversal for as much drama as possible, but it is ultimately quite anticlimactic. This isn’t a real prison, it isn’t even a rogue college experiment from the early 1970s; it’s a Netflix reality show. It’s meaningless! You keep waiting for a hockey brawl to break out, but nothing like that ever happens.

Guard and inmate contestants in The New Stanford Prison Experiment.Netflix

At first, the new guards try to act like “good” guards but soon realize this makes them seem like hypocrites. Instead, they ease up on restrictions, leading to a bit of a party atmosphere. Meanwhile, many of the inmates realize this is all kind of dumb (as will a great number of home viewers, I’m sure!) and start saying “pineapple.” Others are determined to make it to the end, to fulfill some sort of promise they’ve made to themselves. (Does Netflix cut them a bonus check if they last 14 days? None of that is ever discussed.)

Finally (to risk spoiling things), a decision emerges from the ranks. If the inmates all decide to leave as one, as a collective instead of individuals who have had enough, then they will have “taken power” and used it in the name of righteousness. Beaming with pride, our three overseers are delighted to conclude that, wowee, power doesn’t always corrupt! What a relief! The world’s systems can stay in place now. Or something.

If all this sounds preposterous, just know I’m leaving tons of extra nonsense out. I watched this series in awe of its stupidity. I am not one who automatically dismisses all competition shows. The Great British Baking Show is charming and RuPaul’s Drag Race is chock full of puns and creativity. But The New Stanford Prison Experiment is a round peg in a square hole—a ludicrous scenario desperate to rationalize its own existence.

Zimbardo’s experiment may have been unethical, but this is just humiliating, both to the audience and to the people who had to spend nearly two weeks in uncomfortable conditions before landing on a milquetoast and meaningless conclusion. If I were forced to watch all six episodes again, it would feel like a jail sentence.

Jordan Hoffman is a film critic and entertainment journalist living in central New Jersey. He also publishes at Vanity Fair, Entertainment Weekly, and the Times of Israel. He is a member of the New York Film Critics Circle and co-author of The Star Trek Book of Friendship. X: @jhoffman

#6024. Inside top Trump bulldog’s plan to save House GOP majority and defy history

GOP congressional candidate Mike Beltran and Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, discuss Republican momentum in Florida’s 14th district on ‘Fox Report.’

Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, was jumping into the car with his wife on the way to the airport when he took a call from a Fox News Digital reporter on Thursday morning.

It’s a microcosm of what the House Judiciary Committee chairman’s recent weeks and months have been: a seemingly endless series of planes, trains and automobiles across the U.S. campaigning for fellow Republican lawmakers.

House Republicans’ senior leadership is crisscrossing the country raising money and support for their members to win Tuesday’s midterm elections. Jordan, though he’s not part of the trio, has much the same schedule.

"Sometimes they’re fundraisers, sometimes they’re rallies, sometimes they're both," Jordan said. "We're doing everything we can just to help our team win, because… if these Democrats get in there, my real concern, I gotta be honest, is what they're gonna try to do to the structure of our government."

MAPPED: TRUMP’S NONSTOP CAMPAIGN BLITZ SWEEPS KEY STATES

Rep. Jim Jordan leaves a House Republican Conference meeting at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Dec. 10, 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

A source familiar with Jordan’s travel schedule said he’ll have gone to 115 districts across 34 states during this election cycle. That includes 19 consecutive days on the road in the lead-up to Nov. 3 in states such as Washington, Oregon, Texas, Arkansas, Florida, Illinois and South Carolina.

And despite the diverse areas, Jordan said his message is mostly the same: Republicans cut taxes, secured the border and Democrats will make it all worse.

"We understand things cost a little too much, and we're working on that. But remember, most of that's because of the Biden administration and their record inflation. We're bringing that inflation rate down, but you know, we still understand things, things cost too much, and we're gonna keep working on that," Jordan said.

TRUMP VOTERS REVEAL THEIR BIGGEST FEAR HEADING INTO MIDTERMS — AND IT'S NOT RISING PRICES

"But the big issue we talk about is, if these radicals that now control the Democrat Party, if they get control of the government, the crazy things they're gonna do are just frightening."

And because he’s not a member of leadership, he’s not afforded the same charter flights and police motorcades that come with that job.

While he’s had some private flights, most of Jordan’s travel has been comprised of commercial airlines and long drives between destinations — including sitting in traffic.

He said his favorite travel tunes include the greatest hits of late country star Glen Campbell.

But Jordan said he also uses much of that time texting or calling colleagues, asking how their races are going, and talking to staff about what issues to raise at his next event.

House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, speaks at a press conference with other members of House Republican leadership in Washington, D.C., on May 20, 2025. (Getty Images)

He’s also raised a significant amount of cash for their campaigns, donating $1.97 million to Republicans across the country and $2.65 million to the House GOP campaign arm.

10 DEMOCRAT-HELD HOUSE SEATS REPUBLICANS COULD FLIP TO SAVE THEIR MAJORITY

It comes as House Republicans fight an uphill battle to retain their majority, as multiple political forecasts show Democrats poised to take over the chamber.

Jordan’s volume of travel is notable for someone who is not in senior House leadership, but it’s not a surprise, given his years-long high profile.

"His celebrity status is very helpful," one House Republican previously told Fox News Digital. "When Jim Jordan comes to town for you, you put 300 butts in seats."

Another lawmaker shared a similar figure. Rep. Tim Moore, R-N.C., told Fox News Digital that Jordan reached out to him about doing an event in his district that wound up a success.

DEMOCRATS SEE NEW CHANCES TO FLIP RED STATES — BUT A $400M GOP SPENDING ADVANTAGE COULD DERAIL THEIR PLANS

"We had a fundraiser in Gastonia and it was very well attended.  A huge crowd, nearly 300 people there — raised a lot of money, a lot of excitement, a lot of enthusiasm, and so I appreciated him coming down to do that," Moore said. His district also saw a visit from House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., which Moore said also raised a significant sum.

Rep. Tim Moore, R-N.C., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on March 17, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

Jordan has appeared alongside conservatives in deep red districts and moderates in battlegrounds — walking out to Survivor’s "Eye of the Tiger" for many of those appearances — painting a picture of party unity that’s a far cry from his roots as an anti-establishment rebel leading the House Freedom Caucus.

"It’s kind of a Jordan 2.0," the first House Republican said. "He’s just a great citizen of the conference."

A second House Republican told Fox News Digital that a wide range of members see Jordan as a "mentor." They said Jordan’s travels are a mix of Republicans asking him to come out and him extending those offers himself.

"Jim doesn't care if you're moderate or even if you have to lean left to keep your seat, you have to represent your people," the second House Republican said.

Asked whether he’s changed or the party has, Jordan said it was "the overall picture."

"Any differences that exist in the Republican Party are pretty small compared to the differences between Republicans and the left, the hard left, the radical left, which now controls the Democrat Party," Jordan said.

It has also inspired questions about what he wants out of it.

House Republicans and members of the media are widely expecting that Jordan is eyeing a bid for senior leadership after failing to clinch a position in the past.

The U.S. Capitol building on Aug. 7, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

If Republicans lose the majority, he’s expected to run for minority leader, where he’d be Trump’s top defender in Congress.

But Jordan himself has publicly dismissed those notions.

"I’m focused on… Tuesday," he told Fox News Digital. "The way you stop the radicals from making these structural changes to our constitutional form of government, these radical policy positions that they have, the way you stop them is at the ballot box, and that happens on Tuesday."

And then the conversation ended, because Jordan had to catch a flight to campaign with Republican candidates in Florida that night.

Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.
